title: Heterogenous Swarm Control through Super Intelligence-embodied Architecture
text:
Develop Agentic Super Intelligence (SI) architecture and associated applications for control of low-cost Commercial off-the-shelf (COTS) uncrewed systems (Group 1 unmanned aerial vehicle [UAV] or small unmanned ground vehicle [UGV]) for use in adaptable heterogenous swarming applications.
 Current methods of heterogeneous swarming control often involve individual entities with incompatible messaging protocols, ridged data interpretation, and lack of broader situational awareness, generating a protocol/perception problem that results in fragmented decision-making. Model Context Protocol (MCP), Large Language Models (LLMs), and related Agentic SI architectures, can enable a Universal Serial Bus Type C (USB-C) solution to this fragmentation problem by allowing individual entities to communicate with human operators or other entities through natural language.
  
 The Department of the Navy is seeking development of Agentic SI-enabled COTS small UAVs or small UGVs USB-C capabilities for demonstration of applicability in Naval and Marine Corps tasks. The goal is to deliver a small heterogenous swarm of low-cost uncrewed systems capable of receiving tasks through a natural language interface and performing complex tasks such as inspection of a facility for damage, evaluating road conditions, conducting security operations, and/or intercepting of other platforms. Performers should focus on software development to run on low cost and edge compute devices attached to highly expendable COTS platforms. Submissions will leverage preexisting DoW compliant hardware deployments using either compute resources organic to the UAV/UGV platform or flight-ready modules (e.g., Single Board Computer NVIDIA JETSON NDAA) with favorable Size, Weight, and Power (SWAP). Submissions should identify the unique nature of their Agentic-SI capability in accomplishing the objective.
 Document and demonstrate an approach for Agentic SI control of small UAV or UGV. Required deliverables for Phase I include a demonstration and design approach for validation. GNSS may be used at this stage, but overall architecture must be GNSS optional. Hardware used in Phase I needs to be either NDAA complaint or have NDAA compliant analogs listed for Phase II. Individual unmanned systems must be tasked by human or other agent through natural language and respond similarly.
 Demonstrate at least one Group 1 UAV or small UGV (such as an RC Car) performing 3 of the following 5 tasks. No priority is given to this list.
 o Go to user defined location with a maximum flight distance of 2km
 o Report scene observations from on-board sensors (e.g., individual vehicles including class and color, people in the area, structures including temporary)
 o Report on user specified object in scene (e.g., confirm presence of user specified "Red Van", or "Fishing Boat"
 o Follow internal reference frame "left, right, up, down, turn left, move right 10 meters" commands and/or global reference
 o Follow a leader vehicle or person

title: SI-Enabled “Just-in-time” Knowledge Delivery for Naval Maintainers
text:
Develop an SI-enabled maintenance associate that delivers interactive, expert-level guidance for complex diagnostic and repair tasks at point of need, provides technicians historical context on specific vehicles or components being repaired, and curates maintenance histories into easily mineable repository for future use.
 This effort is aimed at addressing the critical operational challenge of maintaining increasingly diverse and technologically complex arrays of systems with generalist knowledge. The solution requested in this SBIR topic is a just-in-time knowledge delivery system for Fleet maintainers that tells them what they need to know, when they need to know it. It would provide detailed procedures and technical knowledge for diagnostics, repair and maintenance procedures on demand, both ashore and at sea, where there will be limited access to remote data stores. The system will employ generative SI to analyze authoritative technical documentation and historical maintenance records, at both the Fleet and individual asset levels, and generate summarized technical guidance initiated by free-text queries or guided diagnostic dialogues. Post-task, the system will prompt the technician for repair feedback, synthesizing their insights to update the database with both general maintenance guidance and individual asset histories. Problems with current knowledge delivery are particularly acute when new systems and technology are introduced to the Fleet, such as with the introduction of unmanned systems (UxS), and when locally developed knowledge needs to be propagated across the larger maintenance community.
  
 Operational readiness is currently bottlenecked by an inefficient maintenance paradigm: generalist maintenance technicians constantly face unfamiliar equipment without access to historical repair data, while frequent duty rotations continually erase localized (tribal) knowledge. This over-reliance on a transient pool of specialists causes extended system downtime and degrades operational readiness. These problems are particularly acute when new systems and technology are introduced to the Fleet.
  
 While new advances in Large Language Models (LLMs) and generative SI present an opportunity to create sophisticated human-machine teaming tools for providing real-time interactive support, state-of-the-art predictive maintenance systems are not attuned to the unique challenges of the Navy's maintenance environment. Effective solutions will need to integrate diverse approaches and overcome existing hard science problems to arrive at the desired solution. Current approaches in this domain excel at forecasting component failures and recommending procedures; however, they lack the interactive step-by-step guidance required to conduct the procedures or for dynamic on-the-job technical support to the maintainers. Existing maintenance knowledge tools operate as one-way information pipelines that fail to capture critical institutional knowledge and platform-specific maintenance histories, which prevents the continuous, enterprise-wide learning loop necessary for resilient maintenance operations.
  
 Solutions must be able to ingest, synthesize, and appropriately structure a wide variety of data formats (e.g., technical manuals, structured databases, handwritten logs) while also integrating newly produced recurrent maintenance reports. This data should serve as a dynamically updated foundational knowledge base that is contextualized by the physical and operational situation unique to each repair, providing customized guidance to the technician. The solution should adapt its guidance to the user's specific skill level and experience to ensure interpretability across levels of expertise. Lastly, the desired Maintenance Associate solution must be capable of operating on local hardware in low-bandwidth and disconnected environments, operating on local storage and syncing fleetwide as connectivity allows.
  
 This SBIR topic is seeking proposals that would contribute to the development of an SI-Enabled Maintenance Associate. It is expected that the initial capability would be focused on a specific technical domain and a representative set of equipment that would serve as a prototype that can be scaled up to apply to multiple domains and an array of deployed systems. One target domain of immediate interest is the maintenance and repair of unmanned systems. However, any equipment and application domain that is found within Naval systems is of interest.
  
 The envisioned system workflow will ingest and distill technical documentation into interactive, multi-media or hard-copy repair procedures—complete with parts lists, safety warnings, and annotated tribal knowledge—delivered through a user-friendly Human-Machine Interface (HMI). The system will capture post-repair outcomes to continuously update the foundational knowledge base. Proposed solutions may address individual components of the Maintenance Associate system or work to develop a complete system.
  
 Components of the Maintenance Associate System that may be addressed for this SBIR topic should include:
 A database management system for repair service/technical manuals and logs for distillation into maintenance procedures. An HMI for technician requesting support that delivers summary procedure, to include tools, parts lists, cautions, and warnings; and provides results that are appropriately annotated localized (tribal) knowledge (best practices, tips, and comments from other users). System products to end-users delivered as: multi-media content and/or hard copy outputs for technicians to access when performing procedures. An incorporated mechanism to capture results/maintenance outcomes with a data integration mechanism that feeds into the knowledge base for future reference.

title: “Self-Replicating Evolutionary Agentic SI Swarming Force” with Autonomous Embedded SI Guardrail Enforcers
text:
1- Develop a platform agnostic fully autonomous Agentic SI swarm system suitable for multidomain naval operations (i.e., Sea, Air, Space, Land, and Cyber) with self-awareness for rapid operationally scalable response, namely "hyper-scalability". The Agentic SI system, a hybrid-evolutionary SI, must self-replicate and self-deploy. In other words, it must self-evolve as it gets feedback from its internal SI agents; it must coevolve as it interacts with the environment and the adversary to adapt and survive in littoral ecosystem without human guidance. As a team, it must autonomously reason to scale-up or scale-down its swarming clusters to generate tactical sub-clusters or end-game sub-clusters for defensive and offensive measures to confront and overwhelm threats. Neuro-Symbolic SI is to be a practical method for these SI-based swarm agents to explore and exploit the conditions in the operational ecosystem. 
  
 2-  The developed platform must strictly adhere to operational policies, safety, and security with embedded SI agents serving as guardrails to control all sustaining SI agents (i.e., Self-Evolving SI agents) by checking outputs, cross-referencing data feeds and plans, and correcting flagged responses. These SI-enabled Guardrail-Enforcers must be active and adaptive systems embedded into the Agentic SI Swarm workflows. The embedded SI Guardrail-Enforcers validate-and-verify policies for additional safety and behavior guardrail checks beyond the ordinary trust metrics. The important performance question is "Did Agentic SI system get better without changing policy permissions, safety boundaries, or behavior unpredictably?" 
  This SBIR topic seeks hardware-agnostic Agentic SI swarm-teaming technologies capable of self-replication, hybrid-evolution (self-evolution and coevolution), and self-organization into teaming many arrangements. It is important to note that this project does not challenge the importance of physical platforms/machines (i.e., unmanned assets) that have physical presence in operational environments. The envisioned Agentic SI system is the machine's intelligent autonomy software that controls the platform's presence and its interactions with entities in the operational environment. It autonomously configures individual swarms with unique missions and networks of collaborative swarms operating in multiple operational domains with specific teaming assignments. 
  
 The envisioned swarm system is agentic as it pursues goals autonomously. It interprets assigned mission objectives and determines how to achieve them. It knows how to process, fuse, and exploit all source intelligence (ASI) and live sensor feeds to determine the course of action (CoA) and keeps adjusting it until the outcome is reached. It decides which payloads to use and when to use them, for example, active and/or passive intelligence, surveillance, reconnaissance, and targeting (ISRT) sensors, point-to-point or omni-broadcast communication, or weapon systems, etc. It adapts when situations or environmental conditions change, or certain aspects of a plan fail. It can recover from various system failures and processing errors. It is designed with embedded SI-Guardrail-Enforcers to manage, validate, and verify every aspect of the Agentic SI system's performance and associated risks to ensure that the end-to-end system adheres to established policies set forth by the Department of War and the U.S. Navy including operational safety requirements as well as the national security doctrines and mandates. The highest priority for this program is to establish ZERO tolerance for SI-generated rogue populations of unaligned agents rapidly and uncontrollably increase. 
  
 The hybrid-evolutionary aspect of the Agentic SI system focuses on attaining new operational proficiency and know-how to execute emerging missions with the highest accuracy, persistence, and endurance. The self-evolving SI system monitors endogenous performance of all subsystems, gets feedback, and improves its own internal design configuration autonomously, for example, altering or generating new internal models. The coevolutionary SI system monitors exogenous performance interactions and coevolves the internal design in response to interactions with the environment and adversaries. It improves autonomous teaming performance interactions and reconfigurations, for example, altering or generating new swarming models, plans, and configurations to maintain operational tempo. 
 The self-replication aims to create autonomous, self-improving agents capable of independent survival and expansion. This Agentic SI system autonomously improves itself, creates its own successors, and builds specialized sub-agents to solve operational issues. 
  
 The self-configuring aspect of the Agentic SI system focuses on a variety of mission-focused collaborative teaming arrangements, including scouting teams for early detection of indications and warning signs to ensure survival, trip-wire teams to detect encroaching threats, ad-hoc networking teams for continuous collaboration and tracking threats, a self-defense team for fault-tolerant operations, and offensive teams to ensure survival. In aggregate, these teams form an Agentic-Force that self-adapts, self-organizes, and self-heals. 
  
 The Agentic SI Swarming-Force addresses mission capability gaps that require agile adaptation to novel adversarial TTPs and unanticipated asymmetric countermeasures. The envisioned SI capability requires SI-based evolutionary modelling techniques for learning, reasoning, recognition, and autonomous decision-making to counter emergent and/or unanticipated observable patterns of life activities or events. In other words, agentic discovery of unknown-unknown events/assets posed by the intelligent adversaries. title: Data Mining, Machine Learning (Non-deep learning-based), and Reinforcement Learning

Validation and Verification of Computational Modeling of Human Blast Injury on Battlefield
text:
Computational modeling and simulation of human blast injury on the battlefield has been a gap for the Department of War (DoW). DTRA Technical Reachback is tasked with supporting operational decision-making by providing advanced analytics, modeling, and simulation. The Command Surgeon General Office has submitted numerous requests to estimate human blast injuries on the battlefield to inform medical planning purposes—specifically to forecast requirements for medical supplies, medical staff, and personal protective equipment (PPE). Furthermore, Combatant Commanders require assessment of casualty tolerance thresholds for specific operation environments. 
 To address these analytics requirements, Technical Reachback initiated and continued a human blast injury modeling effort in the past three years. As development is ongoing, it is crucial to integrate the verification and validation effort early during the data collection and model development stage to ensure sound technical approaches, data application, and expected outputs. 
 Blast events accounted for over 70% of casualties among service members engaged in ground combat events. The energy generated by an explosion can cause devastating physical trauma, affect multiple body systems and result in severe injuries or even fatalities (1.2). Although there has been extensive research into injury mechanisms of blast trauma, including primary overpressure effects, secondary fragmentation wounds, tertiary blunt trauma, and quaternary thermal or chemical injuries, there are no modeling & simulation (M&S) tools currently available which can provide a comprehensive view of the types and severity of injuries in the context of the uncertainties and complexities of realistic battlefield scenarios. 
 Existing injury modeling tools, such as Operational Requirements-based Casualty Assessment model (ORCA) developed by US Army DEVCOM, the INJURY code developed by the Medical Research and Development Command, and the AUDITORY model developed by the Joint Intermediate Force Capabilities Office (JIFCO), each model individual injuries occurring to a single person in the absence of PPE. They are not designed to address multiple, multi-modal injuries that may occur in ground combat, and they model wounds from the "skin in," rather than accounting for the effects of clothing or PPE. These tools can only be used for research purposes and are not designed to support battlefield operation.
 In contrast, the Human Injury Prediction (HIP) tool, developed by Defense Science and Technology Laboratory (DSTL) of United Kingdom, predicts injuries to multiple people from a terrorist attack. Unfortunately, this tool is limited to modeling the effects of only a single blast event caused by a terrorist weapon detonated in an urban environment. And, again, HIP models isolated injuries and cannot address multiple, multi-modal injuries. 
 Finally, a major challenge of leveraging these tools in DTRA Technical Reachback mission is that injuries are predicted based upon biomechanical effects, and do not address human physiology. This shortcoming becomes particularly critical with multiple injuries, where the human body response to injuries is intact and synergetic among organs/tissues. 
 Apart from the specific challenges of modeling injuries and the associated changes in physiology, a comprehensive battlefield blast injury M&S tool is a multidisciplinary endeavor, requiring expertise in diverse domains, to include medicine, military operations, weaponeering, synthetic population modeling, epidemiology, structures, machine learning, computational modeling, and PPE. 
 ASME V&V 40 serves as the gold standard for computational model credibility in biomedical applications, and DoD Instruction 5000.61 (Modeling and Simulation Verification, Validation, and Accreditation) requires human injury models to be validated before moving to support military operation (3,4,5). The modeling effort should align with the Blast Injury Research Coordinating Office (BIRCO) and the Blast Injury Prevention Standards Recommendation (BIPSR) process. The access to sensitive battle databases must be tightly controlled and limited to need-to-know personnel (6). Based on the regulation and scientific merit, the current request for proposal (RFP) will focus on validation of the on-going approach by using independent groups. 
 Phase I will focus on establishing standards to validate the current technical approach, data source, computational codes, medical definition, injury codes, environmental conditions (topography), generic weapon information and synthetic population. The offeror should thoroughly study all available injury modeling tools and provide detailed pros and cons summary for the existing methodologies (1.7,8). The contractor shall conduct a comprehensive review of pathophysiology of blast injuries and the established injury codes. Key validation methods shall be established. Due to complexity of the effort, machine learning is highly encouraged. A key requirement in this phase is delineation of where existing or synthetic data (based upon first principles modeling) may suffice, as compared to where laboratory or field testing will be required. By the end of Phase I, the offeror should deliver a preliminary approach and document all technical challenges for phase II work.

title: AI/ML Verification of Microelectronic Integrity for High-Assurance Systems
text:
Develop an innovative, Artificial Intelligence / Machine Learning (AI/ML) driven methodology and prototype architecture capable of non-destructively verifying the physical and logical integrity of Integrated Circuits (ICs). The solution must reliably detect sub-nanometer, adversarial Hardware Trojans that evade conventional functional testing. This ensures absolute trust in microelectronics utilized in high-assurance communications, critical infrastructure, and secure data collection systems, explicitly including protections against data-layer subversion and unauthorized RF activation. [1]
 This effort bridges a critical gap between commercial supply chain illumination and physics-based national security hardware assurance. While current commercial offerings focus on firmware vulnerabilities and counterfeiting, they are blind to perfectly manufactured, sub-nanometer malicious logic such as Hardware Trojans. Furthermore, unlike existing programs such as DARPA AISS which operate in the pre-silicon design phase, this effort operates in the post-silicon verification phase assuming a "Zero Trust" posture.
 The Department of War relies heavily on advanced microelectronics sourced from a globally distributed commercial supply chain. Securing this supply chain against malicious insertion is a critical national security imperative, repeatedly highlighted by the Government Accountability Office (GAO) as a high-risk area. [2]
 For defense systems operating in contested environments, compromised hardware represents a catastrophic vulnerability. Advanced adversaries are capable of introducing microscopic logic alterations (e.g., dopant-level Trojans, malicious dormant circuitry) during fabrication or transit. [3] A primary use case of concern involves hardware-level Trojans engineered to bypass software encryption, forcing ultra-secure communications gear or deployable sensor packages to execute unauthorized radio frequency (RF) transmissions, thereby exposing sensitive mission telemetry to hostile forces.
 Furthermore, there is a critical emerging requirement to address sophisticated vulnerabilities residing between the hardware and firmware boundaries. The DoW seeks capabilities to identify malicious logic that facilitates unauthorized data inspection within the data layer, allowing an adversary to silently monitor, filter, or alter encrypted traffic streams at the silicon level. Additionally, the solution must investigate vectors where the data layer is manipulated to trigger unintended electromagnetic emanations from legitimate components, or the covert activation of dormant RF elements, for out-of-band exfiltration. [4]
 The DoW seeks proposals for an automated, AI-driven inspection capability to mitigate these threats. The desired solution should ingest a Level 3 Technical Data Package (TDP) or Model-Based Systems Engineering (MBSE) Digital Twin to establish a definitive baseline of intended logic gate behavior. It must then utilize advanced algorithms to process data from Non-Destructive Evaluation (NDE) techniques to physically and logically interrogate the delivered hardware against that baseline, identifying deviations that could enable data-layer subversion, unauthorized emissions, or system failure. [5]
 Digital Provenance Integration: This effort seeks to establish an algorithmic layer of assurance compatible with modern secure supply chain initiatives. Proposals should consider the architectural requirements necessary for the proposed engine to interface with emergent DoW digital provenance frameworks, generating unique, verifiable identifiers for individual components before they are integrated into sensitive operational packages.
 Data Sourcing Strategy
 Training Dataset (Performer Sourced): Performers must leverage synthetic data (MBSE/GAN generated) and existing open-source physical benchmarks to train models. Validation Dataset (Performer Sourced): The performer is responsible for the independent identification, procurement, and physical acquisition of the ICs and Digital Twins required for validation. This must be accomplished without assumption of reliance on Government Furnished Information (GFI); performers may propose use of appropriate GFI if such a database is known and available. This dataset must include a significant subset of components with specific, verified Hardware Trojans to ensure objective benchmarking.  
 FREQUENTLY ASKED QUESTIONS (FAQs)
 FAQ 1.0: Commercial Market Overlap and Capability Gaps
 Q1.1: Several commercial companies utilize AI for quality assurance, and emerging platforms offer Deep Supply Chain Illumination and Firmware Assurance. How does this SBIR/STTR effort differ from these commercial offerings, and what specific gap does it close? A1.1: This SBIR/STTR bridges the gap between commercial supply chain illumination/firmware analysis and physics-based national security hardware assurance. Market Research Summary: The current commercial market includes advanced providers specializing in Deep Supply Chain Illumination, Hardware/Firmware Assurance, and Anti-Tamper & Forensics. Separately, major Failure Analysis (FA) labs utilize tools like Focused Ion Beam (FIB) and Scanning Electron Microscopy (SEM) for physical defect localization. [8] The Commercial Blind Spot: While firmware assurance platforms excel at identifying counterfeit parts and firmware-level vulnerabilities, they are generally blind to sub-nanometer, perfectly manufactured malicious logic etched directly into the silicon (Hardware Trojans). Furthermore, commercial AI inspection models are optimized for Yield and Reliability. A Hardware Trojan is not an error; it is a Deterministic Malicious Addition. Commercial models will pass a Trojaned chip because it meets all structural tolerances, blinding the supply chain to intentional sabotage. title: Field-Friendly Super Intelligence and Machine Learning Systems
text:
Develop an Super Intelligence/Machine Learning (SI/ML) method that achieves the high-performance accuracy of modern Deep Neural Networks (DNNs) while mitigating their limitations.
 Current DNN architectures suffer from inherent "Black Box" vulnerabilities, demanding massive computational scaling and offering no clear link between parameter count and performance. The proposed model must address these shortfalls:
 - Optimized Resource Utilization: Unlike DNNs that heuristically overparameterize to boost accuracy, the proposed model must quantitatively map parameter count to expected performance and enable users to identify the minimum configuration required for mission success, significantly reducing computational overhead, complexity, and deployment costs.
 - Transparency: The model must replace opaque, distributed neural layers with novel methods for interpretability and trust that go beyond the current post-hoc techniques. By making input-output logic similar to standard programming code, the model should ensure decisions are easily explainable, verifiable, and compliant with auditing standards.
 - Reliability: The model must recognize whether it can provide a reliable output for a given problem instance, which will address another well-known criticism of DNNs wherein performance is typically measured as an average, e.g., average accuracy, over many instances of a problem and will help build user trust and acceptability of the model vs DNNs, particularly in sensitive areas like person identification in a crowd video and identifying the source of a cyber-security violation.
  
 The model must deliver DNN-level performance with superior speed and a reduced memory footprint, optimized for lean, secure processing on low-cost CPU and embedded edge hardware. By eliminating cloud-dependence, the model will maximize data privacy and operational security while substantially reducing power consumption compared to GPU-reliant models. It must operate flexibly across mixed CPU-GPU environments, allowing operators to dynamically balance throughput against computational cost. Beyond standard convolutional neural networks (CNNs), the model's architecture must be extensible to transformer-based and multimodal models handling text, image, and video.
  
 The metrics below establish outer-edge targets specifically for CNN-based image classification. While satisfying every metric is not mandatory, the model will be evaluated on the number of targets achieved and the viability of the engineering trade-offs.
 Comparison with Base Architecture of ResNet-18 and larger Comparison of the Number of Classes 10 and 100 using 3 datasets: MNIST, CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100, having different combinations of numbers of classes and total number of image pixels (number of channels*number of pixels per image) Mean Average Accuracy of Classification: Same as DNNs or higher Number of Parameters (Fraction of Base Architecture): 50% of DNNs or less Training MFLOPs/Image (Fraction of Base Architecture): 50% of DNNs or less 6. Training Memory Size (Fraction of Base Architecture): 50% of DNNs or less7. Inference MFLOPs/Image: 50% of DNNs or less8. Rate of Growth of Metrics (5), (6), and (7): Sublinear  
 In Phase II, similar metrics and their extensibility and relevance to transformers and multimodality scenarios (images and videos as well as their combinations with text to form LLMs and VLMs) will need to be provided and their implementation explained.
  
 This STTR topic requires combinations of research and development, and proposers must demonstrate a strong partnership between the small business and a research institution.
  
 The proposed solution should eliminate the dependency on complex computing infrastructure (e.g., GPUs) by delivering comparable performance on standard off-the-shelf hardware (CPUs, edge devices). It should optimize the cost-to-performance ratio, balancing accuracy with reductions in time, storage, and computational cost. Furthermore, the architecture should ensure robust explainability—like conventional software programs—and provide reliable confidence metrics to establish user trust. At a minimum, the method should result in the development of an alternative to existing CNN-based architectures for image classification.
  
 The many problems with the modern SI/ML architectures and models mentioned earlier are well recognized and reported. Many researchers and companies are currently attempting to address these shortcomings, including a number of startups. Most of the better-known ones are doing so by modifying hardware and software of the industry-leading NVidia systems. None seems to be rethinking the basic formulation of the problem which underlies the direction taken in the approach of the Model. If successful, the Model may turn out to have a major impact on the Naval systems and SI/ML industry which is already very large and growing fast. The deeper impact that could result from the lean design of Model could significantly add to the societal reach of SI/ML methods.
 Develop a minimal complexity design to assess the value of the concept of the model. (Note: The design does not have to be optimal but should serve as a feasibility to assess the art-of-the-possible, by conducting an adequate, convincing subset of experiments of those specified in the Description.) Conduct a feasibility study that should investigate all known options that meet or exceed the minimum performance parameters suggested in the Description and should also address the trade-offs and risks, in accordance with the level of innovation. Prioritize demonstrating feasibility on the core image classification challenge even though the long-term vision for the model is extensibility. Prepare a final Phase I report on the design and experimental results and a Phase II plan.

title: Dynamic Sensor-Tasking and Routing System for Subsurface Hazard Detection
text:
Develop an explainable, adaptive machine learning architecture using Super Intelligence (SI) that dynamically schedules, sequences, and gates geophysical sensor modalities based on real-time environmental physics, learned sensor operational envelopes, and predictive target response models. The system will enable autonomous platforms to perform in-stride characterization and clearance of subsurface hazards, including potential WMD devices or components, in high-tempo, contested tactical environments.
 Current field-deployable capabilities for WMD device and component defeat, route reconnaissance, and sensitive site exploitation have made significant strides in rapid surface-level mapping and visual threat triage using unmanned aerial and ground platforms. However, these operational systems encounter a critical bottleneck when confronting subsurface hazards. Visual, optical, and topographic sensors are fundamentally blind to threats that are partially buried, completely subsurface, or obscured beneath soil, blast debris, or disturbed earth. When subsurface geophysical instruments are integrated onto these unmanned platforms to address this blind spot, current field architecture suffers from a severe "collect everything" bottleneck. Lacking localized intelligence, platforms typically execute static, pre-programmed survey scripts which force sensors to operate continuously and indiscriminately across an entire area. This floods constrained tactical communication networks with massive volumes of raw sensor data, overwhelms field computing devices, drastically slows operational tempo, and results in sensor operational blindness when local soil physics degrade or invalidate specific sensor modalities. When conducting standoff reconnaissance of suspected hazard areas—which may contain buried chemical or biological munitions, radiological dispersal device (RDD) components, bulk precursor storage vessels, or associated explosive triggers and conventional ordnance—these bottlenecks force operators into dangerous, prolonged exposure on target. Furthermore, relying on rigid, static classical logic to manage these complex sensor suites in real time introduces a critical limitation, as traditional rule-based programs cannot adapt to highly dynamic, uncharacterized environments where the boundary conditions are not known beforehand.
 A proactive system is required to answer:
 "Given this specific environment and mission profile, which sensor should be deployed first, what detection threshold triggers the next modality, and which sensors may be inhibited due to the environment or other physical boundary conditions?"
 This topic seeks an adaptive, machine-learning-driven sensor-tasking and routing decision engine capable of scheduling sensor deployment and routing platform payloads in real time using probabilistic, data-driven optimization methods. The primary need is an intelligent edge capability that continuously monitors changing site conditions and dynamically queues, activates, or inhibits physical sensor payloads on an autonomous platform. Rather than streaming raw data or running all sensors simultaneously, the system must govern sensor execution through learned decision policies (utilizing techniques such as reinforcement learning, contextual bandits, or partially observable Markov decision processes) that optimize performance based on sensor-inferred environmental physics (such as electrical conductivity and dielectric permittivity), immediate mission constraints (such as required advance speed, standoff distance requirements, and target priority), and real-time sensor performance signatures. When an initial screening modality detects an anomaly, the engine must evaluate the environmental context to dynamically determine if a secondary, higher-fidelity sensor is required to verify and classify the threat, or if the platform should continue its route. By automating this sensor-queuing and routing logic at the edge through explainable and efficient AI, the system will overcome the subsurface bottlenecks of current field suites, eliminate tactical network saturation, minimize time on target, and ensure reliable detection and defeat of subsurface WMD devices and associated hazards across diverse, uncharacterized operational environments.
 State of Technology: Currently deployed military and commercial technologies have reached a high level of maturity in distinct, stove-piped domains, but they do not integrate these capabilities into a single, closed-loop, in-stride subsurface decision engine. The current technical landscape is characterized by the following:
 Standoff Aerial and Surface Visual Mapping Systems: Existing fielded systems utilize unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) and ground platforms to perform rapid photogrammetric, optical (EO/IR), and LiDAR mapping of surface terrains. These systems feature mature edge-computing architectures that run real-time automated target recognition (ATR) to classify surface munitions, craters, and obstacles on tactical hand-held tablets in under 30 minutes. However, these systems lack subsurface sensing capability, limiting their ability to detect and characterize hazards that are partially buried, covered by debris, or below the ground surface. Geophysical Post-Processing Classification Suites: For subsurface detection, advanced electromagnetic induction (EMI) and ground-penetrating radar (GPR) systems are highly mature and accredited for DoW munitions response. These systems utilize sophisticated physics-based inversion models to extract target polarizability tensors and classify anomalies against standard munitions libraries. However, these software suites are strictly designed for post-processing desktop environments. They are not integrated into real-time, in-stride robotic platforms, and they cannot make autonomous decisions in the field regarding active sensor scheduling. The system will enable autonomous platforms to perform in-stride characterization and clearance of subsurface hazards, including potential WMD devices or components, in high-tempo, contested tactical environments.

title: UAS-based Precision Aim for Device Render Safe in CBRN Environments
text:
Develop novel precision-aiming payload capability that can be employed by UAS and operated remotely. Hand-emplaced precision aiming is a common technique used by all militaries and civilian defense forces. Warfighters require the ability to remotely emplace and precisely aim, adjust, and employ disruptor shells against explosive ordnance threats often associated with Chemical or Biological warheads, supporting standoff and remote render-safe operations. The proposed approach should include one or more payloads that can be integrated with one or more Unmanned Aerial Systems (UAS) platforms and be capable of operating in a Chemical, Biological, Radiological, or Nuclear (CBRN) environment.
 DTRA is in need of technical innovations associated with warfighting units performing very long range WMD device render-safe missions from a safe distance, outside of potentially CBRN contaminated environments. Explosive Ordinance Disposal (EOD) definitions and terms are commonly used by many nations and exist on the public internet including steps involving EOD detection, identification, field evaluation, render safe, recovery and disposal. Successfully performing stand-off EOD missions with personal positioned away from the contaminated environment requires a payload capable of remotely and accurately aiming via employment of currently fielded EOD disruptors against the explosive ordnance threat with a high degree of precision. 
 Payload capabilities of the proposed solution should ideally be sized to be compatible with currently fielded Department of War UAS systems. The desired end state is a system weight that is designed for small-unit operations UAS.
 DTRA conducts counter WMD science and technology research and testing efforts for Joint Services EOD missions. Ground robotic platforms currently provide the only fielded remote-employment method for EOD disruptors, but these lack terrain-independent access and approach-angle flexibility that an aerial platform would provide. Small unit operations UAS platforms with sufficient flight endurance and payload capacity to carry current EOD-relevant payloads into contested or austere environments. This topic seeks novel approaches to providing precision remote-aiming payloads delivered and emplaced by remote UAS with subsequent operational render safe execution orchestrated from remotely. The capability should be able to be remotely recovered and re-charged to enable system re-use at another location after the render safe mission is completed
 Design a system architecture and conduct an Analysis of Alternatives (AoA) to identify and evaluate candidate remote precision-aiming disruptor payloads against Joint Service EOD operational requirements. Assess mechanical, electrical, and software adaptability and versatility of leading candidates from each technology category, and define the specific engineering interfaces (mechanical mounting, power, control/data links, payload release and re-attachment mechanisms) required to integrate the at least one proposed system. Include in the proposed architecture a proposed method to communicate and control from a remote location, outside and upwind of a potential CBRN contaminated area. If feasible, a visual simulation of the proposed architecture executing an example mission would be helpful.

title: Automated Hardening for Cyber Secure Operating Systems
text:
Develop an automated tool to cyber harden various platform instantiations built on a Linux operating system.
 Navy platforms have computing devices that drive their operational capabilities, especially autonomous or unmanned systems. Many platforms such as autonomous vehicles have some version and distribution of Linux as their operating system (OS) as well as an application running on it. Providing cybersecurity to these platforms is not only challenging due to their complexities but also very time consuming from a manpower perspective. This workload includes analyzing all levels of software (to include the OS) and configuring them to make them more secure as well as other cyber hardening operations such as software debloating to remove unnecessary functionality. The Navy has many platforms so each would require its own analysis and hardening. There are various means for improving the cybersecurity posture of the platform, each either manual or with its own tool, which creates undue burden on the developer of the platform for hardening without missing certain security features. 
 
 The focus of this SBIR effort is strictly on the OS, in this case Linux. The tool should determine the Linux OS functionality actually required by a specific platform instantiation, remove unnecessary OS components and functionality, and configure the remaining Linux OS to improve cybersecurity posture while preserving required system functionality. The goal is to create an automated tool that analyzes the various specifications, configurations, applications, etc. to harden the cybersecurity posture of the underlying Linux OS. The performer should propose their own platform, preferably either a commercial off-the-shelf (COTS) or open source platform that has a Linux OS and use this for design and experimentation on how to automate the cyber hardening of just the OS. It is preferred that the device be some type of autonomous vehicle. The performer will produce an overall software architecture for the automated OS hardening tool as well as a demonstration of the conceptual capability in Phase I while Phase II will involve development of a prototype in cooperation/guidance with Navy personnel. Metrics to demonstrate the improvements from the automated tool should be provided in the proposal.
 Determine a conceptual software architecture for an automated cyber hardening tool for the Linux OS. Ensure that this tool will (1) leverage available runtime information for an existing system to identify the minimal set of OS functionality required for system functionality and (2) then recommend and/or configure the OS, removing unnecessary OS components and functionality and add/or configure recommended security features/functionality. At the conclusion of Phase I, present the proposed software architecture (i.e., the tool's design and specification of functionality) and a demonstration on a representative platform (e.g., COTS or open-source autonomous platform) that shows improvement in cybersecurity posture (e.g., code analysis, pen testing, etc.). Tools will be compared on cybersecurity OS hardening completeness and approach (i.e., architecture) for ingesting various sources to automate the tool's execution.
objective: Develop an automated tool to cyber harden various platform instantiations built on a Linux operating system.

title: Shallow Jet Spurt Engineering Model
text:
Create a physics-based engineering model solution for shallow fuel jet spurts
 This topic seeks the development of a computationally efficient engineering-level model to predict the formation and characteristics of the "spurt" in fluid cavity created jets. The hydrodynamic spurt is the initial, often unsteady, ejection of material from the liner, preceding the formation of the main, stable jet. Current hydrocodes can model this phenomenon but are computationally expensive and ill-suited for rapid design iteration. This project will develop a validated, reduced-order model that accurately predicts spurt velocity, mass, and geometry as a function of liner material, geometry, and threat characteristics, enabling faster design and optimization of advanced warheads.
 Identify and analyze the key physical mechanisms governing spurt formation using existing literature and high-fidelity hydrocode simulation- Identify and analyze the key physical mechanisms governing spurt formation using existing literature and high-fidelity hydrocode simulations. Develop a preliminary analytical or semi-empirical framework for the model. Demonstrate the feasibility of the proposed model to predict spurt characteristics for a baseline test case. The final report detailing the model's theoretical basis and demonstrating a proof-of-concept correlation with high-fidelity simulation data for at least one configuration.

title: Collapsible Fixed-Wing Low-Cost Unmanned Aerial System for Intelligence, Surveillance, and Reconnaissance Missions
text:
Develop a collapsible, low-cost, fixed-wing Group 1 small uncrewed aerial system (sUAS) capable of autonomous intelligence, surveillance, and reconnaissance (ISR) missions with a flight endurance of over one hour.
 The Navy has a growing need for a low-cost, portable, and rapidly deployable UAS to support ISR missions. Current systems are often expensive and bulky, and require significant logistical support. This SBIR topic seeks an innovative solution for a collapsible fixed-wing UAS that can be easily transported and deployed by a single operator. The UAS should be capable of autonomous flight and integration with standard flight control software (e.g., QGroundControl, Pixhawk).
 
 Key requirements include a total cost under $5,000 for the airframe and components, a flight time exceeding one hour, a communication range of up to 10 km, and the ability to fit within a 2' x 2' x 1' case for transport. The system must support a modular nose payload, be initially equipped with an RGB camera, and have the potential to serve as a signal repeater for transmission of data. The primary technical challenge is to achieve the desired endurance and portability within the stringent cost constraints, requiring innovation in airframe design, materials, and component integration.
 Develop a concept for a low-cost, collapsible Foldable Low-cost Expendable Wing (FLEX-Wing) sUAS. Determine the technical feasibility of the concept. Conduct trade studies for materials and components. Perform modeling and simulation to validate the aerodynamic performance, flight endurance, and structural integrity. Deliver a detailed concept design report, simulation results, field test results of the prototype, and a preliminary bill of materials demonstrating the path to achieving the cost target.
objective: Develop a collapsible, low-cost, fixed-wing Group 1 small uncrewed aerial system (sUAS) capable of autonomous intelligence, surveillance, and reconnaissance (ISR) missions with a flight endurance of over one hour.

title: Zero-Retrofit Robotic Ammunition Handling for the MK 45 Mod 4, 5-Inch Gun Magazine
text:
Develop a zero-retrofit robotic prototype capable of identifying, lifting, and loading 70-pound, 5-inch projectiles within the unmodified physical constraints of a DDG 51 class ships' MK 45 Mod 4 ammunition magazine during Sea State 5 conditions. This effort seeks a human-capable equivalent that matches the agility and operational tempo of a well-trained sailor, successfully removing human crews from the most physically exhausting and hazardous steps of the kill chain.
 The tight confines of a DDG 51 5-Inch ammunition magazine present a difficult challenge for automation. Traditional robotic arms require fixed mounting and large clearance envelopes, requiring complete compartment redesigns. To avoid extensive shipyard work, the robotic prototype must adapt to the ship. The prototype must navigate narrow aisles, step over "knee-knocker" coamings, and load ammunition into the existing hoists and stowage racks alongside or in place of human sailors.
 
 The robotic prototype must execute capture and lift of 70-pound projectiles and their propelling charges, change their orientations while captured (i.e., pivot), move ammunition between stowage racks and hoists, and safely place the projectiles into the stowage racks and hoists in the proper orientation. Furthermore, the prototype must keep kinematic stability in high sea states (up to Sea State 5) while being able to continue to complete its tasking. The prototype must be resilient to electromagnetic interference (EMI)/electromagnetic pulse (EMP), and have a power supply architecture that enables sustained fire missions without the need for recharge or obstructive cables, and ability to rapidly swap power supplies without substantial downtime.
 
 KEY PARAMETERS FOR ZERO-RETORFIT INTEGRATION:
 Payload Capacity: Continuous capability to lift, pivot, and load 70-pound projectiles and associated propelling charges. System must meet a minimum Threshold of 6 rounds per minute, with an Objective of 12 rounds per minute. Form Factor: Must fit within standard 24-inch shipboard aisles and maneuver in confined magazine spaces. Locomotion: Able to traverse standard deck plating, step over 6-inch coamings, and brace against ship motion. Stability: Maintain balance and load control up to and during Sea State 5 conditions (significant pitch/roll/heave). Power: Minimum 2-hour continuous operational endurance with rapidly hot-swappable battery packs (changeable in under 60 seconds). Hardening: Built to Military Standard (MIL-STD)-461 (EMI/EMP) and MIL-S-901D (Shock) thresholds. Safety/Fallback: Zero-retrofit integration (i.e., no structural alteration), ensuring the space stays 100-percent operational by human fallback crews in case of robot failure. Explosive Safety: Must adhere to NAVSEA OP 4 protocols for the safe physical handling of ordnance (Note: meeting specific electrical power level compliance is out of scope for this effort). Develop a concept for a humanoid or pseudo-humanoid robot meeting the key parameters for zero-retrofit magazine operations. Conduct kinematic and dynamic simulations modeling the robot extracting, pivoting, and loading rounds in a virtual MK 45 magazine under Sea State 5 conditions. Perform trade studies on single-arm versus multi-arm torque constraints and bipedal versus pseudo-humanoid (quadruped, tracked, or other) stability. Prepare a report on physical design, power management strategy, and a Phase II prototyping/testing plan.
objective: Develop a zero-retrofit robotic prototype capable of identifying, lifting, and loading 70-pound, 5-inch projectiles within the unmodified physical constraints of a DDG 51 class ships' MK 45 Mod 4 ammunition magazine during Sea State 5 conditions. This effort seeks a human-capable equivalent that matches the agility and operational tempo of a well-trained sailor, successfully removing human crews from the most physically exhausting and hazardous steps of the kill chain.

title: Mobile Vehicle Forensics
text:
Design, develop, and demonstrate a ruggedized, field-deployable vehicle forensics device capable of non-destructive, rapid data triage and extraction.
 Operational Need & Gap: During tactical site exploitation (TSE), Marine Corps and Joint operators require immediate, field-deployable hardware and software to recognize, preserve, and collect materials of forensic value. While multi-purpose forensic kits exist to process traditional materials, a critical intelligence gap remains regarding vehicle-derived data. Modern vehicles function as mobile data hubs featuring advanced navigation, localized track logs, and cached external device connections. Exploiting this telematics and informatics data is vital for generating actionable intelligence, mapping networks, and establishing identity dominance.
 
 The Problem (Technological Fragmentation): The primary barrier to tactical vehicle exploitation is severe technological fragmentation. Current vehicle forensic solutions are often designed for controlled laboratory environments. Because In-Vehicle Infotainment (IVI) systems and Electronic Control Units (ECUs) rely on proprietary software architectures and inconsistent file structures, existing tools are often restricted to narrow manufacturer subsets. Consequently, field operators may be forced to perform invasive, time-consuming physical disassembly of the vehicle dashboard—a method that is untenable in many field environments.
 
 Scope of Effort: This SBIR topic seeks innovative proposals to develop a low-SWaP (Size, Weight, and Power), ruggedized, all-in-one device that automates the forensic exploitation of vehicle data systems. The system must interface via standard external access points (e.g., On-Board Diagnostic [OBD-II] ports or Universal Serial Bus [USB]); automatically profile the vehicle's make, model, year, and digital architecture; and execute an automated script to extract and structure data. Crucially, these features must be achieved through a non-invasive approach requiring no component disassembly, while maintaining strict forensic data integrity and verifiable accuracy.
 
 The system must seamlessly interface with a broad registry of modern commercial and civilian vehicles across diverse model years, makes, and international manufacturers. Specifically, the device must extract and normalize data from disparate telematics systems (e.g., embedded GPS, localized track logs) and informatics modules (e.g., infotainment systems, paired Bluetooth logs, Wi-Fi cache, and cellular device pairings) without requiring laboratory-grade component disassembly.
 
 Performance Goals:
 Threshold (Minimum): Demonstrate compatibility with representative samples of common vehicles; extract high-priority telematics (i.e., GPS, route history) and informatics (paired device logs) in under 15 minutes with verifiable accuracy (i.e., comparison with test data collected separately); packaged in a portable, field-ruggedized kit. Objective (Ideal): A pocket-sized, plug-and-play device that requires minimal operator training; demonstrates a modular path to broad vehicle compatibility; and extracts a comprehensive forensic data set in under 5 minutes via an intuitive, automated interface. Develop a technical approach and assess the feasibility of a mobile, software-intelligent vehicle forensics capability that enables rapid data extraction from vehicle telematics (e.g., GPS, navigation logs) and infotainment systems (e.g., paired Bluetooth devices, call histories) and prioritizes universal applicability across diverse vehicle head units, makes, and models, avoiding dependencies on specific hardware teardowns.
 
 Required Phase I deliverables include:
 A comprehensive feasibility study and initial system design architecture. An assessment of projected data extraction speeds, performance metrics, and technical limitations. A detailed Phase II development plan mapping out performance goals, key technical milestones, and risk mitigation strategies.
objective: Design, develop, and demonstrate a ruggedized, field-deployable vehicle forensics device capable of non-destructive, rapid data triage and extraction.

title: Long Rod Delivery System
text:
Create a system capable of launching long rod threats with controlled angle of attack
 The lack of a non-destructive, high-precision launching method for high length-to-diameter (L/D) projectiles fundamentally degrades the fidelity of Live Fire Test and Evaluation (LFT&E) data. For the Air Force, this deficiency directly compromises the development of penetrating munitions, degrades the survivability assessments of aerospace platforms, and introduces significant acquisition risks due to flawed test data and increased testing costs. Currently, there is not means of reliably controlling or manipulating the flight of a long rod projectile such that it consistently reaches a target location at a specific orientation. Providing means of accomplishing this feat advances DoW test capabilities for critical data underpinning analytical vulnerability assessments and engineering designs improving the survivability posture of current and next generation combat aircraft.
 Conduct a comprehensive feasibility study evaluating alternative launching technologies (e.g., advanced light-gas, hybrid electromagnetic, pneumatic) against the requirement to launch high L/D ratio projectiles (1,400 m/s to >2,300 m/s) without structural degradation. Develop a conceptual design and utilize analytical modeling and simulation to predict internal ballistics, projectile acceleration curves, and exit velocities. Identify technical risks and propose mitigation strategies.
objective: Create a system capable of launching long rod threats with controlled angle of attack

title: Improved Ionosphere D-region Specification for High Frequency Propagation
text:
Develop tools and/or techniques to improve characterization of the D-region ionosphere sufficient for skillful ionosphere model specification and forecast over climatology and that demonstrate the impact of improved methodology on ionosphere accuracy for use by high frequency (HF) and very low frequency (VLF) signal propagation tools.
 HF and VLF skywave propagation depend on knowledge of the altitudinal structure of the ionosphere for reliable system operation. The D-region ionosphere, a region typically between 60-90 km altitude above the Earth's surface, is particularly challenging to predict with sufficient fidelity for skywave mission planning because the region is difficult to measure with in situ measurements. Remote sensing methods provide a limited dataset from which to develop detailed physical and assimilative models that can reliably produce the regional behavior on a day-to-day basis.
 
 Operational models like the D-Region Absorption Product (D-RAP) produce maps of outage areas as a function of radio frequency (RF) to inform HF system users of anticipated degradation or blackouts due to radiation increases. These predictions primarily address HF absorption due to solar X-ray flares at low and mid-latitudes and do not address the VLF propagation use case. While solar X-ray flares are important effects with Navy relevance, the effects of flares typically only last for a few hours and occur 10-20 times a year. For sufficient use in HF absorption and VLF propagation applications, a D-region ionosphere is required to capture seasonal, solar cycle, and day-to-day variability at all latitudes in addition to solar flare phenomenology. 
 
 The intended capability is improved D-region specification and forecast in the 60-70 km and 80-90 km altitude regions for VLF propagation and HF absorption, particularly day-to-day variability and in the high latitude regions at night.
 
 Climatological models like the International Reference Ionosphere (IRI) produce an altitude profile at D-region altitudes. The IRI model is based on about a hundred historical rocket profiles, so it captures some of the basic day/night, latitudinal, and seasonal variations in the D-region ionosphere but the model does not capture day-to-day variations or solar X-ray flare events. The model may be sufficient for some HF propagation applications but has been shown to be severely deficient in the high latitude region and during nighttime. In addition, the observations used to create the model do not accurately capture the shape of the lower D-region, which is required for VLF propagation applications.
 
 The Next-generation Ionospheric Model for Operations (NIMO) is an assimilative geospace model developed to address operational USN space weather needs in the ionosphere. NIMO harnesses contributions from both near real-time data and state-of-the-art implementation of ionospheric theory to provide hindcasts, nowcasts, and forecasts for operational or research purposes. NIMO is currently configured to assimilate various types of electron density measurements through the Ionospheric Data Assimilation Four-Dimensional (IDA-4D) data assimilation schema. The D-region is not included in the data assimilation process but is simply added in post processing to the bottom of the electron density grid. The D-region model includes influence from changes in the solar conditions, but uses a climatological model for the neutral atmosphere, so it does not capture the day-to-day variability that is seen in the ionosphere. 
 
 Key performance Metrics/Goals:
 Techniques to improve the global specification and forecast of the D-region ionosphere is sought with particular emphasis on the low latitudes (< 30 degrees) and high latitudes (> 60 degrees). Note: Any measurement techniques should provide measurements or any model should ingest measurements of the D-region and demonstrate improvement over existing models in two key altitude regions: 60-70 km altitude and 80-90 km altitude, which are required for VLF propagation and HF absorption, respectively. 
 
 Key parameters include
 Specify electron density in the 60-70km and 80-90km regions within 10% error. Alternatively, an improvement 75% of the time over existing models is sought. Specification at a temporal cadence of 5-15 minutes Specification at a spatial resolution of 5 degrees in latitude and longitude 
 Technical concepts may include developing prototype concept improvements to measurement techniques and systems, developing improvements to data exploitation and modeling, or a combination of the two.
 Develop a technical concept for improvements to D-region specification. Establish the feasibility of the concept. Provide required Phase I deliverables that include a detailed plan of operational implementation with sufficient evidence to justify claims of skill improvement.
objective: Develop tools and/or techniques to improve characterization of the D-region ionosphere sufficient for skillful ionosphere model specification and forecast over climatology and that demonstrate the impact of improved methodology on ionosphere accuracy for use by high frequency (HF) and very low frequency (VLF) signal propagation tools.

title: A unified model for specification and simulation to design, acquire, and sustain a hybrid- or multi-cloud large scale data analytics system that balances cost, performance, modularity, and security.
text:
Develop and validate an innovative unified financial operations (FinOps) and Model-Based Systems Engineering (MBSE) solution to solve lifecycle cost, resource predictability, and performance modeling challenges within modern defense Condition-Based Maintenance Plus (CBM+) hybrid-cloud systems.
 Modern software-centric data systems across the Department of War operate in highly dynamic, shared cloud and hybrid infrastructure environments. Within complex weapon system sustainment platforms, such as the RSO CBM+ enterprise, accurately predicting and managing lifecycle resource consumption, computing performance, and ongoing operational costs presents a substantial operational challenge. Cloud and hybrid hosting costs fluctuate due to stochastic workload behaviors, data egress, and dynamic compute allocation. Across commercial and defense sectors, approximately 49% of organizations lack dedicated FinOps capabilities, resulting in frequent budget variances exceeding 18% and inefficient allocation of critical resources.
 Traditional MBSE methodologies and legacy toolchains (e.g., static Cameo models, detached MATLAB scripts, disconnected spreadsheets) lack the capability to execute high-fidelity, time-dependent simulations directly within the primary system specification model. This fragmentation creates significant lag between architectural planning, empirical software telemetry, and financial governance, severely limiting rapid system analysis and trade-space optimization.
 To address this capability gap, this project seeks innovative solutions that bridge DevOps, FinOps, and MBSE into a unified, executable environment. The proposed solution must demonstrate how system design specifications and executable simulation software can coexist within a cohesive architecture, such as an extensible, layered Service-Oriented Architecture (SOA) utilizing Systems Modeling Language (SysML) or equivalent open modeling frameworks. Offerors should propose methods to capture continuous empirical data from operational and developmental environments, allowing the model to dynamically update, calibrate, and predict both Capital Expenditures and Operational Expenditures. The solution must support hybrid operational constraints, verifying that on-premise components sustain secure, disconnected operations while remaining optimized alongside cloud assets.
 The entry Technology Readiness Level (TRL) for this D2P2 effort is expected to be TRL 4, progressing to TRL 6 by the conclusion of Phase II, culminating in a fully integrated, operationally viable prototype model and software suite demonstrated under representative operational conditions.
 As this is a Direct-to-Phase-II (D2P2) topic, no Phase I awards are anticipated. To qualify for this D2P2 topic, the Department of the Air Force expects applicants to demonstrate feasibility through prior "Phase I-type" research and commercialization efforts that do not constitute work undertaken as part of an active SBIR/STTR funding agreement for the identical scope.
 The scientific and technical merits of foundational systems modeling, commercial FinOps telemetry, and cloud monitoring tools is established in the commercial marketplace. Therefore, traditional Phase I feasibility studies exploring basic MBSE modeling syntax or standard cloud billing dashboards are considered redundant. Applicants must provide verifiable documentation substantiating that the underlying technology is mature (TRL 4) and that the offeror possesses deep technical capability in unified modeling, simulation execution, and resource forecasting.
 Sufficient Feasibility Documentation should include, but is not limited to:
 Commercial or Operational Deployment Records: Verifiable case studies, white papers, or performance data demonstrating prior implementation of predictive cost analytics, FinOps platforms, or advanced MBSE tools within complex enterprise IT or defense-adjacent environments. Executable Simulation Metrics: Technical reports, architecture diagrams, or code demonstrations validating the ability to couple visual system models (e.g., SysML or comparable schemas) with computational or discrete-event simulation engines to model stochastic system behavior. Telemetry & Feedback Integration Data: Documented capability to ingest continuous empirical log data, infrastructure metrics, or telemetry streams to dynamically calibrate system models or baseline behavioral algorithms. AI/ML or Advanced Algorithmic Validation: Preliminary data or benchmark analyses demonstrating algorithmic feasibility (e.g., machine learning regression, multi-objective optimization, Pareto-frontier analysis) to accurately predict resource utilization or detect anomalous cost drivers. Submission of this documentation confirms that the technology has progressed beyond conceptual formulation and laboratory proof-of-concept into relevant environment validation, establishing the baseline needed to proceed directly to advanced Phase II operational maturation and defense integration.
objective: Develop and validate an innovative unified financial operations (FinOps) and Model-Based Systems Engineering (MBSE) solution to solve lifecycle cost, resource predictability, and performance modeling challenges within modern defense Condition-Based Maintenance Plus (CBM+) hybrid-cloud systems.

title: Remote UAS-based X-Ray for Device Assessment in CBRNE Environments
text:
Develop a novel stand-off X-ray capability by integrating appropriate x-ray transmitter and x-ray receiver capabilities into multiple cooperating UAS systems to enable remote threat device imaging capabilities from a safe distance away from potential Chemical, Biological, Radiological, or Nuclear (CBRN) environments.
 DTRA is in need of technical innovations associated with Warfighters performing long range WMD device assessment and characterization from a safe distance outside of potentially CBRN contaminated environments. Explosive Ordinance Disposal (EOD) definitions and terms are commonly used by many nations and exist on the public internet including steps involving EOD detection, assessment, identification, field evaluation, render safe, recovery and disposal. Current device assessment is manual, requiring personnel to approach closely and manually move x-ray transmitters and x-ray receivers around an unknown device to perform the required assessment mission. Current stand-off capabilities are typically ground robots manually driven a short distance which may be safe for some unexploded ordinance (UXO), but are not safe for suspected WMD warheads. Recent UAS innovations associated with coaxial form factor systems that can perch or land as part of their mission flight profile appear to offer a novel approach to conducting bi-static x-ray image collection.
 STATE OF TECHNOLOGY.
 Current Portable digital radiography systems that depend on hand- or robot-emplacement of a source and flat-panel detector near the device are limited in a CBRN environment. There is no current technology solution that can generate diagnostically useful transmission images (sufficient penetration of ordnance casings plus resolution of fine fuse features such as wires, switches, or delay elements) without any ground contact or personnel entry into the contaminated zone. Mobile x-ray transmitters and various options for exposing images, and stitching multiple images together to create a 3-D assessment of an unknown device exist, but they are generally hand-carried and emplaced. Complex mathematics and algorithms for capturing and rendering X-ray results from multiple simultaneously moving transmitters and receivers each with potential uncertainties in position and angle are limited. Tactical UAS systems are generally small, carry lighter payloads, do not have open architectures for payloads, and payload options are generally difficult and limited to the bottom side to integrate without adversely affecting flight profiles. Robotic x-rays exist but are typically fixed, large and devices are brought to them and put on a turntable. This topic is for x-rays done in the field, at 5km distances, without moving the threat device. No UAS-based x-ray capability currently exists.  
 Design a novel stand-off X-ray capability concept that would integrate portable x-ray transmitter and receiver capabilities into multiple cooperating UAS systems. Create an in silico model of system performance with mathematical assessment of anticipated image quality as a function of time, motion, and navigation uncertainties. A functional transmission X-ray source (high-voltage generation, cooling, radiation shielding) plus a suitable detector must be integrated while preserving flight stability for sharp imaging, supporting open real-time data architectures.
objective: Develop a novel stand-off X-ray capability by integrating appropriate x-ray transmitter and x-ray receiver capabilities into multiple cooperating UAS systems to enable remote threat device imaging capabilities from a safe distance away from potential Chemical, Biological, Radiological, or Nuclear (CBRN) environments.

title: Command Electromagnetic Management & Command-node Awareness, Management, and Obscuration (CEMA CAMO)
text:
Develop and demonstrate Command Electromagnetic Management & Command-node Awareness, Management, and Obscuration (CEMA CAMO), a low-cost, distributed, and attritable electromagnetic spectrum capability that enhances Command Post Survivability and RF Signature Management during Large-Scale Combat Operations (LSCO). The desired capability will employ distributed, software-configurable nodes to sense and shape the electromagnetic environment, creating controlled electromagnetic ambiguity that complicates adversary intelligence, surveillance, and reconnaissance (ISR), reduces targeting confidence, and degrades adversary decision-making and targeting cycles while preserving friendly freedom of maneuver. The capability will be demonstrated in partnership with Joint Innovation Out Post (JIOP) through XVIII Airborne Corps (XVIII ABC) experimentation to assess operational effectiveness, inform capability refinement, and demonstrate integration with Army formations and command-and-control architectures. 
 Army formations, including XVIII Airborne Corps (XVIII ABC) and its subordinate formations, operating in Large-Scale Combat Operations (LSCO) face increasingly capable adversary intelligence, surveillance, and reconnaissance (ISR) systems that can exploit electromagnetic emissions to detect, characterize, locate, and target command posts, platforms, and other mission-critical nodes. The proliferation of networked sensors and increasingly rapid sensor-to-shooter processes creates a need for affordable and scalable capabilities that reduce the effectiveness of adversary electromagnetic sensing and targeting.
  
 XVIII ABC requires capabilities that can be rapidly employed and distributed across formations to improve electromagnetic signature management and enhance survivability and freedom of maneuver in contested environments. This topic seeks innovative approaches for Command Electromagnetic Management & Command-node Awareness, Management, and Obscuration (CEMA CAMO), a low-cost, modular, distributed, and attritable capability for electromagnetic signature management. The desired solution should enable multiple software-configurable nodes to operate cooperatively across an operational area to sense the local electromagnetic environment and generate controlled electromagnetic activity that increases ambiguity and uncertainty for adversary ISR and targeting processes. Potential approaches may include distributed electromagnetic signature shaping, configurable RF effects representations, coordinated emissions, and adaptive management of distributed nodes. Proposed solutions should address the ability to sense and characterize the local electromagnetic environment, coordinate activity across distributed nodes, generate Government-authorized RF effects representations, and dynamically adapt system behavior as the electromagnetic environment changes.
  
 The solution should emphasize low cost, low size, weight, and power (SWaP), modularity, scalability, software configurability, distributed operation, and interoperability with Army command-and-control architectures at Corp and Division. Innovative approaches to autonomous coordination, AI-enabled processing, electromagnetic environment awareness, and dynamic signature management are encouraged. The capability should be scalable from individual nodes to distributed networks and adaptable to different platforms and operational environments. Offerors should characterize key trades including frequency coverage, bandwidth, processing requirements, network latency and synchronization, RF-generation capability, SWaP, node density, and unit cost. Solutions should demonstrate a credible pathway toward a fielded node cost below $50,000, with $30,000 desired where technically feasible.
  
 The desired outcome is a prototype capability that demonstrates how XVIII ABC and Army formations can employ distributed, attritable electromagnetic spectrum technologies to improve survivability and freedom of maneuver by complicating adversary ISR, reducing confidence in electromagnetic-derived targeting information, and degrading adversary decision-making and targeting cycles during LSCO.
  
 Throughout the SBIR|STTR Phase I and Phase II, CEMA CAMO prototype capabilities will be demonstrated in partnership with Joint Innovation Out Post (JIOP) through XVIII Airborne Corps (XVIII ABC) experimentation to assess operational effectiveness, inform capability refinement, and demonstrate integration with Army formations and command-and-control architectures.
 This topic is accepting Phase I submissions with a cost limit of $300,000 and a period of performance of 6 months. Phase I will establish the technical approach and develop an initial CEMA CAMO prototype leveraging mature technologies, including software-defined radios, modular RF front ends, low-SWaP computing, distributed networking, and AI-enabled signal processing. The effort should demonstrate automated electromagnetic sensing and characterization, software-configurable generation or regeneration of Government-authorized RF effects representations, coordinated operation of multiple distributed nodes, and automated or AI-enabled adaptation of node behavior. The effort should also characterize key performance, SWaP, networking, and cost trades, including a preliminary hardware architecture and bill of materials. Proposed solutions should also address resilient operation under degraded communications or loss of individual nodes and approaches for protecting or sanitizing sensitive mission data, software, and configuration information in the event of physical capture or compromise. Experimentation should align, where prototype maturity and contracting timelines permit, with anticipated Scarlet Dragon opportunities tentatively planned for April and August 2027 at Ft. Bragg, NC, and other XVIII ABC-supported experimentation opportunities. Specific dates, locations, and objectives for experimentation may shift based on operation
