title: Mission-Specialized Large Language Models for Operational Training and Knowledge Integration
text:
Develop and demonstrate an explainable, adaptive super  intelligence (SI) capability that enhances Navy workforce readiness, technical training, knowledge transfer, and personnel development through personalized instructional interaction, competency-based learning support, and integration of authoritative Navy workforce and training resources.
 The Department of the Navy faces increasing challenges associated with workforce modernization, technical skill development, personnel turnover, distributed operations, and the growing complexity of mission systems and operational environments. As experienced personnel retire or transition, critical institutional knowledge and operational expertise are frequently difficult to preserve, transfer, and scale across the workforce.
 
 Simultaneously, Navy training and workforce development communities must support increasingly divergent learning requirements across accession, technical education, and qualification pipelines. Existing training approaches often rely on static instructional materials, fragmented knowledge systems, and limited mechanisms for adaptive or individualized instruction.
 
 Commercial large language models (LLMs) demonstrate strong broad-domain reasoning capabilities but are fundamentally limited in their ability to reliably incorporate organization-specific knowledge without hallucination. They are unable to incorporate organization-specific terminology, mission procedures, technical constraints, and authoritative instructional content unique to mission environments. Additionally, these systems frequently generate responses without traceable references, limiting user trust and reducing suitability for technical learning and operational instruction. This gap creates a strong need for a specialized LLM system precisely tuned to an organization's corpus and operational requirements. 
 
 The Navy seeks development of a hyper-parameterized, explainable LLM framework designed specifically to support mission-focused training and knowledge transfer. The system should enable personnel to learn new technical and operational topics through an interactive interface. Outputs should be grounded in authoritative manpower, personnel, training, and education (MPTE) documentation while also leveraging the broad contextual understanding available from foundation LLMs. The proposed capability shall support accelerated workforce proficiency development, preservation of institutional knowledge, and adaptive learning across operational, technical, and mission-support communities while providing transparent, auditable, and trustworthy instructional guidance tailored to user roles, experience levels, and training objectives.
 
 Explainability is a critical requirement for organization-specific LLMs operating in mission environments. The proposed solution must provide transparent and auditable reasoning pathways that allow users to understand how conclusions, recommendations, or generated outputs were derived.
 
 The proposed capability should function as an intelligent training and instructional assistant capable of:
 Teaching mission-specific topics using authoritative organizational documents and instructional materials Combining proprietary knowledge with broad-domain contextual reasoning from foundational LLMs Guiding users through complex technical, operational, engineering, and/or procedural concepts Adapting explanations and instructional depth based on user role, expertise, and/or training objectives Providing explainable outputs with traceable references to source documentation Reducing hallucination through structured retrieval and grounded response generation Supporting continuous updates as training materials, policies, and mission guidance evolve Phase I will focus on assessing the feasibility of a concept for an explainable, mission-specialized training LLM built on sample Navy corpora. The effort will determine the technical feasibility of integrating organization-specific Navy MPTE corpora into a training-oriented conversational SI system. It will identify and characterize the types of Navy documents to be targeted, such as NETC curricula, qualification standards, MyNavy HR competency frameworks, and technical manuals, and define how each would be ingested and leveraged by the LLM. Building on this, the effort will define a concept for hyper-parameterized LLM fine-tuning and retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) architectures appropriate for Navy instructional environments. It will also develop and validate an initial approach for reducing hallucination through structured retrieval and grounded response generation. Required Phase I deliverables include a technical feasibility report and a Phase II development plan.
objective: Develop and demonstrate an explainable, adaptive super  intelligence (SI) capability that enhances Navy workforce readiness, technical training, knowledge transfer, and personnel development through personalized instructional interaction, competency-based learning support, and integration of authoritative Navy workforce and training resources.

title: Biolab Mirror: Artificial Intelligence / Machine Learning (AI/ML) Digital Twin for Intent Characterization and Bio-Containment Integrity
text:
Develop a high-fidelity "Digital Twin" (The Biolab Mirror) and an advanced Artificial Intelligence / Machine Learning (AI/ML) methodology capable of continuous, non-invasive integrity verification and intent characterization of a mid-size, state-sponsored biological research facility. The solution must fuse continuous physical/biological signatures (e.g., metabolic output, environmental thermodynamics, material logistics) with discrete digital telemetry (e.g., Laboratory Information Management Systems (LIMS) logs, Supervisory Control and Data Acquisition (SCADA) / Building Management Systems (BMS) control data). The objective is to detect clandestine biological activities, containment spoofing, and the subtle operational drift indicative of a transition from peaceful, declared research to unauthorized, non-compliant, or undeclared high-risk biological material production [1][2].
 This effort bridges a critical gap between standard Information Technology (IT) network defense and biological physical reality by establishing a "Zero Trust" posture that cross-validates digital telemetry against the immutable laws of physics. Unlike current commercial cyberbiosecurity offerings that focus solely on the IT perimeter or traditional biosurveillance platforms that are purely reactive, the Biolab Mirror is proactively designed to characterize nefarious intent before unauthorized, non-compliant, or undeclared high-risk biological material production occurs.
 The proliferation of dual-use biological technologies and automated, high-containment laboratories globally presents a profound challenge to arms control verification and biosurveillance [3]. A state-sponsored facility operating under a declared, peaceful mandate (e.g., vaccine development, agricultural research) possesses all the necessary infrastructure, reagents, and personnel to rapidly pivot to unauthorized, non-compliant, or undeclared high-risk biological material production [2]. Current verification methods rely heavily on periodic physical inspections, voluntary declarations, and audits of digital LIMS. However, advanced adversaries can digitally spoof BMS, manipulate LIMS records, and conceal clandestine pathogen scaling through "population ghosting" [4][5]. The Department of War (DoW) requires a "Physics-to-Mesh Zero Trust" architecture [6]. This solicitation seeks proposals for a "Biolab Mirror"—a comprehensive Digital Twin that does not inherently trust digital control logs. Instead, the Mirror must continuously cross-validate digital telemetry against the unalterable laws of physics, chemistry, and biology (Conservation of Mass, Thermodynamics, Metabolic Rates). By establishing a rigorous physical baseline (e.g., correlating total water inflow with Effluent Decontamination System (EDS) out-flow, or matching documented animal feed procurement to autoclave waste mass and vivarium Carbon Dioxide (CO2) exhaust), the AI/ML engine must automatically flag the subtle "Coherence Failures" that betray clandestine pathogen scaling, undeclared animal models, or spoofed containment boundaries.
 SUPPLEMENTAL INFORMATION
 Programmatic Metrics and Data Sourcing Data Sourcing Strategy Synthetic Baseline Generation (Performer Sourced): The performer is responsible for generating the Phase II training and validation datasets using established biological and physical engineering standards. Phase I Exit Metrics Measure of Performance (MOP) 1 (Architecture Delivery): Deliver a Digital Twin architecture mapping cross-domain signatures including specialized cross-domain digital and physical validation points.  
 Strategic Offshoots & Cyber-Physical Emulation Executive Summary: The primary objective of the Biolab Mirror SBIR/STTR is defensive: to establish a high-fidelity "Physics-to-Mesh Zero Trust" baseline to detect clandestine activity and intent. Successful completion yields a secondary strategic asset: a perfect, un-spoofed "Cyber-Terrain" map that can be ported into isolated cyber-ranges to simulate, analyze, and train against multi-domain attacks targeting critical high-containment infrastructure [10]. The Capability Gap in Current Cyber-Ranges: Current cyber-ranges are optimized for IT network emulation and struggle to accurately emulate OT and the physical realities of a BSL-3/BSL-4 environment. The Biolab Mirror as the Emulation Foundation: The Biolab Mirror solves this gap. By mapping the continuous physical signatures directly to the discrete digital telemetry, the performer constructs a fully functional Cyber-Physical Sandbox. The Attack Simulation: Authorized cybersecurity evaluation teams and system auditors can execute multi-stage simulated attacks against this virtual target (e.g., spear-phishing an academic researcher -> pivoting to the BMS network -> manipulating the Effluent Decontamination System). The Red Team must navigate the actual laws of biology and thermodynamics to succeed.
 Strategic ROI & Follow-On Potential: Authorizing the Biolab Mirror effort provides a "two-for-one" return on investment (ROI), yielding a defensive characterization engine and a foundational architecture for dedicated cybersecurity testing and critical infrastructure protection. Architecture & Signature Mapping: Develop the conceptual architecture for the Biolab Mirror. The performer must comprehensively map all critical signatures of a mid-size Biosafety Level 3 (BSL-3) / Biosafety Level 4 (BSL-4) facility, categorizing them into Continuous (Physical/Biological) and Discrete (Digital/Telemetry) domains [7]. • Physics-to-Mesh Framework: Define the "Coherence Fuses" and mathematical models required to cross-validate specific digital assertions (e.g., BMS reporting "Sterilization Complete") with physical ground truth (e.g., calculated facility equipment power utilization metrics or chemical reagent depletion). • Intent Characterization Roadmap: Develop an AI/ML roadmap demonstrating how the Mirror will analyze deviations from the established facility baselin

 Develop a reusable illumination system for high-speed photo-optic data collection used at the Holloman High Speed Test Track (HHSTT) and other sled test tracks.
 The PF300 flash bulbs, that provide high-intensity illumination for high-speed video acquisition, are no longer in production. The objective is to award a contract to a small business to engineer, design, and manufacture a modern, robust, reusable replacement for the legacy PF300 flash bulb. This new system must meet or surpass the existing illumination and performance requirements of the original flash bulbs to ensure seamless integration with current high-speed video systems. The ideal solution would leverage Commercial Off-The-Shelf (COTS) or near-COTS technologies to qualify this project as a direct-to-Phase-II effort. A successful reusable replacement would immediately solve the impending obsolescence issue, securing a reliable illumination source for future missions. Furthermore, transitioning to a reusable system would dramatically reduce consumable cost. This technological update could also pave the way for enhanced capabilities, such as adjustable light intensity and longer duration illumination, offering greater flexibility and improved data quality for high-speed video analysis across various applications
 As this is a Direct-to-Phase-II (D2P2) topic, no Phase I awards will be made as a result of this topic. The technology exists, but the operating environment of the Test Track is unique enough there is not a readily available product.  The objective of this Directed to Phase II (D2P2) SBIR effort is to develop an innovative, secure, and scalable solution for modernizing Technical Data Packages (TDPs) associated with complex Air and Space Force platforms. This initiative seeks to address challenges in managing large, diverse datasets by enhancing configuration control, ensuring data integrity, and strengthening Information Assurance (IA) in support of mission-critical operations. Specifically, the focus of this phase is to demonstrate the feasibility of advanced technologies that enable secure data lifecycle management and seamless data exchange within operational environments. Proposed solutions should align with Trusted AI and Autonomy modernization priorities by incorporating robust cybersecurity measures and leveraging cutting-edge advancements in autonomy, data management, and secure manufacturing capabilities. Outcomes of this phase are expected to validate technical concepts and establish a functional prototype that meets the operational imperative of readiness to deploy and fight, contributing to future scalability and transition opportunities in operational use cases.
 Background and Problem Statement:
 The modernization of Technical Data Packages (TDPs) is imperative to address the Air and Space Force's operational challenges in securely managing large-scale, complex datasets associated with advanced platforms and their sustainment life cycles. Current TDP systems often lack robust Information Assurance (IA) capabilities, seamless integration with Product Lifecycle Management (PLM) environments, and effective mechanisms for secure data exchange across operational networks. This limitation not only hinders data integrity and configuration control but also increases vulnerabilities to cyber threats, jeopardizing mission-critical operations. The rapid pace of platform evolution and the increasing reliance on Model-Based Definition (MBD) and digital twin technologies further exacerbate the need for a comprehensive solution that ensures TDP security, scalability, and operational readiness.
  
 Opportunity and Desired Outcome:
 This Directed to Phase II (D2P2) SBIR effort aims to develop an innovative, scalable, and secure solution to modernize TDPs to support the lifecycle of highly complex Air and Space Force platforms. The envisioned solution will integrate advanced IA protocols, cryptographic protections, and tools for encrypted data exchange to facilitate the secure management of the "as-sustained" configuration state of critical assets. The outcome will be a functional prototype capable of enabling secure TDP lifecycle management while aligning with the Trusted AI and Autonomy modernization priorities and Zero Trust Architecture principles. The proposed solution will enhance operational efficiency, minimize cyber risks, and establish a foundation for scalable implementation across DoD platforms.
  
 The project's Technology Readiness Level (TRL) at the start is anticipated to be TRL 4, with the target of reaching a minimum TRL 6 by the conclusion of Phase II, including validation of core capabilities in a relevant operational environment.
  
 Required Efforts and Phase Activities:
 To achieve the stated objectives, the following efforts and activities are required for each phase of the project:
  
 Phase II:
 Develop a secure visualization tool for displaying large-scale MBD geometry and associated data through encrypted web-based interfaces.
 Implement an encrypted configuration management system to maintain and update the "as-sustained" asset state while ensuring strict data integrity.
 Create advanced tools for automated data quality checks, incorporating rules-based IA compliance validation to ensure all TDPs meet security and contractual requirements.
 Design an end-to-end encrypted exchange framework for TDPs, incorporating user authentication, authorization, and audit trails while conforming to DoD Zero Trust Architecture guidelines.
 Integrate AI/ML methodologies to enable secure damage detection, sustainment planning, and actionable insights into asset health.
 Demonstrate the prototype in an operationally relevant environment, proving feasibility, security compliance, and system performance in handling large and diverse data streams.
  
 Minimum Deliverables:
 A secure web-based MBD visualization prototype capable of rendering large-scale geometry and TDP datasets with sub-second response times and role-based access controls.
 Tools for encrypted configuration management and secure "as-sustained" state maintenance, integrated with PLM systems.
 An automated framework for data quality checks and IA compliance validation of TDPs using defined security protocols and rules-based engines.
 A cryptographic data transfer and exchange framework, with test results demonstrating alignment with DoD security policies and successful inter-organizational data exchange.
 Technical documentation detailing methodologies, system architecture, and IA protocols implemented during the project, including recommendations for further scaling and operationalization.
 A transition plan for integrating the developed TDP modernization technology into operational envir

title: US Production of Ultra-High Temperature Ceramic-Yielding Preceramic Polymers
text:
The Department of the Air Force seeks to establish the domestic production of ultra-high temperature ceramic (UHTC)-yielding preceramic polymers. UHTCs are used for demanding aerospace applications, including propulsion and aeroshell components.
 The scaled production of C/C-UHTCs composites (UHTCMCs) for defense applications requires the manufacturing of UHTC precursors in quantities sufficient to support acquisition programs. This SBIR will establish production of an AFRL-patented UHTC preceramic polymers so that the materials are available, at scale and affordable price point, to the high-temperature composite production community.
 This topic is intended for technologies ready to move directly into a Phase II program. As this is a Direct-to-Phase-II (D2P2) topic, no Phase I awards will be made. Offerors must demonstrate completion of Phase I feasibility research and development that is not based upon or logically extend from any prior or ongoing federally funded SBIR or STTR work. Offerors must provide detailed documentation in their Direct to Phase II (D2P2) proposal that demonstrates the successful completion of a "Phase I-like" effort. This includes a feasibility study showing expertise in synthesizing and handling air/water-sensitive chemical compounds. Demonstrated experience in scaling chemical synthesis processes from the lab to pilot scale (e.g., 5-50 kg batches) is required. The feasibility study should clearly illustrate past successes in producing high-purity materials and a foundational understanding of the safety protocols necessary for handling the relevant precursors and reagents.

title: Low SWaP, 2-micron Fiber Amplifiers
text:
Develop and demonstrate a rugged, kilowatt class 2-micron fiber amplifier module that matches size, weight, and power metrics of state-of-the-art 1-micron systems to accelerate the transition of laboratory technology to operational Department of the Air Force capabilities. 
 High-power fiber lasers operating in the 2-micron regime offer critical advantages for defense, medical, and industrial applications, including eye-safer directed energy, advanced sensing, and precision materials processing. While kilowatt-class, narrow-linewidth thulium-doped fiber amplifiers have been demonstrated, the Department of the Air Force aims to reduce the size and weight of existing kilowatt-class 2-micron fiber amplifiers into a highly compact system with similar size, weight, and power metrics of existing 1-micron fiber amplifiers. This topic seeks to leverage existing Air Force laboratory architectures to prime industry for production of robust 2-micron fiber amplifiers, paving the way for transition into active directed energy programs.
 This topic is intended for technologies ready to move directly into a Phase II program. As this is a Direct-to-Phase-II (D2P2) topic, no Phase I awards will be made. title: Agile Wire Harness Manipulation and Installation for Unmanned Aerial Systems
text:
Develop and demonstrate a modular, agile robotic manufacturing workcell capable of autonomously routing, aligning, inserting, and verifying flexible, non-rigid wire harnesses and electrical connectors within the highly constrained physical geometries of Unmanned Aerial Systems (UAS) and advanced munitions.
 As a Direct-to-Phase-II (D2P2) topic, the immediate goal is to transition a validated proof-of-concept software and mechanical baseline (Technology Readiness Level 4) into fully integrated, operationally viable production workcells evaluated at defense prime contractor manufacturing sites. The system must eliminate the need for hard-tooled, single-product automation by delivering an agile platform that integrates deterministic planning models with real-time, adaptive online sensory feedback. This enables the robot to navigate the unpredictable, non-rigid deformation behaviors of flexible cabling, achieve sub-millimeter positioning tolerances, and safely execute intricate "blind-mate" connection sequences within tight bulkhead quarters without manual intervention.
 To support a dynamic, high-mix/low-volume defense production environment, the workcell must be designed for rapid retaskability. Offerors must demonstrate a system architecture that allows shop-floor operators to completely retask the workcell to handle an entirely different munitions or UAS harness family within a single eight-hour shift. Furthermore, the platform must establish the first end-to-end digital thread for harness operations, generating machine-readable traceability records for every routing, tensioning, and insertion step to prevent latent defects and ensure 100% military standard compliance.
 The ultimate phase outcome must demonstrate a two-to-four-times cycle time improvement over legacy manual wiring techniques and a reduction in skilled labor hours per unit by at least 50%. This will directly remove the primary assembly bottleneck constraining the scale-up, surge capacity, and high-rate production of critical defense systems.
 Context & BackgroundModern Department of Defense (DoD) manufacturing and depot sustainment environments increasingly depend on agile automation to scale up production and maintain rapid operational readiness. While automated assembly technologies have matured substantially for rigid components with predictable geometries, the handling of flexible materials remains a persistent challenge. Specifically, wire harness routing, connector inspection, and insertion operations are ubiquitous across the production lines of Unmanned Aerial Systems (UAS), advanced munitions families, and autonomous collaborative platforms. Currently, these intricate electrical assembly processes represent a bottleneck in UAS assembly operations. Assembly technicians must manually route non-rigid cables through confined structural cavities and execute high-precision connection steps under high-mix, low-volume production conditions. Traditional industrial robotics break down when tasked with these operations because flexible wiring deforms unpredictably during manipulation, completely violating the rigid-part assumptions and fixed, hard-tooled rules of standard automation. Problem, Opportunity, & Unmet Need The complete reliance on manual wire harness installation creates a critical capability deficiency that severely penalizes DoD manufacturing agility and surge capacity. Manual operations are fundamentally non-scalable, meaning production lines cannot dynamically "ramp-to-rate" to meet sudden spikes in theater demand. Furthermore, manual wire routing and insertion introduce human-induced variability, resulting in unquantifiable defects such as partially seated connectors, overstressed wires, or compromised bend radii. These latent defects frequently slip past standard visual inspections and surface as catastrophic electrical or communication failures during critical mission times. Aerospace prime contractors and program offices have identified this manual chokepoint as the largest automation gap in UAS and munitions production. This deficiency creates a major opportunity to implement a flexible automation solution. Resolving this challenge requires a modular, adaptive robotic workcell that handles deformable materials, operates with high positional accuracy in restricted footprints, and can be rapidly retasked between completely different product designs within a single factory shift. Desired Outcome & Technological Improvement The desired outcome of this research and development effort is a fully integrated, single-arm modular robotic manufacturing workcell capable of autonomously handling the core manipulation and installation scenarios for flexible UAS and munitions wiring harnesses. Shifting the technology from manual assembly to adaptive, sensor-driven automation will fundamentally advance the DoD technological state of the art by achieving the following targeted improvements: Deformable Material Control: The platform will combine deterministic offline path planning with adaptive, real-time online sensory feedback (such as tactile, force-torque, and vision monitoring). This closed-loop configuration enables "search and settle" machine behaviors to dynamically correct for micro-misalignments and part variability on the fly. Sub-Millimeter Tolerances: The workcell will successfully execute precise connector insertion and blind-mate assembly steps within tightly constrained geometries to a targeted positioning tolerance of $\le$ 0.5 mm.Rapid Retaskability: The system will break the paradigm of dedicated single-product manufacturing by allowing shop-floor operators to ingest new geometric data and completely retask the workcell to a novel harness family in less than 8 hours.End-to-End Digital Thread: The workcell will generate machine-readable traceability records of every insertion force profile and routing path.  Develop and demonstrate advanced power source technologies capable of meeting weapon requirements with specific energy and power equal to or greater than current reserve battery technologies.
 Power source performance in terms of power and energy density is the major objective with affordability, safety, and reliability secondary objectives of Air Force Armament Directorate programs for advanced reserve power sources for weapon systems. Secondary objectives are not distant relative to the major objective, but power and energy density is emphasized in order to enable new concepts and integration strategies. Current reserve thermally activated battery technology is at risk of becoming obsolete due to increasing specific power and specific energy requirements, while other battery technologies with similar or greater specific energy suffer from multiple failure modes, have limited storage life, or have not been tailored to meet the unique requirements for Air Force weapon programs. An advanced reserve power source lasting 20+ years without the need for maintenance or significant energy loss while in storage, is reliable, and is inherently safe, e.g. is not susceptible to thermal runaway, is required. Weapons typically have storage lifetimes of 20+ years; and must maintain reliable operation at any point within this time period without the power source being inadvertently activated. When the power source is activated, it must rise to full voltage within 600 ms and have an activated life of 5+ minutes. The power source must be able to survive shock, vibration, and temperatures (MIL-HDBK-310 1% Hot/ 1% Cold Days, worldwide) associated with external and internal carriage, high speed free flight, and storage environments. The power source will be required to provide power for weapon avionics, guidance, and ordnance initiation events for the entire flight profile. The load on the power source must be capable of periods of pulse power with an average 2.5 kW/kg minimum and a goal to exceed 5 kW/kg load over 60 seconds. The goal of this technology development is to design, develop, and test an advanced design for a power source capable of 20+ years of storage, 5+ minutes of activated life, with a specific energy at a minimum of 40 Wh/kg and a goal to exceed 100 Wh/kg. The power source must be inherently safe during its entire lifetime. Due to the safety issues associated with lithium battery technologies and the process to receive certification through the Naval Ordnance Security and Safety Activity (NOSSA) for use on an ordnance system, lithium battery technologies will need to demonstrate no venting under NAVSEA S9310-AQ-SAF-010 test conditions.

title: Optimally Packaged Assembly for Laser Systems (OPALS)
text:
High-energy lasers integrated onto airborne platforms hold immense potential for a variety of applications, relevant to DAF missions. However, the demanding operational environments encountered by airborne systems, characterized by factors like vibration, shock, temperature fluctuations, and pressure variations, pose significant challenges to the performance and reliability of traditional optical systems. To achieve demanding pointing and line of sight stabilization requirements necessary for the laser to have the desired effect on target, a precision optical beam control system is required to sense and correct platform induced disturbances, acquire and track targets, and sense and compensate for atmospheric and aero-optical disturbances. Historically these optical systems are implemented on flat optical benches or breadboards, in a similar manner to a ground-based laboratory. To fully realize the potential of airborne laser systems, there is a critical need for innovative optical systems designed specifically for ruggedness and environmental stability. This research effort aims to develop and demonstrate a ruggedized, environmentally stable, and optimally packaged optical beam control system specifically tailored for airborne high-energy laser applications, in a more optimized form factor for an airborne system than a conventional flat optical bench or breadboard. 
 The Air Force requires light weight, compactly packaged optical systems to perform critical beam control functions for airborne high energy laser systems. The purpose of this topic is not to develop new outer moldlines or turret designs for airborne systems but rather focus on optimizing the packaging and performance of the internal optical system required to perform the core beam control functions. A canonical layout of such system is available in Reference 1. The Government expects the designed beam control system will perform all functions laid out in the canonical design - or that any deviations are thoroughly understood and technically justified. Additionally, designs should prioritize ease of alignment and component replacement, potential for line replaceable units, beam path conditioning, and material free of shedding contaminants which could lead to foreign object damage. In order to achieve these objectives, the Government anticipates investigations into the following areas, although this list is informational and is intended to be neither proscriptive nor comprehensive:Ruggedized Optical Design and MaterialsRobust Packaging and Assembly TechniquesNovel Optical Architectures: Explore and develop innovative optical designs inherently tolerant to vibrations, shocks, and thermal gradients.Advanced Materials Selection: Investigate and characterize advanced materials with superior thermo-mechanical properties. This includes exploring specialized glasses, ceramics, and composites for optical elements and mounting structures.Advanced Manufacturing and Assembly Processes: Investigate and implement advanced manufacturing techniques, such as additive manufacturing and precision micro-assembly, to fabricate intricate components and achieve high-precision alignment and bonding of optical elements.Athermalized Design Strategies: Implement passive and active athermalization techniques to mitigate the performance degradation caused by temperature fluctuations. This involves optimizing material choices, employing thermal compensation methods.
 In phase I the basic concept for the beam control mounting structure will be developed and investigated. Initial performance estimates will be modeled and an initial estimate of size and weight will be calculated. The Government anticipates numerous trade studies and design excursions to create the conceptual design for the OPALS beam control subsystem. During Phase I, concepts developed should be as platform agnostic as feasible. The Government will provide platform representative vibration spectra for performance analysis. The Government anticipates the majority of the concept development to support a Phase II prototype capable of propagating an up to ~20kW laser. However, the concept should also address issues relating to the transition to the phase III operationalized system, capable of accepting a laser of at least 300kW.

title: Multiple Telemetry Site Signal Source Synchronization
text:
The objective of this project is to study, develop, test, and field a system that addresses a critical gap in pre-mission verification and validation of receive systems supporting flight test missions that transition between multiple, geographically diverse Test and Training Ranges. The end goal is to achieve a fully operational system that enables synchronized telemetry test signals across all participating ranges. This will allow for a comprehensive, end-to-end system checkout before a live test, significantly reducing operational and data fidelity risks, enhancing test accuracy, and strengthening mission readiness for advanced DoW test scenarios.
 Flight test missions that traverse multiple Test Ranges (e.g. hypersonic vehicles/weapons, cruise missiles, long-range weapon systems etc.) or that require different test support infrastructures (e.g. sea range, targets, threat simulators, etc.) at remote Test Ranges, require telemetry receive stations along the flight paths to receive real-time telemetry and then relay that data via ground networks to the control room monitoring the mission. In past mission pre-flight scenarios, remote telemetry receive site to control room links were checked individually. This was accomplished with a local bore sight signal simulator that transmitted a known test pattern at the center frequency of the actual test article. The telemetry receive site would receive the radio frequency signal, demodulate/decode it, then send the data via Internet protocol (IP) networks to the control room. In the control room the received data was verified to be correct as the bit pattern received could be compared to the bit pattern transmitted. This was accomplished for each local and remote telemetry receive site prior to the mission.During the test, each local and remote telemetry receive site would send data to the control room and a manual switch would be accomplished between each data source based on data quality that was determined manually. Note, this selection was not automated.With the invent of best source selection using data quality metrics transferred over IP networks via data quality encapsulation [1], no longer is election of multiple data sources done manually. Telemetry receivers now assess received data quality and assign a bit error probability to a packet of data prior to sending it to the best source selector in the control room. A best source selector (BSS) inputs these multiple streams, performs time alignment, then using the data quality metric, selects the best data to output on a bit-by-bit basis. This output is the best data using all available data streams from diverse receive sites.Though higher quality, near error-free data is now provided to the control room, the addition of the BSS has revealed a shortfall. The entire data path from remote receive sites to transport through best source selection to control room cannot be tested as a complete system to assess mission readiness. The traditional method of pre-flight checks cannot be used. Why? The best source selector will not be able to correlate the multiple data streams from remote sites as the signal sources will not be correlated. This results in the configuration and operation of the BSS being unknown until the test mission. The proposed work will focus on solving this shortfall resulting in a networked, synchronized telemetry validation system capable of simulating a test vehicle's telemetry signal at multiple ground stations simultaneously. Stated another way, the proposed system must simulate the test article signal as if all telemetry receive stations could "see" the test article and simultaneously receive the telemetry signal. This capability will allow test ranges to perform pre-mission verification of the entire telemetry infrastructure. This would include all participating receive antennas, distribution networks, and best source selector(s) to control room displays to ensure full system connectivity and performance before supporting a live mission.
 Phase I should assess the scientific and technical merit and feasibility of the concept proposed for Inter-Range telemetry receive system synchronization and signal source correlation. Objectives and expectations in Phase I are as follows: Thoroughly describe the shortfall identifying all components and interfaces. Reference all appropriate standards and provide a use case(s) that clearly illustrates the shortfall.Propose an architecture that addresses and solves this shortfall. A solution should provide a solution that incorporates multiple, spatially diverse telemetry signal sources/simulators and synchronizes these sources with precise, common time and frequency reference across all sites.Derive a master-client network architecture with a centralized command and control graphical user interface. This will allow an operator to remotely configure, manage, and monitor all signal sources/simulators from a centralized location.At the core of this solution, develop a protocol that precisely aligns all remote pseudo-random bit sequences (PRBS) generated by each simulator.

The end goal is to achieve a fully operational system that enables synchronized telemetry test signals across all participating ranges. This will allow for a comprehensive, end-to-end system checkout before a live test, significantly reducing operational and data fidelity risks, enhancing test accuracy, and strengthening mission readiness for advanced DoW test scenarios.

title: Luminescence-Based Surface Measurement Technique for Simultaneous Pressure and Temperature Measurements within Non-Oxygen Based Hypersonic Ground Test Facilities
text:
Develop and validate a non-intrusive, luminescence-based surface measurement technique for simultaneous pressure and temperature measurements within non-oxygen-based hypersonic ground test facilities.
 Within aerodynamic testing, pressure sensitive paint (PSP) provides crucial global surface pressure data that is utilized in calculating aerodynamic loads [1] and identifying small scale features within the flow. The working principle behind PSP involves luminophores that fluoresce at an intensity inversely proportional to the number of oxygen molecules present i.e., oxygen quenching [2].
 While these paints/luminophores have been sufficiently researched, the use-case of these paints is severely limited due to the requirement of oxygen in the flow field. Advanced hypersonic wind tunnels such as the blowdown facility at AEDC Tunnel No. 9 which utilizes nitrogen as the working fluid, are unable to utilize PSP to capture global pressure data with this method and are therefore severely limited to discrete measurement techniques. It is required that a novel technique be developed to capture simultaneous global pressure and temperature measurements in nonoxygen-based hypersonic wind tunnels.
 Phase I efforts outline technique/paint development and establish feasibility through thorough characterization of the paint properties/sensitivities and reduction process using benchtop testing and testing within small-scale (educational) supersonic/hypersonic facilities.
objective: Develop and validate a non-intrusive, luminescence-based surface measurement technique for simultaneous pressure and temperature measurements within non-oxygen-based hypersonic ground test facilities.

title: AI-Enabled Computed Vision Air-to-Air Refueling Performance Assessment and Automated Pilot Debrief System
text:
Develop, integrate, and demonstrate an artificial intelligence (AI)-enabled computed vision and human-machine interface capability that transforms aerial refueling operations from subjective, observation-based evaluation into an objective, data-driven performance assessment and adaptive training environment. The system shall leverage advanced computer vision, machine learning, and aviation (flight dynamics) analytics techniques to automatically extract operationally relevant performance metrics from aerial refueling events, quantify deviations from desired flight profiles, and generate actionable post-flight feedback to improve aircrew proficiency, reduce human-factor-driven mishaps, and enhance mission readiness.The capability shall analyze video from cameras mounted on the tanker (esp. the KC-46) to provide near-real-time post-flight reconstruction of aerial refueling engagements by correlating aircraft position, motion dynamics, refueling geometry, pilot inputs, and operational context to identify performance trends and training opportunities. The developed system shall perform automated assessment of complex aerial refueling behaviors including aircraft stability, closure rate management, alignment accuracy, control surface position, other situational awareness indicators, and adherence to established refueling procedures.The objective is to mature existing advanced AI-enabled aviation analytics into an operationally relevant post-flight "hotwash" and training capability that increases the instructional value of each aerial refueling sortie, reduces reliance on subjective human assessment, accelerates pilot proficiency development, decreases equipment damage associated with refueling deviations, and establishes a scalable foundation for future intelligent aviation training systems across Department of the Air Force and joint aviation communities.The resulting prototype shall demonstrate the ability to ingest operational aerial refueling data, autonomously generate objective performance assessments, provide intuitive visualization and debrief products, and support transition into existing aviation training, evaluation, and modernization ecosystems. Importantly, the system will also include automated security management of the video so that implementation is seamless and complies with security classification guidance.
 Air-to-air refueling (AAR) is a critical Department of the Air Force and Department of the Navy capability enabling global mobility, long-range strike, combat airpower projection, and sustained aviation operations. However, aerial refueling remains one of the most technically demanding and safety-critical aviation tasks performed by aircrews. Successful execution requires precise aircraft positioning, coordinated control inputs, accurate closure rate management, continuous situational awareness, and effective crew coordination between tanker and receiver aircraft.Current aerial refueling training and post-flight assessment processes rely heavily on instructor observation, pilot self-assessment, manual video review, and subjective evaluation of performance. These approaches provide limited ability to quantitatively assess the thousands of individual performance variables that influence successful refueling operations. Existing methods do not provide pilots with objective, moment-by-moment feedback on aircraft positioning, closure rates, control inputs, deviations from desired procedures, or trends in individual performance over time.This topic seeks to develop, demonstrate, and transition an artificial intelligence (AI)-enabled computed vision capability that (post-flight) automatically analyzes aerial refueling operations and provides objective, data-driven pilot performance feedback. The desired capability will mature existing advances in autonomous aerial refueling analytics and apply them toward training, readiness, and safety improvement by transforming aerial refueling video and available aircraft performance data into actionable post-flight debrief products.The developed system shall provide an automated "hot wash" which analyzes aerial refueling events, identifies performance deviations, and generates intuitive visualizations that allow pilots and instructors to better understand execution quality and areas for improvement. The system shall reduce reliance on subjective recollection and manual review by providing objective measurements of aircraft performance throughout the refueling profile.The capability shall focus on analysis of tanker-mounted video data, such as KC-46 aerial refueling camera systems, while maintaining an architecture capable of expanding across additional tanker and receiver platforms. The vendor may pick (with Government concurrence) the first 3-5 receiver platforms to use in developing this system. Future applicability includes KC-135, C-17, all fighter receiver aircraft, naval aviation communities, autonomous aerial refueling systems, and other aviation training environments requiring advanced performance analytics.The desired solution shall leverage artificial intelligence, machine learning, computer vision, and advanced human-machine interfaces to provide capabilities including:• Automated detection and tracking of tanker (boom and hose) and receiver aircraft during aerial refueling operations.• Measurement of relative aircraft position, movement, velocity, and alignment throughout the refueling engagement.• Assessment of aircraft position within the approved refueling envelope.• Analysis of closure rates, approach vectors, aircraft stability, and deviations from nominal procedures.• Ability to correlate video with other aircraft data if/as available (e.g. telemetry, fuel transfer rate, fuel state, and pilot inputs) to evaluate performance drivers.• Generation of objective performance scores and trend analysis across multiple training events.• Creation of visual performance assessment products for receiver pilot post-flight review of the

title: Fusion of Cooperative Information Sharing for Uncrewed Air Systems (FOCISAUS)
text:
The Department of the Air Force seeks mature, innovative solutions ready for prototype development and demonstration in cooperative perception for uncrewed or autonomous air systems. The objective of this topic is to develop and demonstrate a scalable prototype that enables distributed sensing nodes to share, prioritize, and fuse mission-relevant information in near real time to improve object detection, tracking, navigation, and operator situational awareness in cluttered and bandwidth-constrained environments.
 Solutions should support efficient information exchange, adaptive transmission under changing network conditions, and a credible data fusion design that converts distributed sensor observations into actionable fused products. Offerors should propose technologies with demonstrated Phase I-type maturity and a clear path to prototype integration, testing, and transition.
 Distributed air operations increasingly depend on timely awareness of objects, hazards, and activities beyond the field of view of any individual platform. Cooperative perception offers a path to extend sensing coverage and reduce blind spots by allowing multiple platforms and supporting nodes to share sensor-derived information. Yet this benefit is limited by the large size of modern sensor data, the variability of wireless links, the need for rapid decision making, and the difficulty of combining observations from different platforms, geometries, and sensing modalities.
 This topic seeks prototype-ready solutions that build on prior feasibility work in distributed information sharing, compression, adaptive transmission, and sensor data fusion. The government is interested in capabilities that can select and transmit the most relevant information, manage latency and bandwidth constraints, and fuse data from multiple sources into improved perception outputs for autonomy or operator use.
 Offerors should address the data fusion aspect as a core requirement of the overall solution, whether through point cloud fusion, image or radar correlation, feature or object fusion, track association, or other mission-appropriate methods. Solutions should also describe how fused outputs are exposed to mission applications, edge processing nodes, or user interfaces. Approaches that can operate under degraded or intermittent communications and can scale across multiple sensing platforms are of particular interest.
 Prototype capabilities may include, but are not limited to: Distributed organization, naming, publication, discovery, or retrieval of sensor information; Adaptive data selection, fidelity control, compression, and transmission policies; Real-time or near-real-time fusion and correlation of data from multiple platforms or sensor types; Delivery of fused perception products to autonomy software, edge analytics, or mobile mission applications; and Measurable improvements in latency, bandwidth efficiency, blind-spot reduction, and detection or tracking performance.
 This topic is intended for technologies that are sufficiently mature to proceed directly into prototype development. Therefore, Phase I awards will not be made for this topic and Phase I proposals will not be accepted. Offerors must provide detail and documentation in the D2P2 proposal demonstrating completion of a Phase I-type effort. This should include evidence of scientific and technical feasibility, relevance to a Department of the Air Force need, and a clear basis for moving directly into integrated prototype development.

title: ONR Open Topic for Low-Cost Heads Up Displays (HUDs) for Virtual & Augmented Reality (VR/AR)
text:
Develop a commercial technology to address Navy and USMC gaps regarding low-cost, NDAA-compliant heads-up displays (HUDs) with on-board 6 degrees-of-freedom (6DOF) tracking.
 ONR requests proposals for existing technology demonstration platforms, prototypes, and commercial products that provide domestically-sourced, low-cost HUDs) for first-person view (FPV) drone pilots, and augmented reality (AR) capabilities for Forward Observers (FOs) and Joint Terminal Air Controllers (JTACs). For Phase I awardees, ONR will provide operational context and technical thresholds against which technologies will be assessed and provide feedback and guidance on enhancements to align with warfighting objectives. 
 
 The proposing small business should have an existing hardware solution that meets one or both technical areas listed below:
 - HUD for FPV pilot operations including integrated display, signal inputs, and locations for mounting organic FPV equipment including antennas, transmitters, and power supplies
 - Integrated HUD with native 6DOF tracking, using on-board sensors and modalities (cameras, Inertial Measurement or Measuring Units [IMUs], magnetometers), compute, and power (battery)
 The DON is planning to issue multiple Phase I awards for this topic but reserves the right to issue no awards. Each Phase I proposal must include a Base and Option period of performance. The Phase I Base must have a period of performance of six (6) months at a cost not to exceed $200,000. The Phase I Option must have a period of performance of six (6) months at a cost not to exceed $115,000. Phase I feasibility will describe the existing proposed technology, existing DON system(s) to improve/replace, expected improvements to existing capabilities, and a transition approach to both the DON system and commercial sector. Phase I results will be detailed in a final technical report (Final Report) and presented during the project outbrief one month prior to Final Report submission.
 Phase I deliverables include:
 - Kick-Off Briefing, due 15 days from start of Base award
 - Progress Report, due 90 days from start of Base award
 - Final Report, due 180 days from start of Base award
 - Quad Chart, due 180 days from start of Base award
 - Initial Phase II Proposal, due 180 days from start of Base award
 
 The Phase I Option, if exercised, will include the initial design specifications and capabilities description to build and deliver a prototype solution in Phase II.
objective: Develop a commercial technology to address Navy and USMC gaps regarding low-cost, NDAA-compliant heads-up displays (HUDs) with on-board 6 degrees-of-freedom (6DOF) tracking.

title: Cleaner for the Time Domain Reflectometer Tank Level Indicator
text:
Develop a technology to clean and potentially reverse fouling on Time Domain Reflectometer (TDR) Tank Level Indicating (TLI) components in-place. The solution must function within fully compensated fuel tanks aboard DDG 51 class ships without requiring depressurization, defueling, or dewatering.
 Fouling on the TDR sensor used for TLI is a persistent problem. The TDR is necessary to provide accurate and precise readings for fuel measurement. Over time, TDRs can experience sensor fouling through a buildup of crystallization and other contaminants on TDR rods and tubes, contributing to false readings or other failures if not properly maintained and cleaned.
 
 The operational readiness of the U.S. Navy's DDG 51 Arleigh Burke-class destroyers is being undermined by a persistent and unsolved equipment failure. The TDR sensors, a TLI technique, which are critical for managing fuel, buoyancy, and stability, are consistently rendered unreliable due to fouling. Current cleaning methods are operationally untenable; they require taking fuel compensating tanks offline, emptying fuel and/or compensating seawater, and significant follow-on maintenance, which directly reduces the Fleet's readiness and deployability. These efforts are not a permanent solution and often fail to resolve the underlying issue, making this a high-priority challenge for the DDG 51 Program Office.
 
 The Navy urgently seeks an innovative solution that remedies fouled TDR units without requiring ships to cease operations or undergo costly, invasive maintenance, thereby increasing mission readiness and reducing the risk of fuel spills.
 
 Effective methods for cleaning these sensors in-situ are very limited. The existing approach involves decompensation of fuel tanks (removal of fuel and compensating seawater) and manual removal of TDR sensors for cleaning, which can be costly and time consuming. It is not generally feasible while the ship is underway. Removal of TDR sensors during these manpower-intensive efforts can sometimes lead to TDR sensor miscalibration during re-installation.
 
 The inability to effectively clean TDR sensor fouling is a critical point of failure. The buildup of crystallization and other contaminants on TDR rods and tubes creates false readings and electrical shorts, leading to inaccurate fuel measurement and extensive tracking errors. This directly compromises the precise fuel management necessary for the ship's stability and mission readiness. Current ships have had fuel spills due to TDR TLI fouling. Additionally, scheduled maintenance periods to remove and clean fouled TDR TLI units inherently cause time delays and ship-wide disruptions affecting other planned work. . 
 
 The Navy seeks a product that cleans and potentially reverses the fouling buildup throughout the entire TDR assembly while being compatible with the existing sensor architecture. The technology must return the installed TDR and TLI technique to full operational status upon one execution of the developed technology/technique over an objective period of 36 months, but not less than a threshold period of 8 months of full TDR TLI operability. This effort is required to develop a comprehensive technique that resolves this persistent reliability challenge. A more precise fuel management and reduction in potential failures will result in greater ship stability and increased mission readiness.
 Develop a concept for a product/technology to clean a fouled TDR TLI in-situ, returning it to full operational status within the challenging environment of a compensated fuel tank. Detail how the cleaning technology would be employed on an in-service ship while underway. Establish feasibility through small-scale testing, analysis, or modeling. If the Phase I Option is exercised, include the initial design specifications and capabilities description to build a prototype solution in a Phase II plan.
objective: Develop a technology to clean and potentially reverse fouling on Time Domain Reflectometer (TDR) Tank Level Indicating (TLI) components in-place. The solution must function within fully compensated fuel tanks aboard DDG 51 class ships without requiring depressurization, defueling, or dewatering.

title: Fire Resistant Joiner Bulkhead
text:
Develop a material/system to increase the fire-resistance of joiner bulkheads on ships and compartment-level fire containment while meeting Navy requirements for weight, fit, cost, fire, smoke and toxicity.
 Fire represents a grave hazard to Navy vessels. Recent fire events have propagated through joiner bulkheads and resulted in significant fire damage, which poses a substantial threat to personnel and equipment. Uncontrolled fires can propagate throughout a ship and cause extensive damage to machinery, equipment, and ship compartments; additionally, fires represent an extreme risk to ship personnel. The Navy has made numerous improvements to make ships more fire-resistant but is seeking improvement for containment of compartment-level fire events seen in recent and historical ship fires (i.e., USS OSCAR AUSTIN, USS CONYNGHAM, USS STARK, and the cruise ship Star Princess). More fire-resistant joiner bulkheads would allow damage control teams to contain and extinguish fires more easily before they could grow to threaten the ship. Innovation is needed to meet Navy goals with regard to weight, cost, fit, and performance.
 
 The Navy seeks an improved fire-resistant joiner bulkhead that would reduce the damage ships sustain during fires, as well as improve safety for the crew. 
 
 Development of a fire-resistant joiner bulkhead faces several technical challenges. First, any fire-resistant joiner bulkhead must not have a significant weight increase. Given the quantity of joiner bulkheads onboard ships, any weight increase could add significant weight to the ships, which will impair and degrade ship performance. Second, the improved joiner bulkheads must not excessively exceed the width of current joiner bulkheads. Destroyers have confined spaces and for the comfort and operational capability of the crew, any new joiner bulkhead cannot greatly exceed the dimensions of the existing panels. Third, any fire-resistant joiner bulkhead must be a cost-effective solution for the Navy. In particular, the fire-resistant joiner bulkhead must not substantially increase the costs to install at the shipyard. The reason for this concern is that joiner bulkheads sometimes require modification at the shipyards to fit the exact dimensions of the ship. Any solution that requires expensive edge treating or would otherwise be cost-prohibitive to modify at the shipyards will not be considered. Lastly, the improved joiner bulkhead must meet or exceed the requirements to be certified for shock and fire performance as AN-30 class per MIL-STD-3020 and pass Navy Fire, Smoke, Toxicity (FST) testing per MIL-STD-1623. This is a vital requirement to demonstrate that any new material in the joiner bulkhead will not release dangerous particulates as it burns or fails if there is an impact.
 
 Research into fire-resistant materials has revealed several technology advances in the areas of intumescent coatings, coatings that incorporate nanomaterials to aid in thermal regulation, or advanced high-performance fibers; however, there is no current commercial solution available. The Navy is also open to bio-composites, bio-polymers, or other materials that have the potential to provide superior fire-resistance with reduced toxicity as compared to many commercially available products.
 Develop a concept for a fire-resistant joiner bulkhead that meets the requirements above. Demonstrate the feasibility of the concept in meeting the Navy needs prescribed above and establish that the concept can be developed into a useful product for the Navy. Establish feasibility of a new fire-resistant material/system via small-scale testing. If the Phase I Option is exercised, include the initial design specifications and a capabilities description to build a prototype solution in Phase II.
objective: Develop a material/system to increase the fire-resistance of joiner bulkheads on ships and compartment-level fire containment while meeting Navy requirements for weight, fit, cost, fire, smoke and toxicity.

title: Input-Output Unit (IOU) for Secure Processing and Routing of Hull, Mechanical, & Electrical (HM&E) and Navigation Signals
text:
Develop a dust-protected, water splash-resistant Input-Output Unit (IOU) capable of interfacing with legacy and modern equipment to send, receive, process, and route signals throughout the hull and superstructure of naval vessels.
 IOUs are used on all Navy DDG 51 class ships to transfer Steering Control, Machinery Control, and Damage Control signals, as well as Interior Communication Alarm and Indication, Synchro and Digital Navigation data. They are also used on USN LHA(R) class ships, in Aegis Ashore facilities, and across a variety of Foreign Military Sales (FMS) cases. IOUs serve as a translation point when sending and receiving non-Ethernet traffic, such as synchro and low-level serial data, to Ethernet user systems. 
 
 IOUs are installed in a variety of air-conditioned and non-air-conditioned spaces. Their use in engineering spaces that historically have relied on Halon 1301 (safe for sensitive electronics) for fire suppression has been complicated by the Navy's transition away from Halon and toward water mist protection systems. Additionally, existing IOUs rely on the integration of a wide variety of circuit card assemblies (CCA) to process different types of signals, creating hardware challenges for lifetime support and technology refresh. 
 
 The Navy seeks to reduce lifecycle costs with a simplified design that has fewer hardware dependencies, hardware component updates, and more open and modular system architectures. 
 
 The IOU is intended to be operated continuously. The IOU shall be designed to permit routine maintenance and troubleshooting. Repair actions should be possible while the IOU is energized without loss of required functionality and operating. Reliability and Survivability are essential and all IOU components must demonstrate Mean Time Between Failures (MTBF) in excess of 10,000 hours. While the IOU as a whole product does not exist commercially, the base technology required is available in industry. The focus of this SBIR topic is to integrate the capabilities into a synergized product.
 
 Requirements:
 The Navy requires a dust-protected, water splash-resistant (IEC 60529 IP54-rated) IOU capable of interfacing with legacy and future equipment to send, receive, process, and route signals throughout the hull and superstructure of naval vessels. The enclosure must protect the power supply, cooling components, and electronics necessary to connect serial (RS-232, RS-422, RS-485, NTDS-E), fiber Ethernet, Cat 5 Ethernet (unicast, multicast), analog synchro (60 and 400 Hertz), and analog voltage (AC and DC) capabilities. External connections are made by triaxial, 42-pin, and 92-pin cables, as well as fiber optic connectors to redundant Gigabit Ethernet (GbE) shipboard networks. 
 
 Design must accommodate an additional fifty percent capacity for future growth from initial defined design specifications and capability descriptions. It must also provide adequate internal cooling while meeting or exceeding IP54 dust and spray requirements.
 
 All hardware components must be compliant with Restriction of Hazardous Substances (RoHS) directive 2011/65/EU.
 
 Enclosure:
 Maximum size and weight (excludes external mounting dimensions): 
 Weight: 188 pounds; Depth: 17 inches; Width: 26 inches; Height: 27 inches.
 
 The IOU must be mountable from the rear or the bottom and allow cable attachment/removal and reasonable access to all user interfaces and cable attachment points in any mounted configuration.
 
 Power Supply:
 Internal Alternating Current (AC) power supply will connect to two independent 120V, 60Hz shipboard lighting circuits (2 of 3 phases) for redundancy. Synchro reference power (400Hz and 60Hz) is necessary for some user interfaces (separate from IOU AC power). IOUs should require less than 600 Watts of power when fully loaded. 
 
 IOU must strictly comply with MIL-STD-1399-300, operating reliably on both Type I and Type II power. The design must tolerate all specified voltage and frequency fluctuations, withstand severe voltage spikes, and limit maximum instantaneous input current (inrush current) when initially energized. To maintain ship-wide power quality and ensure system compatibility, the IOU must also adhere to strict limits on harmonic distortion, maintain a high-power factor, and meet the electromagnetic interference (EMI) and electromagnetic compatibility (EMC) requirements of MIL-STD-461. To ensure the IOU design is suitable for shipboard environments, the IOU must meet the requirements of the latest revisions of MIL-STD-810 (currently Rev H with Change Notice 1), MIL-DTL-901 (currently Rev E), MIL-STD-167 (currently Rev 1A with Validation Notice 1), and MIL-HDBK-2164 (currently Rev A), 
 
 IOU must remain fully operational through momentary power interruptions from the selected power source. If all AC power is lost, the IOU will automatically restart within 30 seconds following restoration of at least one power source. Adequate cooling must be maintained in any power-on condition. 
 
 User Interfaces, Routing, Processing:
 IOU must adhere to a defined set of core networking standards. The unit must ensure full compliance with the foundational protocols for internetworking, including IPv4 (RFC 791) and IPv6 (RFC 8200). To support efficient one-to-many data distribution, the IOU must implement IP Multicasting (RFC 1112). For high-availability and fault tolerance, the IOU must also support the Parallel Redundancy Protocol (PRP) in accordance with IEC 62439-3.
 
 Fiber optic cables connecting the IOU to shipboard networks will be supplied by the shipbuilders and will utilize a four-fiber cable per MIL-PRF-85045/18 with a fiber cable class of single mode per MIL-PRF-49291/7. 
 
 Reliance on legacy hardware and proprietary data currently limits the Navy's ability to use open competition. Updating the design to include commercially available components will eliminate these constraints and significantly reduce lifecycle costs.

title: TRIAGE-X: Autonomous Casualty Triage and Treatment in Chemically Contaminated Mass Casualty Events
text:
Develop and demonstrate capability with autonomous medical triage systems to recognize chemical toxidromes and physically deliver the corresponding antidote or life-saving intervention.
 DARPA seeks innovative approaches to autonomous chemical, biological, radioactive, and nuclear (CBRN) triage that measurably improve casualty survival and increase the effective capacity of a medical response during CBRN disasters. Early situational awareness and timely treatment is a matter of life and death in battlefield and disaster medical triage. Responder vulnerability in hazardous environments caused by CBRN attacks adds significant difficulty to the medical response. When a mass casualty incident (MCI) occurs within a chemically contaminated area, the medical response is hindered by uncertainty while the threat is assessed and characterized. To ensure safety of the responders, they must don protective equipment before entry, delaying initial assessment, triage, and treatment with life-saving interventions (LSIs). Personal protective equipment (PPE) also imposes a physiological and functional penalty on responders resulting in slower movement, higher energy expenditure, heat stress, impaired respiration, and reduced manual dexterity; these penalties further impede responders' ability to perform life-saving interventions. Effective stabilization occurs in the cold zone after casualties have been decontaminated [1,2], compounding the delay to evacuation and definitive care. The DARPA Triage Challenge (DTC) has demonstrated that autonomous air and ground systems, using standoff sensors, can locate casualties, characterize injury patterns, and support triage prioritization in realistic MCI conditions [3]. Using DTC triage support capabilities as a starting point, this solicitation aims to extend capabilities to operating in chemically hazardous environments where injury patterns have distinct signatures or toxidromes. Success here extends proven autonomous triage into the one of the most challenging settings where human entry is dangerous and delayed, and where early antidote delivery most directly determines casualty survival [4].Proposed systems should be able to locate and assess casualties for traumatic injuries and chemical toxidromes, generate triage recommendations, and deliver appropriate initial treatments to reverse, stabilize, or prevent the toxic effects of chemicals. Solutions should be designed for realistic operational use in difficult terrain under challenging environmental conditions. DARPA does not prescribe a specific platform, sensor suite, or level of autonomy. Offerors are encouraged to propose the human-machine teaming arrangement that best improves decision quality and casualty outcomes, and to define how their system fails safely when conditions exceed its competence. Approaches should be realistic in scope, repurposed within the period of performance, and grounded in how CBRN mass casualty response actually unfolds.At minimum, the effort shall deliver a demonstrated prototype that detects at least two representative chemical toxidromes and applies appropriate initial treatments for the assessed toxidrome following human-in-the-loop treatment approval.
 Phase I work is expected to have been completed before award. Proposers must submit evidence that their existing prototype can:• Autonomously find and localize casualties and report their location to within 2m• Assess trauma patterns and assign a trauma triage category• Perform accurate standoff vital-signs assessment, including at minimum heart rate and respiratory rate • Operate at scale o At least 20 casualties in a single scenario o Perform assessment in <90 seconds for each casualtyo Survey a 30,000sqft area without battery change• Operate across diverse, realistic environments: indoor and outdoor, daytime and nighttime, ideally (but not required) in adverse weather conditions (rain, smoke)• Produce a human-interpretable output through a graphical interface that conveys casualty locations and priorities of care.• System must be portable. All components should be easily transported by a vehicle or drone.Capability demonstration:A written technical description or published report supported by data and video(s) demonstrating the prototype performing the capabilities above in the stated environments are required (provided via link).
objective: Develop and demonstrate capability with autonomous medical triage systems to recognize chemical toxidromes and physically deliver the corresponding antidote or life-saving intervention.

title: Counter-Unmanned Aerial Systems Rapid Maturation
text:
Mature commercial and dual-use technologies that detect, track, identify, or defeat small low-flying drones (Group 1 and Group 2 unmanned aerial systems) in hostile or contested areas.
 Inexpensive, highly maneuverable, commercially available unmanned aerial systems (UAS) threaten tactical forces, critical infrastructure, and installations. Current defenses are limited by cost, by the operator attention they require, and by their vulnerability to countermeasures. A capability gap against Group 1 and Group 2 UAS remains.
 
 This topic seeks mature or maturing technology at any point in the counter-UAS kill chain. The three areas below are where capability is most needed. They are examples. A proposal may address one area, more than one, or a gap not listed here.
 
 Detection and Tracking. Detect and hold track on highly agile targets in cluttered low-altitude airspace. The proposer selects the sensing modality. Approaches that hold track when the target is not emitting are preferred. Solutions that require permanent site infrastructure or mains power, including fixed perimeter sensor installations, are out of scope for this area. The system must move with the force.
 
 Identification and Decision Support. Classify and identify unauthorized platforms and support an engagement decision. Processing must run on tactical computing hardware carried or emplaced with the force. Proposals should describe a pathway to interoperate with existing command and control. Conformance to a named standard is not required at this stage and will not be scored.
 
 Mitigation and Defeat. Kinetic, non-kinetic, or cyber approaches that defeat hostile UAS in remote tactical theaters and in densely populated areas. Proposals must address collateral effects.
 Operating preferences. The operating environment is denied, contested, and unattended. The four conditions below are preferences, not eligibility requirements. 
 
 Every proposal must state where it stands against each one.
 (a) The system does not require the target to emit radio frequency (RF) energy. Passive RF may be part of a solution; the preference is that track holds when the target is silent.
 (b) The system does not radiate. The Government favors kinetic and cyber defeat over approaches that require the friendly system to emit. Jamming, active illumination, and transmission into a target's control or navigation link are in scope. A proposal that uses any of them must say so and describe the operational effect.
 (c) The system does not require cloud services or reachback. Training and analytics may occur off-platform. The processing that produces the operational output should run on the platform, and the system should continue to function with all external network interfaces disabled.
 (d) The system does not require a dedicated operator, meaning no person whose only task is attending it. Human judgment over the use of force is expected and is not addressed by this preference.
 
 Out of scope: work requiring classified access or a facility clearance at the time of award, and approaches that depend on cooperative identification, including Remote ID broadcast.
 This topic solicits Direct-to-Phase-II (DP2) proposals only. Direct to Phase II proposers shall submit documentation showing that Phase I-equivalent feasibility has already been achieved outside the SBIR/STTR program. Adequate documentation is a written record of at least one test of the proposed approach stating the conditions under which the test was conducted, the dates, the target, threat, or surrogate used, the measured result, and how it was measured.Test data, technical reports, and third-party evaluation metrics are acceptable. A system design alone is not sufficient. A self-declared technology readiness level unsupported by a documented test is not sufficient.
 As required by the DoW solicitation, the feasibility documented may not rest solely upon, or logically extend from, prior or ongoing federally funded SBIR or STTR work; the proposing firm and/or the principal investigator must have substantially performed the work relied upon; and the firm must demonstrate ownership or licensure of the associated intellectual property prior to proposal submission.
objective: Mature commercial and dual-use technologies that detect, track, identify, or defeat small low-flying drones (Group 1 and Group 2 unmanned aerial systems) in hostile or contested areas.
