Work may include developing a concept architecture, modeling critical software components, or bench testing key hardware elements. Phase I deliverables are a feasibility study, a technical report, and an initial system design package showing the path to a prototype.
  
 The technical report shall state the conditions, dates, and target or threat surrogate used in any testing performed, and the measured result. It shall also state where the approach stands against each of the four operating preferences.
objective: Mature commercial and dual-use technologies that detect, track, identify, or defeat small low-flying drones (Group 1 and Group 2 unmanned aerial systems) in hostile or contested areas.

title: xTech|Kinetic Reach Competition
text:
The U.S. Army is seeking innovative force sustainment solutions from eligible small businesses across the U.S. through the xTech Kinetic Reach competition. This platform offers participants the opportunity to engage with the Department of War (DoW), earn prize money and submit a Direct to Phase II Army Small Business Innovation Research (SBIR) proposal. 
 
 The U.S. Army FUZE xTech Program, in partnership with the U.S. Army Europe and Africa (USAREUR-AF) and Global Tactical Edge Acquisition Directorate (G-TEAD) is executing the xTech|Kinetic Reach competition as part of the G-TEAD Accelerated Capability Event (ACE) series. xTech|Kinetic Reach addresses the growing uncrewed aerial system (UAS) threat by identifying high-potential solutions and accelerating transition through funding and integration into live USAREUR-AF-led exercises. Integrating into a USAREUR-AF-led exercise is critical to: (1) validate capabilities under operationally realistic conditions, (2) inform acquisition and integration decisions, and (3) address near-term gaps in autonomous ground operations and effects delivery in contested environments. 
 
 The Army recognizes that the DoW must enhance engagements with U.S. small businesses by (1) understanding the spectrum of world-class technologies being developed commercially that may benefit the DoW; (2) integrating the sector of non-traditional innovators into the DoW Science and Technology (S&T) ecosystem; and (3) providing expertise and feedback to accelerate, mature, and transition technologies of interest to the DoW. 
 xTech|Kinetic Reach is a focused open-topic competition designed to identify cutting-edge technology solutions that will drive significant advancements in military capabilities while addressing complex challenges and enhancing national security. In largescale combat operations, U.S. Army forces must sustain dispersed, continuously moving formations while operating inside highly contested environments characterized by persistent observation, long range fires, electromagnetic interference, degraded mobility corridors, and severely constrained logistics. Current sustainment and recovery methods rely heavily on manned systems that are increasingly vulnerable, slow to adapt, and unable to meet the demands of operations conducted near or within the Autonomous Zone. The Army requires a suite of interoperable, autonomous or minimally manned capabilities - spanning ground and air distribution, power generation, forward arming and refueling, and vehicle recovery - that can operate with minimal oversight, low signatures, reduced logistical burden, and seamless command and control (C2) integration. These capabilities must sustain tempo, reduce soldier exposure, and ensure survivability and mission continuity across the entire sustainment and recovery enterprise in high-threat, GPS and communications degraded environments where traditional methods are no longer feasible or survivable. 
 
 The Army is seeking to evaluate capabilities that demonstrate performance in one of six (6) capability areas, and meet the following criteria for its capability area: 
 
 Topic 1: Uncrewed Ground Payload Transportation 
 
 Topic 2: Autonomous container Handling/Movement System 
 
 Topic 3: Future Power Generation 
 
 Topic 4: Autonomous UAV/UGV Forward Arming and Refueling Point (FARP) System 
 
 Topic 5: Uncrewed Aerial Payload Transportation 
 
 Topic 6: Uncrewed, Automated, Ground Recovery System 
 
 Full competition details including details on these 6 topic areas of interest can be found in Appendix A section of the xTech|Kinetic Reach competition RFI here: https://www.xtech.army.mil/competitions/.

title: Ground-Based Affordable Mass (G-BAM)
text:
The United States currently faces an "unprecedented" military buildup by China and increasing air and missile threats that demand a robust deterrent. However, the current inventory of long-range strike weapons is dominated by high-cost, low-volume systems or aging strategic assets like the Minuteman III, which dates back to the 1960s. The lack of a cost-effective, ground-launched payload delivery system prevents the Joint Force from achieving producibility at scale, leaving the U.S. vulnerable in high-intensity, multi-domain environments where high-end munitions would be rapidly depleted. The objective of this topic is to facilitate innovative research on low-cost, rapidly manufacturable, payload delivery systems.
 The Department of War (DoW) is pivotally shifting toward "affordable mass" to counter peer adversaries who are rapidly expanding their military capabilities. While hypersonic systems offer high speeds, their exorbitant costs—exceeding $50 million per round—limit the military's ability to achieve the "magazine depth" necessary for prolonged conflict. This project proposes a ground-based, non-hypersonic, long-range precision payload delivery system that leverages low-cost production methods and commercial technologies to provide a scalable, high-volume alternative that is a tenth of the price of current high-end munitions. NOTE: The following topic number, ARM26BX04-DV011 - Ground-Based Affordable Mass (G-BAM), in this release is tied to a Defense Innovation Unit (DIU) Challenge Commercial Solutions Openings. The DIU G-BAM Challenge will be used to identify small business concerns that meet the criteria for a potential SBIR Direct-to-Phase II (DP2) award under this topic. Winners selected from the DIU G-BAM Challenge will be the only firms eligible to submit an SBIR DP2 proposal under this topic. Proposals submitted to this topic by non-winners of the DIU G-BAM Challenge will not be evaluated.
  
 How to Apply: Visit the DIU Open Solicitations page to read the full Challenge Announcement, topic details, and application instructions here:
  
  
 https://www.diu.mil/work-with-us/open-solicitations
 This topic is accepting Direct to Phase II submissions for a cost limit up to $2,000,000 and an 18-24-month period of performance.

title: Low - Cost Neuromorphic Edge Intelligence for Persistent Autonomous Change Detection and Machine Situational Memory
text:
Develop, integrate, and demonstrate a low-SWaP-C neuromorphic IR sensor to support celestial navigation to enable position and navigation of sUAS in a Global Navigation Satellite Systems (GNSS) denied environment in day and nighttime for world-wide operations. The desired system should allow an autonomous aircraft to establish a persistent machine representation of an area, recognize operationally meaningful changes, and communicate primarily what changed rather than continuously transmitting full-motion imagery or raw sensor data.
 Traditional airborne ISR architectures frequently collect and transmit large quantities of data even when little or nothing within the observed environment has changed. This creates substantial burdens on: Communications bandwidth. Processing. Storage. Power. Analysts. Command-and-control systems. Neuromorphic and event-driven sensors offer a fundamentally different sensing architecture in which the system responds primarily to changes within the observed environment.
 The desired capability should combine event-driven sensing with onboard edge intelligence and temporal machine memory. Fundamental engineering considerations include: Event-driven/neuromorphic sensor characterization. Low-latency onboard processing. Low power consumption. Detection of operationally relevant changes. Rejection of irrelevant changes caused by lighting, weather, vegetation, shadows, sensor motion, or environmental clutter. Temporal comparison across repeated observations. Persistent representation of previous environmental state. Confidence scoring for detected changes. Autonomous prioritization of significant changes. Ability to cue additional onboard sensors. Generation of compact change products instead of continuous raw-data transmission. Multi-UAS sharing of relevant environmental changes. Open interfaces for integration with aircraft mission systems. Desired change classes may include movement, addition, removal, modification, displacement, construction, damage, altered activity patterns, or other Government-defined changes.
 As this is a Direct-to-Phase II (D2P2) topic, no Phase I awards will be made. To qualify, applicant(s) must provide Feasibility Documentation demonstrating prior completion of Phase I-equivalent efforts outside SBIR funding. Offerors should demonstrate feasibility through existing neuromorphic sensing, event-driven vision, edge AI, machine perception, autonomous change detection, or related capabilities.
 Relevant evidence includes:
 Prototype sensors. Hardware demonstrations. Airborne testing. Edge-processing demonstrations. Power/SWaP measurements. Change-detection performance. False-alarm characterization. Relevant commercial deployments.
 Preferred maturity is TRL 5-6, although compelling TRL 4 technologies may be considered when the underlying sensor and processing architecture has been demonstrated and can reach operational relevance within approximately three years.

title: High-Efficiency Expeditionary Group 2 and Group 3 VTOL UAS for Long-Range Distributed ISR/SOF Operations
text:
Develop, mature, integrate, and flight-demonstrate technologies enabling an autonomous, runway-independent Group 2/3 VTOL UAS capable of persistent ISR/SOF operations, extended-duration flight, modular payload employment, resilient beyond-line-of-sight communications, and integration into distributed mission architectures.
 Runway independence provides substantial operational flexibility for ISR/SOF missions but creates significant technical penalties in aircraft weight, propulsion complexity, energy consumption, endurance, payload, reliability, and cost. The research challenge is to minimize these penalties while enabling a persistent, expeditionary autonomous aircraft capable of operating from austere and distributed locations. The Government seeks emerging VTOL technologies combining reliable vertical operations with efficient forward flight, extended endurance, useful payload capacity, resilient communications, and autonomous mission execution. Solutions may employ tilt-wing, tilt-rotor, lift-plus-cruise, tailsitter, distributed propulsion, hybrid propulsion, or other technically viable architectures. Companies should specifically highlight demonstrated capabilities, current maturity, projected performance, and remaining technical risks in the following areas:
 VTOL Endurance: Capability to achieve 12-15 hours of flight time is critical. Offerors should identify payload, speed, altitude, loiter profile, environmental assumptions, and propulsion configuration associated with demonstrated or projected endurance. Propulsion: Gas-powered propulsion is of particular interest for meeting extended sortie-duration requirements. Fully electric, hybrid-electric, or alternative propulsion solutions are acceptable if they can meet the required sortie duration and mission-performance objectives. In-Flight Recharge: Technologies enabling in-flight energy replenishment or recharge are of interest, including architectures supporting a six B.A. battery configuration, where applicable. Payload: Adjustable and modular payload capacity with a minimum desired capability greater than 60 pounds while maintaining an 12-15-hour loiter/endurance profile. Offerors should additionally characterize performance and design tradeoffs associated with payload growth toward 75 pounds. 
 Network Node / Layered Effects / Force Packaging: Ability to operate as an airborne network node and participate in distributed, layered effects and multi-platform force packages. BLOS: Resilient beyond-line-of-sight communications and autonomous mission execution without reliance upon continuous line-of-sight C2. Vigilant Spirit: Existing integration, interoperability, or a clearly defined integration pathway with Vigilant Spirit. Dynamic Targeting: Ability to receive mission updates and dynamically retask, revisit/retest areas or objects of interest, reassess previous observations or effects, and conduct authorized subsequent mission actions. NKE / ESM: Ability to host, support, and employ modular non-kinetic effects and Electronic Support Measures payloads. Extended Autonomy: Architecture capable of supporting autonomous missions approaching 15 hours, including reliable operation for representative periods of at least 5 minutes without human intervention. Companies should characterize autonomy reliability, intervention rate, failure modes, contingency behavior, recovery, and lost-link performance. VTOL Efficiency Demonstrate autonomous vertical takeoff and recovery. Quantify hover and VTOL fuel/energy consumption. Demonstrate efficient transition between vertical and forward flight. Quantify VTOL energy penalty relative to total mission energy. Range and Endurance Demonstrate or substantiate a credible path to8 hours of flight endurance with representative payload. Characterize mission radius, maximum range, endurance, and loiter time. Quantify payload/range/endurance trade space. Characterize forward-flight propulsion efficiency. Identify fuel or energy requirements associated with representative ISR/SOF mission profiles. For fully electric systems, demonstrate the ability to achieve required sortie duration. Where proposed, characterize in-flight recharge or energy replenishment. Payload and Mission Systems Support an adjustable/modular payload of at least 25 pounds at the desired 8-hour profile. Characterize growth potential toward60 pounds. Characterize payload mass, volume, power, data, thermal, RF, and mechanical interfaces. Support Government or third-party payload integration. Support NKE and ESM payloads. Support airborne network-node functionality. Provide documented interfaces supporting integration with Vigilant Spirit and other Government mission systems. Expeditionary Operations
 Minimize launch/recovery footprint. Minimize personnel and ground-support equipment. Minimize arrival-to-launch and recovery-to-relaunch timelines. Minimize assembly, disassembly, maintenance, and site-preparation requirements. Support distributed ISR/SOF employment from austere locations. Autonomy and Dynamic Mission Execution Autonomous takeoff and landing. Autonomous transition. Autonomous navigation, loiter, mission execution, return, and precision recovery. Dynamic inflight mission retasking. Support dynamic targeting and authorized retest/revisit and reattack/re-engagement sequences. Deterministic contingency and lost-link behavior. Architecture capable of missions approaching12 hours of autonomous operation. Demonstrate representative mission periods of at least5 minutes without human intervention. Characterize autonomy reliability, intervention frequency, mission-completion rate, fault tolerance, failure modes, and recovery behavior. Resilient Communications and Operations
 Maintain useful navigation and mission capability during GNSS degradation or loss. Support BLOS communications and mission operations. Maintain autonomous mission capability during intermittent, degraded, or lost C2. Demonstrate deterministic lost-link behavior. Sup
objective: Develop, mature, integrate, and flight-demonstrate technologies enabling an autonomous, runway-independent Group 2/3 VTOL UAS capable of persistent ISR/SOF operations, extended-duration flight, modular payload employment, resilient beyond-line-of-sight communications, and integration into distributed mission architectures.

title: Collaborative Autonomous UAS for Distributed Non-Kinetic Effects
text:
Develop, integrate, and demonstrate modular technologies enabling Group 2/3 UAS or similarly expendable autonomous aircraft to collaboratively generate distributed non-kinetic mission effects in contested environments.
 The objective is to enable multiple low-cost autonomous platforms to coordinate sensing, positioning, task allocation, timing, communications, and payload employment to produce useful mission-level effects without requiring continuous human control or persistent high-bandwidth communications.
 The desired architecture should employ a human-on-the-loop approach, allowing autonomous systems to conduct distributed mission execution while retaining oversight, positive control, and the ability for human operators to intervene when required.
 The Government is particularly interested in technologies that distribute mission capability across multiple affordable aircraft rather than concentrating sensing, processing, communications, or effects on a single exquisite platform.
 Traditional non-kinetic capabilities can be constrained by platform availability, cost, survivability, operator workload, communications requirements, and centralized mission architectures.
 Distributed autonomous UAS create the opportunity to separate the mission effect from a single exquisite platform and distribute sensing, decision-making, communications, and payload employment across multiple lower-cost aircraft.
 The Government seeks modular technologies enabling Group 2/3 UAS and similarly expendable autonomous aircraft to collaboratively carry and employ Government-approved non-kinetic payloads while operating under a human-on-the-loop command architecture.
 Potential mission functions may include lawful and authorized:
 Electronic support. Communications relay. Spectrum sensing. Deception and decoy functions. Distributed RF effects. Cooperative sensing. Network extension. Authorized cyber-physical mission effects. Signature generation. Mission-support effects. Other non-destructive effects.
 This topic is focused on enabling technologies, payload integration, distributed autonomy, mission coordination, and command-and-control architecture, not development of offensive cyber capabilities.
 Fundamental engineering considerations include:
 Modular Mission Systems
 Modular payload integration. Open mechanical, electrical, power, data, RF, and software interfaces. Integration of Government or third-party payloads without fundamental aircraft redesign. Support for multiple payload types and aircraft architectures. Low-SWaP-C implementation suitable for expendable UAS.
 Collaborative Autonomy
 Autonomous task allocation. Collaborative mission planning and execution. Distributed decision-making. Dynamic reassignment of tasks following aircraft or payload loss. Cooperative sensing and information sharing. Graceful degradation as individual aircraft become unavailable. Quantifiable collaborative mission performance.
 Human-on-the-Loop Control
 Human-on-the-loop mission command and authorization. Positive control over initiation and termination of mission effects. Operator ability to modify objectives, constraints, or mission priorities. Deterministic responses to loss of communications. Abort and safe-state functionality. Appropriate human authorization for mission functions requiring Government approval.
 Communications and Distributed Operations
 Operation with intermittent, degraded, or unavailable communications. Distributed decision-making without persistent centralized control. Low-bandwidth coordination methods. Time and spatial synchronization. Network extension and relay capability. Resilient interfaces with Government mission and C2 systems.
 Mission Assurance
 Geographical, temporal, frequency, target-set, or mission-based constraints as applicable. Prevention of unintended or unauthorized effects. Defined operating boundaries. Fault detection and graceful degradation. Quantifiable reliability and mission-effect performance.
 As this is a Direct-to-Phase II (D2P2) topic, no Phase I awards will be made. To qualify, applicant(s) must provide Feasibility Documentation demonstrating prior completion of Phase I-equivalent efforts outside SBIR funding. Offerors should possess existing technology applicable to autonomous UAS, collaborative autonomy, spectrum operations, modular payloads, resilient communications, electronic support, distributed mission systems, human-machine teaming, or related capabilities.
 Phase I-equivalent evidence may include:
 Hardware demonstrations. Flight demonstrations. Collaborative autonomy testing. Multi-aircraft demonstrations. Modular payload integration. Electronic support or spectrum-sensing demonstrations. Communications relay or network-extension demonstrations. Distributed task-allocation demonstrations. Human-on-the-loop mission-control demonstrations. Degraded-communications testing. Hardware-in-the-loop or system-level testing. Relevant modeling supported by physical test data. Operational experimentation.
 Offerors should identify:
 Number and type of aircraft previously demonstrated collaboratively. Level and duration of autonomous operation. Human intervention requirements. Communications architecture and bandwidth requirements. Behavior during communications degradation or loss. Payload interfaces. Supported non-kinetic mission functions. Current aircraft and payload SWaP-C. Collaborative autonomy reliability. Current TRL and remaining technical risks.
 Preferred entry maturity is TRL 5-6, with TRL 4 considered where the core technology has been demonstrated and can credibly mature within approximately three years.

title: Long-Range, Expendable Autonomous Air Vehicle for Distributed Effects in Contested Environments
text:
Develop, integrate, flight-test, and demonstrate an affordable, expendable autonomous air "One-Way Attack" (OWA) vehicle capable of delivering a mission-relevant payload over operational ranges of 400 nautical miles threshold to 1,200 nautical miles at varying ranges in between while operating in communications-degraded and GNSS-degraded or denied environments.
 Future contested operations may require the ability to generate large numbers of distributed airborne effects at ranges beyond those achievable by many existing Group 2/3 UAS.
 The desired system should combine sufficient aerodynamic efficiency, propulsion performance, autonomous mission execution, modular payload integration, resilient navigation, and low-cost manufacturing to enable operations at ranges between approximately 400 and 1,200 NM.
 Solutions should emphasize a modular vehicle architecture allowing Government or third-party payloads, autonomy, navigation, and communications components to be integrated without redesigning the entire aircraft.
 Range and Mission Performance
 ≥400 NM threshold to 1,200 NM with demonstrable varying ranges under a clearly defined mission profile. Document payload/range/endurance trade space. Characterize representative payload, launch conditions, altitude, speed, propulsion configuration, and mission profile. Demonstrate sufficient aerodynamic and propulsion efficiency to achieve long-range operation at acceptable recurring cost.
 Autonomous Mission Execution
 Autonomous launch and transition to mission flight. Autonomous navigation and mission execution. Autonomous terminal mission functions appropriate to the proposed concept. Continued mission execution during intermittent or extended loss of command-and-control connectivity. Deterministic and configurable lost-link behavior. Mission-planning interfaces that minimize operator workload. Architecture capable of incorporating Government-provided autonomy.
 Resilient Navigation
 Maintain useful navigation during representative GNSS degradation, denial, interference, or loss. Characterize navigation performance, accumulated error, availability, and recovery. Support integration of complementary navigation sources. Collaborative navigation approaches are of interest where sufficiently mature for Phase II integration and flight demonstration. Navigation technologies should be mature enough to support the overall D2P2 schedule; maturation of 5-6 TRL fundamental navigation concepts is not the primary intent of this effort.
 Modular Mission Architecture
 Modular mechanical, electrical, power, data, and software interfaces. Integration of Government or third-party payloads without fundamental air-vehicle redesign. Architecture capable of accepting Government-provided autonomy, navigation, communications, and payload components. Document Government-accessible interfaces necessary for transition.
 Propulsion
 Characterize propulsion performance. Quantify fuel/energy consumption across representative mission profiles. Identify propulsion reliability and remaining maturation risks. Characterize range, payload, and propulsion trade space.
 Environmental and Structural Performance
 Demonstrate environmental and structural suitability for representative operational employment. Characterize launch loads, flight loads, environmental limitations, and relevant storage/transport constraints.
 Affordability and Scalable Manufacturing
 Treat recurring unit cost as a primary system-level design consideration. Identify major unit-cost drivers. Demonstrate production-relevant manufacturing approaches. Reduce dependence on scarce materials, specialized tooling, and labor-intensive production where technically feasible. Quantify production scalability, lead time, labor content, and supply-chain risks. Consider rapid, distributed, or high-rate manufacturing approaches.
 The Government is interested in existing technologies requiring integration and maturation, not clean-sheet conceptual aircraft requiring extended basic research.
 As this is a Direct-to-Phase II (D2P2) topic, no Phase I awards will be made. To qualify, applicant(s) must provide Feasibility Documentation demonstrating prior completion of Phase I-equivalent efforts outside SBIR funding. Offerors should demonstrate Phase I-equivalent prior work establishing that the underlying air vehicle and critical subsystems are technically viable. Relevant evidence may include:
 Existing aircraft or representative flight testing.
 Long-range flight performance.
 Propulsion testing.
 Aerodynamic analysis supported by test data.
 Autonomous flight demonstrations.
 Resilient-navigation testing.
 Collaborative-navigation demonstrations, where proposed.
 Payload integration.
 Structural and environmental testing.
 Manufacturing demonstrations.
 Hardware-in-the-loop or system-level testing.
 
 Offerors should provide available measured data characterizing:
 Current maximum demonstrated range.
 Payload associated with demonstrated range.
 Propulsion efficiency and fuel/energy consumption.
 Aircraft aerodynamic performance.
 Autonomous mission capability.
 Performance under degraded or unavailable GNSS.
 Lost-link and degraded-C2 behavior.
 Payload interfaces.
 Current recurring-cost estimate and principal cost drivers.
 Manufacturing maturity and achievable production rate.
objective: Develop, integrate, flight-test, and demonstrate an affordable, expendable autonomous air "One-Way Attack" (OWA) vehicle capable of delivering a mission-relevant payload over operational ranges of 400 nautical miles threshold to 1,200 nautical miles at varying ranges in between while operating in communications-degraded and GNSS-degraded or denied environments.

title: Rapidly Reconfigurable Pod-Based System Survivability Suite for Air Operations in Contested Environments
text:
Investigate, design, prototype, and experimentally evaluate advanced open-architecture methodologies and reconfigurable subsystem integration concepts within an external modular pod construct (threshold baseline: Air Force Research Laboratory [AFRL] Agile Pod). The primary R&D objective is to explore novel approaches for abstracting platform-to-payload interdependencies, solving multi-physics obscuration and thermal/electromagnetic boundary problems, and demonstrating dynamic, autonomous self-protection threat-warning, correlation, and countermeasure techniques via distributed edge compute without requiring host-platform system recertification.
 Modern multi-domain operational environments present increasingly agile, multi-spectral threat emitters spanning radio frequency (RF), infrared (IR), and electro-optical (EO) regimes. Conventional aircraft survivability equipment (ASE) suffers from hardwired, federated implementations, tightly coupled mechanical and electrical host dependencies, and high-latency upgrade cycles. Overcoming these barriers requires foundational research into containerized, hardware-agnostic modular payloads, high-efficiency edge processing architectures, and adaptive aperture configurations that can operate autonomously while remaining fully interoperable with joint command-and-control networks.
 This topic solicits applied research and experimental development into an externally carried, modular open-system survivability architecture. While leveraging mature sensing and countermeasure components where appropriate, the primary technical investigation focuses on heterogeneous compute abstraction and advanced processing architectures. This entails researching novel architectural patterns that abstract diverse federated signal processing, countermeasure arbitration, threat correlation, and cross-platform networking into a unified, modular, software-defined compute environment. Key research activities include evaluating containerization paradigms, real-time deterministic virtualization, and Open Mission Systems / Universal Command and Control Interface (OMS/UCI) standard execution under strict size, weight, power, and thermal (SWaP-C) limitations.
 Simultaneously, the effort must resolve multi-physics boundary constraints and sensor obscuration challenges. This requires developing high-fidelity analytical, computational fluid dynamic (CFD), and electro-optical/electromagnetic models to characterize and mitigate aircraft-induced obscuration and aero-optical distortion across diverse carriage regimes. Research will further focus on distributed aperture hand-off algorithms and multi-pod sensor correlation to synthesize complete, gapless spherical coverage (steradian field-of-regard) across heterogeneous, dynamic flight profiles.
 Finally, the investigation addresses dynamic interoperability and low-latency autonomous response mechanisms. Investigation is needed into machine-to-machine autonomy algorithms capable of conducting real-time threat detection, localized track clustering, and immediate self-protection countermeasure dispense and pointing without operator-in-the-loop dependencies, while concurrently synthesizing threat telemetry for dissemination across communications links. Underpinning this entire capability is the design of open, non-proprietary physical and logical interface syntax aligned with Modular Open Systems Approach (MOSA) guidelines to enable zero-rework substitution of future experimental payloads.
 As this is a Direct-to-Phase II (D2P2) topic, no Phase I awards will be made. To qualify, applicant(s) must provide Feasibility Documentation demonstrating prior completion of Phase I-equivalent efforts outside SBIR funding. Evidence must include: Architectural Trade Studies & Modeling (comparative performance models evaluating physical, thermal, and electrical integration of multi-spectral survivability components inside modular pod form factors), Algorithm & Interface Simulation (preliminary software simulations validating hardware abstraction layers, synthetic threat correlation pipelines, and OMS/UCI-compliant data schemas), Aero-Optical and Sensor Obscuration Analysis (ray-tracing, installed field-of-regard modeling, and host aircraft interaction analyses proving the conceptual viability of 360-degree coverage via single or distributed pod arrangements), and Bench-Scale Experimental Data (measured bench-test, hardware-in-the-loop (HWIL), or prototype range test results verifying core detection, processing latency, and countermeasure control feasibility).

title: Multi-Function Processor, Rapid Architecture, Miniaturized (MFP-RAM)
text:
Develop and flight-demonstrate a standards-compliant, rapidly reconfigurable hybrid communications system using a SOSA Small Form Factor Line Replaceable Unit capable of supporting multiple waveforms, frequency bands, and Multi-Level Security.
 Tactical communications systems must operate in RF-dense and contested environments while adapting to changing mission requirements. Current tightly coupled, proprietary, single-purpose hardware limits rapid technology insertion and the coexistence of multiple security domains. The Government seeks a COTS-first, modular, reconfigurable hybrid communications Line Replaceable Unit that integrates multi-band Software Defined Radios, modular open-system interfaces, secure RED/BLACK separation, and a containerized software environment. The capability must support integration into representative air platforms while reducing host-aircraft modification burden and enabling future waveform or payload changes with minimal redesign. Proposals must address the remaining system-level research and development required to integrate, validate, qualify, and flight-demonstrate the hybrid communications capability. Proposals do not have to result in a production-ready capability, but must be sufficient to facilitate a minimum viable product (MVP) which can be used in a surrogate flight demonstration. 
 As this is a Direct-to-Phase-II (D2P2) topic, no Phase I awards will be made. Applicants must demonstrate readiness for Phase II through prior Phase I-type efforts. Required evidence shall include validated data, prototype performance metrics, subsystem-integration results, and evidence of compliance with applicable SOSA standards. Applicants must demonstrate successful multi-band waveform operation, modularity, and secure RED/BLACK separation. The submitted evidence must identify the remaining system-level architecture, integration, qualification, validation, and flight-demonstration work proposed for Phase II.
objective: Develop and flight-demonstrate a standards-compliant, rapidly reconfigurable hybrid communications system using a SOSA Small Form Factor Line Replaceable Unit capable of supporting multiple waveforms, frequency bands, and Multi-Level Security.

title: Mobile Expeditionary 3D Concrete Printer (MX3DCP)
text:
Mature and validate expeditionary 3D concrete printing technologies, materials, and geometries so military personnel can rapidly construct combat-relevant, blast-resistant force-protection structures at contested airbases. 
 Problem: The U.S. Air Force faces an urgent and growing gap in its ability to rapidly harden, repair, and reconstitute expeditionary airbase infrastructure during combat operations. Recent attacks against airbase infrastructure in the Middle East have reinforced a reality already evident in planning for the Indo-Pacific and other contested theaters: U.S. forces must be able to operate from bases that are vulnerable to missiles, rockets, artillery, one-way unmanned aircraft, and fragmentation-producing weapons. Current expeditionary infrastructure is often too slow to construct, too logistics-intensive to transport, or too lightly protected to provide meaningful survivability under modern attack conditions. Put bluntly, the Air Force has spent decades building exquisite kill chains while too often housing the Airmen who sustain them in tents, trailers, and flat-walled structures that were never designed for the threat environment now arriving overhead.
 Opportunity: 3D concrete printing offers a potential step-change in expeditionary construction by enabling military engineers to rapidly print protective structures using automated or semi-automated construction workflows, reduced skilled labor, and locally available cementitious materials where feasible. Prior work has demonstrated that cementitious materials can be printed, that full-scale structures can be produced with mobile 3DCP systems, and that limited blast testing can be performed on printed wall assemblies. However, the existing state of the art has not yet fully addressed the combined problem that matters most for combat survivability: printable expeditionary materials, field-executable operator workflows, and structure geometry deliberately optimized to mitigate blast-wave behavior and fragmentation effects.
 This Direct-to-Phase II effort will improve the current DoD technological state by integrating three related areas of technical development: advanced cementitious materials suitable for expeditionary printing; mobile, field-operable 3D concrete printing systems and workflows; and printable protective geometries designed to mitigate blast and fragmentation effects. First, the project will evaluate advanced cementitious materials, including Air Force Civil Engineer Center-developed materials and other candidate mixes, for printability, strength gain, curing behavior, environmental tolerance, pumpability, layer adhesion, and compatibility with native or in situ material sourcing. Second, the effort will develop and evaluate novel printable geometries that improve survivability beyond conventional flat-wall construction, including shapes intended to reduce blast reflection, limit pressure amplification, interrupt fragmentation paths, and improve internal occupant protection. Third, the project will validate these material and geometry combinations through representative printing, structural evaluation, and controlled blast/fragmentation testing.
 The initial technology readiness level is estimated at TRL 5, with discrete material, printer, and structure demonstrations approaching TRL 6. The current manufacturing readiness level is estimated at MRL 4 to 5, because the underlying processes exist but require maturation for repeatable production in austere conditions by lightly trained military personnel. The target at the end of Phase II is TRL 6 to 7 and MRL 5 to 6, supported by relevant-environment demonstrations, printed test articles, validated print parameters, documented material performance, and blast-response data suitable for transition planning.
 The required Phase II effort will include material screening and characterization; evaluation of locally sourced or partially substituted cementitious feedstocks; printability testing under relevant environmental conditions; development of candidate protective geometries; computational modeling of blast interaction and fragmentation exposure; printing of representative components and structure sections; controlled structural, blast, and fragmentation testing; operator workflow development; logistics and deployment analysis; and documentation of design rules, print parameters, safety considerations, and transition recommendations.
 Minimum deliverables will include a material characterization report; a printability and expeditionary logistics assessment; a geometry design and modeling report; representative printed test articles; blast and fragmentation test results; validated print parameters for selected material/geometry combinations; operator-ready draft technical procedures; and a final transition package identifying recommended use cases, limitations, equipment requirements, training requirements, and follow-on test needs.
 The desired outcome is a validated technical foundation for rapidly printed protective infrastructure that can be employed by Air Force civil engineers in expeditionary and combat environments. A successful effort will not replace all conventional construction, but it may give commanders a faster and more survivable option when the choice is currently between slow construction, vulnerable temporary shelters, or telling Airmen to make do with whatever was shipped before the shooting started.

title: Wide Pass Bandwidth, High Selectivity, Continuously Tunable Notch Filters
text:
Wideband receivers used in electronic warfare (EW), signals intelligence (SigInt), and electronic support measures (ESM) need to instantaneously capture broad swaths of spectrum to avoid missing frequency agile radio frequency (RF) signals. Wideband receivers, however, lack the dynamic range to capture wide bandwidths of spectrum containing both large interferers and weak signals of interest. Thus, multiple receivers are needed in these applications which results in large size and power consumption. 
 The objective of this topic is to develop miniature, low power, and high selectivity tunable notch filters capable of protecting wideband receivers from large interferers. The effort will target the largest interferers which are in L, S, C, and X bands with tunable notch filters, while allowing pass bandwidths spanning L through Ku bands. Each notch filter must be continuously tunable across a minimum of 3 of the 4 targeted bands (L, S, C, and X) while having a notch depth > 20 dB and a notch bandwidth < 1 % across all tuned frequencies. With a narrow notch bandwidth, each notch filter must be programmable and maintained with an accuracy of 50% of the notch bandwidth and should maintain this accuracy over temperature. The notch filters must be able to reject large interfering signals and therefore should be able to notch receive interference levels greater than 5 dBm. In the bandpass each filter must cover L-Ku band (1-18 GHz) while maintaining a low insertion loss and noise figure of less than 1.5 dB and low passband distortion with an IIP3 > +50 dBm. Each notch filter must be small, less than 3 cc, and should be connectable in series without interfering with one another to notch multiple frequencies in the same receive chain. Finally, the power consumption, including any tuning electronics, of each notch filter should be less than 100 mW. The required metrics are: 
 Passband frequency range (GHz)1 - 18
 Maximum passband insertion loss or noise figure (dB) ≤ 1.5
 Passband IIP3 (dBm)≥ 50
 Notch band tunable frequency range (GHz)1 - 12
 Number of bands covered by a single, continuously tunable notch≥ 3
 Minimum notch depth across all tuned notch states (dB)≥ 20
 Maximum notch fractional bandwidth (%)≤ 1Size (cc)≤ 3
 Power consumption (mW)≤ 100
 This topic is intended for a technology proven ready to move directly into a Phase II program. A Phase I SBIR award will not be made. The offeror is required to provide details and documentation in the Direct to Phase II (D2P2) proposal which demonstrates accomplishments of a "Phase I-like" effort, including demonstrating the expertise needed to design and fabricate miniature, high selectivity tunable notch filters. The offeror should have demonstrated, in a laboratory environment (TRL3), a notch filter achieving a 20dB deep notch with a bandwidth less than 5% of the tuned frequency, a continuous tuning range of at least 3:1, and a passband insertion loss below 3 dB across a wide frequency range. Demonstration of zero static power tuning and a filter volume of approximately 1 cc is desired. The offeror should have demonstrated the capability of maintaining low passband distortion and high notch depth across all tuned states. The proposal should illustrate past success at the aforementioned performance levels with tunable notch filter technologies fitting the above descriptions

Wideband receivers, however, lack the dynamic range to capture wide bandwidths of spectrum containing both large interferers and weak signals of interest. Thus, multiple receivers are needed in these applications which results in large size and power consumption.

title: Domestic Liquid Phase Epitaxy of Yttrium Iron Garnet Films for Resilient Microwave Filter Supply Chains
text:
The United States Air Force relies on yttrium iron garnet (YIG)-based microwave filters for critical radar, electronic warfare, and communications systems. These components require high-quality YIG epitaxial films in the 10-150 µm thickness range grown by liquid phase epitaxy (LPE). Domestic production capability for LPE-grown YIG films does not currently exist, and the entirety of this supply chain depends on foreign sources — representing a significant vulnerability to Air Force readiness, modernization programs, and long-term system sustainment.
 This topics seeks proposals to design, procure, and commission a fully domestic LPE growth facility capable of producing device-grade YIG films on gadolinium gallium garnet (GGG) substrates across the 10-150 µm thickness range. Efforts shall demonstrate system integration, process optimization, and material qualification sufficient for insertion into operational microwave filter architectures. Required technical performance thresholds include film thickness uniformity of ±5% across 1-inch wafers, surface roughness below 5 nm RMS, and saturation magnetization (4πMs) values within ±50 Gauss of specification. Offerors shall employ a systematic process characterization approach — such as design-of-experiments (DOE) methodology — to establish repeatable, production-ready growth processes governing flux composition, growth temperature, rotation rate, and cooling profile.Proposed solutions shall include a structured material qualification program incorporating X-ray diffraction (XRD), profilometry, vibrating sample magnetometry (VSM), and FMR spectroscopy. Qualified films shall be suitable for delivery to government-designated filter manufacturers and laboratories for device-level insertion and performance verification.Successful Phase II performance shall result in a domestic LPE production capability with documented process controls, material qualification data packages, and a clear transition roadmap to Phase III commercialization and direct supply to DoW prime contractors. This topic directly supports the AFRL strategic priority of eliminating foreign single-source dependencies for critical electronic materials and establishing a sovereign U.S. industrial base for high-performance garnet magnetic films.
 This topic is intended for a technology proven ready to move directly into a Phase II program. A Phase I SBIR award will not be made. The offeror is required to provide details and documentation in the Direct to Phase II (D2P2) proposal which demonstrates accomplishments of a 'Phase I-like' effort, including demonstrating the expertise needed to grow, characterize, and qualify device-grade magnetic garnet epitaxial films. The offeror should have demonstrated experience with liquid phase epitaxy (LPE) or a comparable epitaxial growth method for yttrium iron garnet (YIG) or related magnetic garnet films on gadolinium gallium garnet (GGG) substrates, and should be able to show prior films characterized for crystalline quality, thickness, surface roughness, saturation magnetization, and ferromagnetic resonance (FMR) linewidth. Demonstration of prior films approaching device-grade quality - low FMR linewidth, good thickness uniformity, and low surface roughness - is desired, as is evidence of a systematic process characterization approach (such as design-of-experiments methodology) governing flux composition, growth temperature, rotation rate, and cooling profile. The offeror should also demonstrate an understanding of the material qualification tools required for device insertion, including X-ray diffraction (XRD), profilometry, vibrating sample magnetometry (VSM), and FMR spectroscopy. The proposal should illustrate past success at the aforementioned activities with magnetic garnet or comparable single-crystal oxide film technologies fitting the above descriptions, sufficient to substantiate that the small business is positioned to design, commission, and operate a domestic LPE production capability without a preceding Phase I effort.

These components require high-quality YIG epitaxial films in the 10-150 µm thickness range grown by liquid phase epitaxy (LPE). Domestic production capability for LPE-grown YIG films does not currently exist, and the entirety of this supply chain depends on foreign sources — representing a significant vulnerability to Air Force readiness, modernization programs, and long-term system sustainment.

title: Quantum Sensing Analyzer
text:
Investigate and validate the feasibility of developing a novel quantum-based sensing technology utilizing Rydberg atomic sensors as an ultra-wideband universal measurement standard for electromagnetic systems. Demonstrate the potential of these sensors in a calibrated and highly sensitive universal measurement standard to enhance radar, electronic warfare, and antenna characterization.
 The "Quantum Sensing Analyzer" project aims to address critical limitations in existing electromagnetic measurement technologies by developing a novel quantum-based sensing capability utilizing Rydberg atomic sensors. These sensors, leveraging quantum properties, exhibit extraordinary sensitivity and accuracy over a widespread frequency spectrum ranging from DC to 1 THz, with potential scalability to even broader ranges. This initiative is designed to modernize and standardize test and evaluation processes within the Department of Defense (DoD), particularly benefiting the Benefield Anechoic Facility (BAF) and its mission to support advanced electromagnetic system testing.
 Problem Statement and Opportunity:
 Current electromagnetic measurement techniques rely on diverse and complex instruments, which introduce inefficiencies, inconsistencies, and increased costs for the acquisition, testing, and integration of modern radar systems, electronic warfare platforms, communication systems, and antennas. These existing systems also face challenges in maintaining accuracy and repeatability, particularly when evaluating performance across a wide range of radio frequencies or within controlled environments like anechoic chambers.
 The introduction of Rydberg sensor technology represents a disruptive opportunity to establish a universal, high-precision, SI-traceable standard for electromagnetic measurements. By adopting a single, compact, and adaptable sensor for diverse measurement tasks—including spectrum analysis, field strength monitoring, and chamber characterization—this capability promises to significantly reduce infrastructure requirements, simplify operational workflows, and enhance confidence in test data accuracy.
 Project Objectives:
 ● Develop and validate a proof-of-concept Rydberg-based quantum sensing system capable of performing highly accurate and repeatable electromagnetic measurements across 1.5 MHz to 40 GHz.
 ● Demonstrate the ability of the sensor to serve as a universal measurement standard for radar, electronic warfare, communication systems, and antenna evaluation.
 ● Establish enhanced chamber characterization capabilities, including electromagnetic leakage detection, direction finding, near-field measurement, reflection mitigation, and quiet zone mapping, to improve the testing environment quality.
 ● Progress the technology readiness level (TRL) from TRL 2 at project initiation to TRL 6 by the conclusion of Phase II.
 Required Efforts and Phase Activities:
 Phase I:
 ● Perform a comprehensive feasibility study to assess the applicability of Rydberg atomic sensors as a universal electromagnetic measurement standard.
 ● Evaluate the sensors' technical attributes, including sensitivity (targeting sub-microvolt/meter thresholds), dynamic range, and bandwidth.
 ● Identify potential integration challenges with existing test facilities and systems, particularly those used in the BAF.
 ● Deliverables: Feasibility study report detailing technical analyses, identified challenges, and potential solutions; preliminary system design for a prototype quantum sensing analyzer.
 Phase II:
 ● Develop, fabricate, and demonstrate a functional prototype of the Rydberg-based quantum sensing system, incorporating key findings from Phase I.
 ● Conduct extensive testing and validation of the prototype in operationally relevant environments, including the BAF, with emphasis on precision, SI-traceability, and repeatability of electromagnetic measurements.
 ● Integrate the system into existing DoD testing workflows, showcasing improvements in efficiency, reduced equipment requirements, and testing performance.
 ● Deliverables: Fully operational prototype, detailed test and evaluation report, system integration plan, and transition strategy for scaling and deployment within the DoD.
 Desired Outcome:
 The successful development of a Quantum Sensing Analyzer will revolutionize the DoD's electromagnetic measurement and testing capabilities by delivering a single, universal, quantum-enabled sensing standard. This solution will eliminate the need for multiple specialized instruments, streamline developmental and operational testing, and significantly enhance test accuracy and repeatability. Furthermore, the technology will address critical modernization priorities, such as advancing quantum science and enabling operationally focused Advanced Battle Management Systems (ABMS). This effort aligns with the Air Force's strategic goals to improve mission readiness, accelerate technology deployment to the warfighter, and invest in cutting-edge testing capabilities that sustain innovation and technical superiority in defense systems.
 Phase I will assess the feasibility of Rydberg sensors for precise electromagnetic measurements (1.5 MHz-40 GHz). Goals include evaluating sensitivity, bandwidth, and range while addressing DoD test needs. Deliverables: technical feasibility analysis, preliminary design, and simulated performance data to validate the sensors' potential as a scalable, SI-traceable measurement standard for advanced defense applications.
objective: Investigate and validate the feasibility of developing a novel quantum-based sensing technology utilizing Rydberg atomic sensors as an ultra-wideband universal measurement standard for electromagnetic systems. Demonstrate the potential of these sensors in a calibrated and highly sensitive universal measurement standard to enhance radar, electronic warfare, and antenna characterization.

title: Solid Propellant Environmental Effects Digital Twin
text:
The objective of the proposed effort is twofold: 1) Model and simulate the combined effects of thermal, temporal, chemical, and geometric changes to solid propellants that occur over time for in rocket motor grains, and 2) integrate predictive behavior tools into solid rocket motor design tools for decision-quality models and simulations. The intended result is a solid propellant aging and environmental process digital twin.
 Solid Rocket Motors (SRMs) provide propulsion for many critical defense applications including surface launched, air launched, ballistic, and space vehicles. The propellant that creates acceleration through these SRMs is a complex active material that can be sensitive to environmental effects from thermal loads, exposure to air or humidity, chemical changes, pressure, or vibration loads due to time or ingredient changes. Both mechanical response characteristics and ballistic properties can be affected. This topic requests projects that will combine computational modeling and design capability from several sources to simulate aging responses due to environmental effects. The framework must follow Modular Open Systems Approach standards mandated in 10 U.S.C. § 4401 for compatibility with several commercially available computational tools such as ANSYS, ABAQUS, Python, MatLab, SysML, and others.
 Define a ballistic or structural degradation mechanism in solid propellent that can be implemented in a damage tolerant design process for solid rocket motors. Develop the technical argument for transitioning non-continuum mechanisms to a continuum-based analysis techniques. Develop a Digital Engineering plan to create the desired capability to model Solid Rocket Propellant and predict behavior over extended periods of time and environmental conditions.

The intended result is a solid propellant aging and environmental process digital twin.

title: Next-generation Green Monopropellant Gas Generation
text:
Develop a low-power, real-time precision liquid-to-gas phase-change feed system featuring active molecular feedback control to enable the seamless integration of liquid propellants (including next-generation green liquid propellants such as ASCENT and LMP-103S) with high-efficiency in-space plasma propulsion systems. While legacy propellants like hydrazine vaporize with relative ease, next-generation green propellants possess near-zero vapor pressures that streamline ground operations but make efficient vaporization and stable gas-phase molecular composition extremely difficult to control. Proposed solutions must actively monitor and modulate the vaporization process in real time to deliver precise molecular species fractions under tight power constraints, ultimately establishing a versatile, fuel-agnostic propellant conditioning capability to support dynamic space operations and emerging in-space refueling architectures.
 The USSF has a desire to use liquid monopropellants for high thrust propulsion (natively in chemical thrusters) and for low-thrust, very energetic missions (in electric propulsion thrusters) - so called Multimode Propulsion (MMP) capabilities - to support Dynamic Space Operations. Such MMP capabilities have a number of very favorable characteristics including high propellant density, reduced need for high pressure storage systems, continued need for chemical propulsion on DoW assets for high thrust prompt maneuver, and compatibility with future on-orbit liquid propellant refueling capabilities.
 
 One critical capability gap is an energy efficient, precision propellant feed system which efficiently converts next-generation liquid monopropellant into non-reactive vapor phase products which can be fed into the electric propulsion (EP) thruster. Key challenges arise from the fact that next-generation monopropellants have negligible vapor pressure and are extremely difficult to combust at low temperature and pressure. 
 
 The desired technology should present a solution for a feed system capable of supporting sub-kW to 100 kW class EP systems: 
 - Operation at minimum on ASCENT propellant (T) or on ASCENT and other monopropellant formulations (O)
 - Realtime telemetry, including mass flow rate, species composition, and temperature as inputs to the EP device 
 - Maintain consistently characterized molecular composition (T) and extremely stable molecular composition (O) of the output vapor and support both steady-state and pulsed operation at frequencies greater than 5 Hz
 - Minimal SWaP with particular focus on low power consumption
 - Incorporate fluid/vapor facing materials that can reliably withstand long-term exposure to green monopropellants and their breakdown products over the required lifespan. Potential issues also include condensation or freezing for long-duration propellant storage in ullage and plenums if these or similar components are used
 - Demonstrate rapid warmup/gas generation in less than 10 minutes (T) or on-demand (O)
 - Ensure lifetime design consideration for future multiple refueling opportunities
 
 This work directly supports the Contested Logistics Technologies (LOG) Critical Technology Area with respect to space mobility operations.

Offerors responding to this topic shall demonstrate "Phase I-type" technical feasibility through prior research, development, laboratory validation, commercial development, or operational demonstrations performed outside of the SBIR/STTR program. Phase I proposals will not be evaluated and will be rejected as nonresponsive. 
 For this D2P2 topic, the Government expects that the small business would have accomplished the following in a "Phase I-type" effort via some other means (e.g. IRAD, or other funded work). Proposal may provide example cases of this new capability on a specific application. The documentation provided must substantiate that the proposer has developed a preliminary understanding of the technology to be applied in their Phase II proposal to meet the objectives of this topic. Documentation should include all relevant information including, but not limited to, technical reports, test data, prototype designs/models, and performance goals/results.

title: B-52 Multi-Factor AI Performance Charts
text:
Develop and validate a capability that modernizes B-52 AI Performance Chart capability that automates approved performance calculations, supports disconnected EFB operations, and provides accurate, auditable outputs for aircrew decision-making. 
 The B-52 Stratofortress has been the backbone of the United States Air Force's long-range strategic bomber capability for more than six decades. Despite multiple upgrades to its avionics and mission systems, aircrews continue to rely on labor-intensive, manually interpreted paper Technical Order performance charts and multi-step worksheets to calculate critical operational calculations such as takeoff and landing distances, brake energy limits, crosswind restrictions, runway condition impacts, directional control limits, and degraded-performance scenarios. These manual processes are time-consuming, increase cognitive workload and introduce opportunities for human error, and require aircrews to make high-stakes decisions under challenging time constraints, often during dynamic operational scenarios. Continued reliance on manual processes reduces operational efficiency, increases crew workload, and can negatively impact decision-making, especially in contested or degraded environments. 
 
 The current state of the art within commercial aviation utilizes Electronic Flight Bag (EFB)-based performance planning tools capable of rapidly calculating aircraft performance using approved aircraft data and validated calculation methodologies. While these solutions demonstrate the feasibility of digital performance-planning capabilities, they do not incorporate B-52-specific TO data, military performance procedures, cybersecurity requirements, airworthiness considerations, or Department of the Air Force EFB integration requirements. As a result, a capability gap exists between current B-52 performance-planning processes and modern digital aviation decision-support systems. The proposed effort will begin at approximately TRL 3-4, leveraging prior Phase-I-like work including operational requirements analysis, commercial market research, chart digitization methodologies, deterministic algorithm concepts, and successful demonstrations of related technologies in both government and commercial aviation sectors. Commercial aviation performance applications, technical-order digitization technologies, and deterministic calculation engines have demonstrated feasibility and provide a strong foundation for this effort. The objective of the Phase II effort is to advance the capability to TRL 6 through development, validation, and operational demonstration of a prototype capability suitable for transition into the Air Force EFB ecosystem. The Government is particularly interested in approaches that leverage secure research infrastructure, advanced computing resources, AI-assisted data extraction capabilities, and development of government-owned intellectual property to accelerate chart digitization, data validation, and long-term sustainment. Additionally, the Government seeks to leverage existing federally funded research investments such as those within U.S. National Laboratories or other Federally Funded Research & Development Centers (FFRDCs) to the maximum extent possible. Leveraging existing investments around AI security, vulnerability assessments, red teaming, model assurance, secure deployment of advanced models, and evaluation of AI systems supporting national security missions will help accelerate technology maturation and transition. 
 
 To meet this goal, the Phase II D2P2 effort is expected to include the following activities: 
 
 Integration of the AI-driven solution for chart mining and digitization to extract data; Refinement of deterministic algorithms to calculate performance metrics (e.g., takeoff/landing distances, brake energy limits, crosswind tolerances) based on TO and other authoritative data sources. 
 Development of intuitive user interface and operational workflows that align with aircrew feedback and mission requirements, ensuring a transparent and user-friendly application. 
 Rigorous testing and validation of algorithm accuracy, decision-support reliability, and adherence to airworthiness and compliance standards, incorporating inputs from operational stakeholders and SMEs. 
 Coordination with USG relevant Program Offices and certification authorities to support EFB system accreditation, operational testing, and fielding - this would translate into the existing U.S. Government EFB system with offline capabilities to ensure reliable operation in contested, degraded, or denied environments. 
 Coordination with U.S. National Laboratories or FFRDCs already investing in similar capabilities to enable rapid technology advancement, alignment of development roadmaps towards broader national security priorities, and aid in the transition into operational systems. This STTR effort stands to vastly improve the DoW's technological state by eliminating the inefficiencies of current manual performance calculations and transitioning the B-52 platform into a new era of data-driven, AI-enhanced operations that rapidly generate transparent and auditable aircraft performance assessments using approved source data. The capability shall not generate unvalidated performance estimates, extrapolated values, or inferred outputs when required data are unavailable or outside approved limits. The resulting solution will enable faster, more reliable decision-making, directly enhancing safety and mission outcomes while reducing aircrew workload. Moreover, the offline functionality ensures the tool's efficacy in a range of operational environments, including denied, degraded, and contested settings. Minimum acceptable deliverables include:
 A prototype closed loop EFB-compatible software capability suitable for operational evaluation. Digitized and validated performance datasets derived from approved B-52 source material. Verified and validated calculation methodologies
objective: Develop and validate a capability that modernizes B-52 AI Performance Chart capability that automates approved performance calculations, supports disconnected EFB operations, and provides accurate, auditable outputs for aircrew decision-making.

title: RF Spectrum Operations Enhanced with Distributed AI-Assisted Sharing of Knowledge Sharing (RF-DASK)
text:
Develop a dynamic and scalable signal representation to describe complex waveforms in a compressed format for RF spectrum knowledge sharing between Electronic Support (ES) systems and control the deployment and operation of Electronic Countermeasures. The proposed solution should support distributed operation in a network along with perform emitter detection, classification and geolocation.
 Current ES systems are designed to detect enemy electronic signals by extracting Pulse Descriptor Words (PDWs) from these signals. Modern radar systems used by adversaries increasingly employ Artificial Intelligence (AI) and it is becoming increasingly difficult to identify, characterize, and represent their waveforms using PDWs alone. To deploy effective Electronic Countermeasures (ECM), there is a need to develop novel methods, including machine learning (ML) [1,2] to enable dynamic and scalable data representation and compression methods that represent complex waveforms, which can be efficiently shared with other nodes in the network. The main goal of this project is to develop advanced techniques for dynamic and scalable signal representation to describe complex waveforms in a compressed format for radio frequency (RF) spectrum knowledge sharing and support network level information dissemination for emitter detection, classification and geolocation representative of activity segmentation [3]. Operational size, weight and power (SWaP) constraints should be determined to implement the proposed algorithms on hardware platforms and the developed techniques should be evaluated and demonstrated with hardware-in-the-loop experiments in relevant spectrum environments.
 As this is a Direct-to-Phase II (D2P2) topic, no Phase I awards will be made. The offeror is required to provide detail and documentation in the Direct to Phase II proposal which demonstrates accomplishment of a "Phase I-like" effort, including a feasibility study. This includes determining, insofar as possible, the scientific and technical merit and feasibility of ideas appearing to have commercial potential. It must have validated the product-market fit between the proposed solution and a potential Air Force stakeholder. The offeror should have defined a clear, immediately actionable plan with the proposed solution and the AF customer. Relevant areas of demonstrated experience and success include high-fidelity M&S, solutions to complex RF problems using AI/ML, concept development, solution demonstration and product evaluation.
objective: Develop a dynamic and scalable signal representation to describe complex waveforms in a compressed format for RF spectrum knowledge sharing between Electronic Support (ES) systems and control the deployment and operation of Electronic Countermeasures. The proposed solution should support distributed operation in a network along with perform emitter detection, classification and geolocation.

title: Wideband Antenna for RF Photonics Modules
text:
Design, fabricate, and experimentally test a wideband antenna solution ready to be integrated with standard RF-photonics transceiver modules. The antenna module must satisfy two key requirements. First, they should be fully compatible with standard packaging assemblies of RF-photonic modules. Second, they must deliver stable and efficient performance across a broad frequency bandwidth. However, integrating antennas with RF-photonic modules presents a significant challenge due to the electrically small size of the antennas and the bandwidth limitations imposed by Chu's limit. To address this challenge, innovative antenna designs are required. These solutions may incorporate passive and/or nonlinear materials or elements to counteract the dispersive behavior of the antenna and enable broadband radiation while remaining suitable for integration with RF-photonic modules. The final design should ensure seamless integration of the RF-photonic and antenna modules, enabling them to work synergistically with minimized size, weight, power, and cost (SWaP-C).
 Given its inherent broadband capabilities, RF photonics is a promising technology for both civilian and military applications. It is employed in several platforms, including autonomous vehicles, UAVs, and mobile devices, to sense and navigate complex environments and detect and track mobile targets, among many other use-case scenarios. Current studies are establishing and advancing RF photonic technology for several applications. However, these advances, especially in the radio frequencies or lower millimeter-wave regime, are still based on bulky antenna solutions, preventing the realization of compact systems that can be easily accommodated in small platforms. Proposals are sought to provide innovative antenna solutions addressing the need for integration with commonly packaged RF photonic modules without impacting their operation bandwidth. The proposed efforts shall build upon the existing integration-friendly antenna solutions to develop a novel antenna technology amenable to integrating electrically small broadband RF-photonic modules. By the end of Phase I, a broadband antenna module compatible with RF-photonics should be numerically analyzed. Phase II should focus on a proof-of-concept experiment of the integrated broadband antenna module with a selected RF photonics system. Overall, this topic aims to advance RF photonics technology with integrated antennas to meet demanding requirements, such as large bandwidth, reduced size and weight, and low profile. Relevant metrics that the proposers should consider are an antenna solution fully compatible to be integrated with the standard packaging topologies of RF photonic modules, an antenna module with excellent performance in the high RF regime, and with a bandwidth beyond Chu's limit. 
 As this is a Direct-to-Phase II (D2P2) topic, no Phase I awards will be made. In the Phase I effort, a feasibility study and initial development of the proposed antenna solution will be carried out. This endeavor should involve the design of the antenna module. Comparison between the proposed and the simulation-backed-up performance metrics, including the level of integration and isolation, the operational bandwidth, return loss, and radiation efficiency, should be carried out. At the completion of this phase, a preliminary design of the antenna module, meeting the indicated metrics for the proof-of-concept experiment, will be demonstrated and reported.

title: DIRECT TO PHASE II: Frequency-Based Persistent Super Intelligence Tracking and Surveillance Capability
text:
Develop and demonstrate an super intelligence (SI)-driven signal processing framework that leverages high-dimensional spectral feature extraction, adaptive neural control loops, and secure human-machine teaming to detect, classify, and characterize covert and agile waveforms in complex electromagnetic environment.
 The Navy faces acute operational challenges in intercepting and characterizing covert, highly agile adversarial emissions across dense electromagnetic operational environments. Modern threat systems increasingly utilize Low Probability of Intercept and Low Probability of Detection (LPI/LPD) techniques—such as Direct-Sequence Spread Spectrum (DSSS), ultra-fast frequency hopping (UFLH), wideband Linear Frequency Modulation (LFM), Costas frequency coding, and polyphase pulse compression (e.g., Frank, P1-P4 codes)—deliberately depressing emission power densities below the thermal noise floor [Refs 1, 2]. Consequently, conventional Electronic Support Measures (ESM) and wideband radiometer/energy-detection receivers exhibit severe performance degradation, failing to detect stealth radar transmissions, covert datalinks, and distributed sensor relays. This visibility shortfall undermines the tactical sensor-to-shooter timelines foundational to Combined Joint All-Domain Command and Control (CJADC2) and Distributed Maritime Operations (DMO).
 
 To counter advanced stealth emitters, an AI-driven signal processing framework can draw upon several modular algorithmic pathways and candidate techniques, such as:
 
 Sub-Noise-Floor Cyclostationary Analysis: For instance, computing the spectral correlation density (SCD) or cyclic autocorrelation can expose covert signal periodicities (e.g., symbol rates, chipping sequences, and carrier modulation artifacts), isolating structured LPI/LPD waveforms from stationary thermal background noise and Gaussian interference [Refs 3, 4].
 
 Time-Frequency Deep Learning Architectures: As an example for intra-pulse modulation recognition, raw wideband In-phase/Quadrature (I/Q) samples can be transformed into high-resolution time-frequency representations—such as Wigner-Ville Distributions (WVD) or Continuous Wavelet Transforms (CWT)—and processed by deep convolutional or recurrent neural networks (CNN/RNN) to classify polyphase or frequency-coded pulses without requiring prior waveform templates [Refs 5, 6].
 
 Adaptive Multi-Channel De-interleaving: For high-density pulse environments, candidate approaches include reinforcement-learning-guided spectral search or adaptive filter banks to isolate agile hopping channels and separate co-channel, overlapping LPI signals across wide instantaneous bandwidths [Ref 7].
 
 Calibrated Operator Decision Metrics: To support tactical watchstanders, Bayesian neural networks or conformal prediction methods can be applied to generate uncertainty bounds alongside extracted parameters (e.g., pulse repetition intervals, modulation bandwidths, chirp rates), providing validated, interpretable indicators of stealth emitter activity. 
 
 SWaP-Constrained Edge Optimization: Potential implementation paths for tactical platforms include neural network quantization, weight pruning, and tensor acceleration to facilitate low-latency inference on Size, Weight, and Power (SWaP)-constrained naval edge computing hardware.
