title: DIRECT TO PHASE II: Ultra-Low Latency Technology for Radio Applications 5G
text:
Develop ultra-low latency audio data obscuration techniques optimized for Internet Protocol (IP)-based communications over Fifth Generation (5G) frequency bands to enhance the resilience and operational effectiveness of Command and Control, Communications (C3).
 Modern C3 operations increasingly depend on commercial 5G and IP-based network infrastructures, which are vulnerable to latency, jitter, packet loss, and adversarial interference. As highlighted in recent industry consensus on how 5G technology is going to transform the Department of War (DoW) [Ref 2], in contested and congested environments, these challenges jeopardize mission-critical data flows, particularly time-sensitive audio communications essential for tactical decision-making. While the Multifunctional Information Distribution System (MIDS) Joint Tactical Radio System (JTRS) is the current standard for secure, jam-resistant tactical data links, it must be modernized to interoperate with these evolving network environments.
  
 To maintain a strategic advantage in alignment with the National Defense Strategy (NDS), the Department of Defense Private 5G Deployment Strategy [Ref 1], and Joint All-Domain Command and Control (JADC2) initiatives, the Navy seeks to design, develop, and prototype a software-only solution for ultra-low latency audio data obscuration. This technology must be tailored for IP-based communications operating across 5G and Open Radio Access Network (O-RAN) environments and be seamlessly integrable into existing MIDS JTRS platforms.
  
 These software-only innovations will strengthen C3 links in real-time operational scenarios, drawing technical parallels from critical commercial capabilities such as ultra-reliable low-latency 5G for industrial automation [Ref 3] to support high-precision activities including cooperative motion control, video-guided remote operations, and node-to-node tactical communications. By integrating these technologies into existing communication infrastructures, the DoW aims to ensure robust, secure, and resilient communication channels, even in congested spectrum environments or under adversarial jamming and electronic interference.
  
 The proposed solution should:
  
 Achieve Ultra-Low Latency Audio Transmission: Develop software-based obscuration methods capable of delivering secure, intelligible audio over IP-based 5G networks. The threshold goal is an end-to-end latency of under 20 milliseconds, with an objective goal of 1 millisecond to meet JADC2 and NDS real-time operational requirements.
  
 Enhance Resilience in Contested Environments: Ensure audio data integrity and communication continuity in environments affected by spectrum congestion, electromagnetic interference, or intentional jamming, using robust data hiding and spread-spectrum techniques. To satisfy PMO requirements, system resilience and audio intelligibility must be demonstrated and verified against the following representative operational profiles:
 1. Network Packet Loss Resilience: The software-based recovery and reconstruction algorithms must maintain communication continuity under severe channel degradation: Threshold Target: Maintain continuous link and zero audio stream dropouts under a continuous random packet loss profile of up to 10%. Objective Target: Maintain link alignment and intelligibility under burst/consecutive packet loss profiles of up to 30%. 2. Spectrum Congestion Performance: Under simulated high-traffic 5G slice congestion (congested multi-user IP environments): Threshold Target: End-to-end processing and transmission latency must remain under 20 milliseconds. Objective Target: End-to-end processing and transmission latency must remain under 1 millisecond. 3. Jamming and Interference Immunity: The spread-spectrum and data-hiding layers must resist intentional electromagnetic interference: Threshold Target: Maintain link stability and synchronization under narrow-band and barrage jamming up to a Jamming-to-Signal (J/S) ratio of 15 dB. Objective Target: Maintain link stability under dynamic tracking jamming up to a J/S ratio of 30 dB. 4. Audio Intelligibility Standards: Restored and unobscured audio streams must meet standard military voice intelligibility baselines: Threshold Target: Achieve a Perceptual Evaluation of Speech Quality (PESQ) score of 3.0 or higher (providing fully intelligible, clear voice communication). Objective Target: Achieve a PESQ score of 4.0 or higher (delivering excellent, high-fidelity voice reproduction).  
 Enable Scalable Integration with Existing DoW Systems: Design modular, software-defined solutions for seamless integration into platforms such as the MIDS JTRS SDR, supporting the modernization of tactical communication networks under the MIDS Program Office.
  
 Support Seamless Transition to Operational Systems: Ensure the final solution supports a seamless transition to operational systems, including full integration into the MIDS JTRS platform.

title: DIRECT TO PHASE II: Advanced Multi-User Signal Separation for Tactical Waveforms
text:
Develop and demonstrate a robust multi-user signal separation for tactical waveforms to improve the quality of likelihoods prior to being processed by soft-decision decoding algorithms.
 The Program Office championing this effort is PMW/A 101 that manages and delivers advanced, secure tactical communication systems for naval platforms. A core mandate of this office is to continuously integrate next-generation capabilities that enhance waveform resilience, increase spectral efficiency, and ensure robust connectivity for warfighters operating in highly congested and contested electromagnetic environments. The technology developed under this SBIR Direct to Phase II topic is intended to transition directly into the PMW 101 portfolio of tactical radio systems.
 
 In modern tactical networks, the proliferation of friendly assets creates a dense signal environment where simultaneous transmissions on the same frequency cause multi-user collisions and limit operational effectiveness. This problem is exacerbated in contested domains where very low Signal-to-Noise Ratios (SNRs) are common. Current baseline receiver systems typically treat these overlapping friendly signals as insurmountable noise. Because legacy systems lack the ability to untangle these collisions, they simply drop the packets or fail to decode them entirely, which severely limits network throughput and the real-time data exchange required for mission-critical operations.
 
 To overcome these limitations and maintain a critical operational advantage, this SBIR Direct to Phase II topic seeks the development of an advanced signal processing core capable of robust multi-user signal separation for tactical waveforms. By enabling non-orthogonal multiple access-like schemes, this capability will significantly increase network capacity and user count without requiring additional spectrum. 
 
 The goal is to deliver high-quality soft signal likelihoods recovered from simultaneous-user collisions to downstream soft-decision decoding algorithms. To achieve close-to-optimal performance in two-user collisions, proposed approaches must operate effectively at very low SNRs and mitigate intermittent interference by dynamically detecting burst collisions and nullifying compromised likelihood data. While advanced joint demodulation represents one viable pathway, proposers are highly encouraged to suggest any innovative framework that targets an approximate 3dB improvement over current baselines. The targeted improvement will be measured against the current baseline receiver under comparable two-user collision conditions and will reflect improvement in multi-user separation and downstream decoding performance rather than overall receiver sensitivity. This 3dB gain will translate directly to longer communication ranges, higher data rates, and increased resilience against jamming.
 
 This effort requires the performer to:
 
 Develop an advanced algorithm for multi-user separation that is effective in low SNR and interference-prone environments.
 
 Generate high-quality Log-Likelihood Ratios (LLRs) for modern soft-decision forward error correction (FEC) decoders, utilizing novel, proposer-defined technical approaches.
 
 Implement a mechanism to detect burst collisions and erase or correct corrupted likelihood data to prevent decoder failure.
 
 Design, implement, and test the algorithm within a modular Field Programmable Gate Array (FPGA) core based on open-systems principles.
 
 The successful transition of this capability will fundamentally improve the resilience of tactical networks. By delivering a modular FPGA core built on open-systems principles, the solution could be seamlessly integrated into a wide range of current and future Original Equipment Manufacturer (OEM) radio platforms, which could significantly reduce the life-cycle costs associated with developing entirely new systems to achieve these capabilities. This Direct to Phase II effort seeks proposers who can rapidly demonstrate these advanced receiver techniques with a clear transition path into operational military hardware.

title: DIRECT TO PHASE II: Modular Software Reference Implementation for Waveforms
text:
Develop and demonstrate a modular software reference implementation of a government-specified tactical waveform on a Digital Transceiver to establish an open architecture that leverages novel processing to transition from legacy Field-Programmable Gate Array (FPGA)-based systems.
 The Multifunctional Information Distribution System (MIDS) Program Office (PMA/PMW-101) is driving a critical architectural pivot in tactical data link (TDL) communications. Historically, the defense sector has relied heavily on FPGAs to host complex tactical waveforms due to strict RF timing constraints. However, as noted in recent software-defined radio (SDR) surveys, this hardware-centric approach suffers from severe developmental friction [Ref 1]. Programming FPGAs via Hardware Description Languages (HDL) requires lengthy synthesis, complex place-and-route cycles, and difficult timing closures. Because software compilation bypasses these physical routing and synthesis barriers, transitioning from HDL to high-order software languages (C/C++) on general-purpose architectures typically reduces development timelines by 50% to 80%—compressing multi-year hardware upgrade cycles into a matter of months.
  
 To overcome legacy constraints, this initiative mandates a transition toward a modular open systems architecture (MOSA). By decoupling the physical layer (PHY) from the underlying hardware, containerized Software-Defined Waveforms (SDWs) can be deployed across modern processing. Because standard Central Processing Units (CPUs) often lack the deterministic throughput required for heavy RF pipelines, modern SDR frameworks dynamically offload computationally intensive PHY tasks to coprocessors like GPUs, Neural Processing Units (NPUs), or adaptive System-on-Chips (SoCs).
  
 This heterogeneous approach enables the execution of highly parallel mathematical pipelines via software Application Programming Interfaces (APIs), including:
  
 Vectorized Signal Processing on GPUs or NPU cores:
 Executing Fast Fourier Transforms (FFTs) High-throughput Forward Error Correction (FEC) Matrix Multiplications  
 AI-Driven Cognitive Radio: As demonstrated by O'Shea and Hoydis [Ref 2], traditional heuristic PHY blocks can be replaced by "neural receivers" and deep learning autoencoders. By reusing embedded AI inference blocks, radios can perform real-time channel estimation, signal classification, and non-linear error correction at the tactical edge.
  
 By migrating to this software-first model, the Navy ensures rapid portability across joint-force platforms to provide highly scalable parallelism, allowing waveforms and AI-enhanced microservices to execute, reconfigure, and recover dynamically, ensuring maximum resiliency in contested electronic warfare environments.

Offerors must detail their practical experience in optimizing these waveforms for modern, heterogeneous compute environments—specifically multi-core CPUs, GPUs, and NPUs—and demonstrate scalability from enterprise server environments down to constrained tactical radio form factors.

title: Lightweight, Energy-Efficient Portable Nitrogen Generator for Expeditionary Operations
text:
Develop and demonstrate a man-portable, self-contained nitrogen generator capable of producing high-purity (equal to or less than 99.5%) nitrogen at 1,800 to 3,500 pounds per square inch (PSI), operating strictly within a 120-volt, 25-Amp single-phase electrical limit to support United States Marine Corps (USMC) expeditionary maintenance operations. While utilizing common enabling gas-separation technologies similar to topic N244-P02, this effort is strictly distinguished by its unique requirement for a highly modular, lightweight, two-man portable form factor engineered specifically for point-of-need operations in austere, forward-deployed environments.
 The United States Marine Corps (USMC) requires high-pressure nitrogen gas at forward operating locations to perform essential maintenance tasks, including aircraft and ground vehicle tire servicing, recoil mechanism servicing, recharging of gas suspension and accumulator components, and filling gas cylinders. Historically, the military relies on pre-filled, heavy steel gas cylinders resupplied through a vulnerable logistics chain. This process creates a severe logistical burden and hazardous material handling risk. Generating nitrogen at the point of need is essential to sustaining mission readiness in distributed, austere, and expeditionary environments consistent with USMC Force Design 2030 and Expeditionary Advanced Base Operations (EABO) concepts. The final product will be employed by USMC maintainers operating from forward tactical enclosures, specifically integrating with the JLTV Electronic Maintenance Shelter (JEMS). The system will provide point-of-need, high-purity nitrogen to service tactical vehicle and aircraft tires, hydraulic accumulators, recoil mechanisms, and suspension struts in support of distributed expeditionary operations.
 
 While the USMC currently utilizes a legacy portable nitrogen generation system, it presents severe technical limitations that hinder expeditionary operations. First, the legacy system weighs 450 pounds, severely limiting mobility and requiring a four-person lift. Second, it requires 240-volt single-phase electrical power drawing 25 Amps. This exceeds the standard 120-volt, 25-Amp electrical limits of forward tactical enclosures, such as the Joint Expeditionary Maintenance Shelter (JEMS). Third, the current system only achieves 99.0% nitrogen purity (falling short of the required 99.5% for sensitive aviation and vehicle struts) and suffers from extremely slow flow rates, taking up to 6 hours to fill a standard 244-cubic-foot cylinder.
 
 Commercial industry has introduced 120-volt single-phase configurations that achieve high purity. However, these state-of-the-art commercial units fall short of expeditionary physical requirements: they weigh in excess of 650 pounds, require separate external air compressors to operate, and maximize output at only 3,000 pounds per square inch (PSI). No known existing solution simultaneously achieves man-portable weight limits, 120-volt/25-Amp operation, self-contained air compression, high purity (Develop and demonstrate a man-portable, self-contained nitrogen generator capable of producing high-purity (equal to or less than 99.5%) nitrogen at 1,800 to 3,500 pounds per square inch (PSI), operating strictly within a 120-volt, 25-Amp single-phase electrical limit to support United States Marine Corps (USMC) expeditionary maintenance operations.
 
 This SBIR topic seeks innovative small business proposals to design, develop, demonstrate, and deliver a prototype device for a man-portable, energy-efficient, self-contained nitrogen generator that overcomes the stated limitations. Proposed approaches may include advanced membrane separation, pressure swing adsorption (PSA) with novel sorbent materials, hybrid separation architectures, lightweight composite enclosures, advanced electric motor/compressor technologies, intelligent power management, or other innovative approaches that meaningfully advance the state of the art. The prototype device must address extreme environmental challenges, specifically maintaining gas separation efficiency in high heat and high humidity, and must physically fit within tactical maintenance shelters.
 
 The prototype device shall target the following performance parameters to bound the scope of effort, while remaining open to innovative approaches that may refine specific parameters:

System can break down into modular components where no single module exceeds the two-person lift limits defined in MIL-STD-1472 (T); =/+ 150 lbs total. title: Integrated Multi-Spectral Periscope for the Amphibious Combat Vehicle (ACV)
text:
Develop and demonstrate a ruggedized, multi-spectral imaging, 360-degree-capable camera system capable of integration into Amphibious Combat Vehicle (ACV) periscopes.
 Current periscopic vision systems on Marine Corps combat vehicles are limited to daylight optical performance, over a limited Field of View (FoV), and lack the ability to integrate modern digital imaging, thermal, and night vision technologies. The new system shall provide daylight, low-light/night vision, and thermal (IR) imaging capabilities through a single, compact, and modular unit; and enhance situational awareness, target detection, and crew safety for Marines during water, transition, and land operating environments.
  
 This SBIR topic seeks to develop an integrated camera-based periscope module that:
 Provides visible (Electro-Optical [EO]), night vision (Near-Infrared Low-Level Laser (or Light) [NIR/LLL]), and long-wave infrared (LWIR) imaging in a compact unit. Is retrofit-compatible with existing periscope housings used in the USMC ACV FOV, or is capable of replacing optical viewports with an electronic display module. Includes onboard image fusion and low-latency video output for vehicle displays and augmented-reality systems. Meets ruggedization standards (MIL-STD-810H, MIL-STD-461D, and EC Standard 60529, rating IP66) for temperature, shock, vibration, EMI, dust and water resistance. Provides hardware resistance to seawater corrosion, as tested in accordance with GMW 14872, "Exterior, Exposure D" as stated in Table A3. Does not result in significant weight increase over that of the standard periscope. Supports integration with vehicle electronics architectures, including Vehicular Integration for C4ISR/EW Interoperability (VICTORY) and NATO STANAG 4609 standards.  
 Novel design approaches may include:
 Digital overlay in periscope eyepieces, merging optical and sensor imagery for seamless situational awareness. Edge processing and SI-assisted fusion of EO/NIR/LWIR feeds to highlight threats or movement. Wireless or wired integration with crew display systems such as: o Integrated Visual Augmentation System (IVAS)
 o Enhanced Night Vision Goggle - Binocular (ENVG-B)
 o Joint Mounted Display System (JMDS)

title: Distributed Multispectral Event-Driven Integrated Sensing and Communications
text:
Develop a distributed multispectral event-driven integrated sensing and communications capability that can timely provide robust detection of a wide range of objects and integrate into existing onboard sensors to expand operational battlespace.
 The Navy Aegis Program Office is interested in expanding battlespace awareness to support cross-domain operations through the integration of remote passive sensors. Currently, these sensors rely on real-time frame-based processing that generates large volumes of data, requiring significant processing power and energy and creating constraints for resource-limited hardware platforms with finite battery life, processing capabilities, and memory. In addition, transmitting large volumes of data over dynamic communication links can introduce delays and encounter bandwidth limitations that cannot meet time-critical operational needs. The complexity of the battlespace and electromagnetic environment further presents challenges for robust detection, classification, and identification. Advanced remote passive-sensor technologies that enable efficient and distributed sensing and processing will support multidomain operations by providing timely and resilient battlespace awareness. Successful technologies will be transitioned to the Aegis Combat System (ACS) to enhance distributed sensing, accelerate decision-making, and enable cross-domain operations.
 
 The Navy is seeking to develop Multispectral Integrated Neuromorphic Sensing and Communications (MINSC) technology to support endurant remote sensing capability. MINSC is an event-driven sensor featuring low-probability-of-intercept (LPI) data transmission that can timely identify a wide range of objects and transmit the information to remote platforms to integrate into the existing decision-making process. Neuromorphic computing can provide energy efficient, parallel processing, and low-latency framework for passive sensing, edge computing, and remote inference. 
 
 Neuromorphic sensors deliver high temporal resolution, asynchronous, energy and bandwidth efficient data inspired by biological vision. The Navy seeks to build an Event-Driven Energy-Efficient Ecosystem to support Endurant Long-Range Sensing and Communications capability. Solutions can be software, neuromorphic hardware, and/or end-to-end neuromorphic system that can deliver robust information and fuse with existing sensors to provide improved tracking, detection, classification, and identification. The Navy is open to innovative ideas of novel system design that can make decisions locally and communicate sparingly or timely send out the event-driven information for remote inference. The intended capability is an integrated remote passive-sensing capability that performs event-driven local sensing and processing, communicating only the information necessary to enhance remote awareness, and fuses with existing sensors to improve tracking, detection, classification and identification. 
 
 Distributed MINSC will provide advantages in dynamic environment and resilience to noise and debris associated with military applications. Incorporating event-based multispectral remote sensors with onboard sensors will expand operational battlespace, contribute to robust Common Operational Picture (COP) and enhance situational awareness. It will integrate with the Aegis and permit realistic testing of all threat types and configurations in a dynamic testing environment. Track visualization will be delivered through the existing ACS console Graphical User Interfaces (GUIs). The solution will support current operator track management and decision-making and integrate with the AEGIS Test Bed (ATB) to facilitate system evaluation against more advanced threats. The solution will provide an enhanced capability to address targets in all configurations and optimal engagement options to the sailors, which will increase mission capability and effectiveness against the latest threats.
 
 Work produced in Phase II may become classified. Demonstrate the feasibility in meeting the requirements in the Description to support the tests and operational environments. Establish feasibility through analysis and modeling. title: Low-cost Mid-wave Infrared Focal-Plane Array (FPA) Fabrication through Direct-bond Interconnection
text:
Develop a focal-plane array (FPA) fabrication process based on wafer-scale 3D-heterogeneous integration that enables a mid-wave infrared (MWIR) III-V detector epi-layer wafer to be directly bonded to a Silicon-based read-out integrated circuit (Si-ROIC) wafer, thereby eliminating the inefficient die-level Indium (In) bump-bonding process currently required to assemble Mid-wave Infrared (MWIR) FPA sensor chips.
 Electro-Optic and Infrared (EO/IR) sensors are used in a wide variety of applications, such as navigation, wide-area surveillance, and targeting. Operating in the visible and near-IR bands, EO sensors are available with small pixels and in large arrays at low cost, because the Si-detector wafer and Si-ROIC wafer can be 3D-integrated directly through wafer-to-wafer bonding with high yield at high volume based on material and complementary metal-oxide-semiconductor (CMOS)-process compatibility. By contrast, sensors operating in the MWIR employ III-V detector materials, which are not CMOS-process compatible, while III-V epi-layer detectors cannot be epitaxially grown directly on Si, as required to produce the crystalline order of high-quality detectors [Refs 1-2]. Instead, the III-V detector epi-layer is grown on a lattice-compatible substrate wafer, which is then flip-chip bonded to a Si-ROIC through a dense array of sub-pixel indium bumps placed on each wafer, followed by detector-substrate removal. The technically demanding process of depositing, aligning, and compressing the dense arrays of indium bumps on detector and ROIC die, results in a labor-intensive, inefficient, low-yield process for IR FPA fabrication, which greatly increases cost. 
 
 In recent years, 3D-heterogeneous integration has enabled a single integrated chip of greater overall functionality to be realized at reduced cost by assembling multiple smaller chips, each having unique functionality, material, node size, and/or foundry origin. Direct-bond interconnection (DBI) [Refs 3-5] is a 3D-heterogeneous integration technique that can potentially enable low-cost MWIR FPA fabrication. In principle, DBI should enable very large format FPAs with small pixels to be fabricated, as the process is largely independent of wafer and pixel size, in contrast to conventional bump-bonding. Moreover, the DBI process utilizes a temperature range that is compatible with MWIR IR detector materials. 
 
 The goal of this SBIR topic is to demonstrate the use of DBI or a similar process for fabrication of high-performance, large format, small-pixel, MWIR FPAs at low cost with the objective of refining the technique sufficiently to potentially replace conventional bump-bonding.
 Plan a detailed concept for a FPA fabrication and characterization process, including a risk assessment. While the pixel unit cell design is flexible, a pixel size of less than or equal to 10 micro-meters (um) and format of at least 2K x 2K are required, but otherwise any existing or commercially available Si-based ROIC can potentially be used for this effort. The III-V detector epi-layer spectral response must cover at least the MWIR band (3-5 um). The specific foundry and fabrication process steps will be determined in Phase I. Develop a detailed FPA characterization plan, including measurement of inter-wafer voids, pixel operability, and yield. Perform a per-FPA cost analysis that compares DBI or the selected alternative process to conventional bump-bonding and includes an assessment of the cost impact of process selection trade-offs.
objective: Develop a focal-plane array (FPA) fabrication process based on wafer-scale 3D-heterogeneous integration that enables a mid-wave infrared (MWIR) III-V detector epi-layer wafer to be directly bonded to a Silicon-based read-out integrated circuit (Si-ROIC) wafer, thereby eliminating the inefficient die-level Indium (In) bump-bonding process currently required to assemble Mid-wave Infrared (MWIR) FPA sensor chips.

title: Electro-Optical/Infrared Tactical Decision Aid
text:
Develop an Electro-Optical/Infrared (EO/IR) Tactical Decision Aid (TDA) for surface and air sensors in maritime, littoral, and inland environments.
 The United States Navy (USN) requires the capability to rapidly predict the performance of sensors that depend on the propagation of electro-optical/infrared (EO/IR) radiation (i.e., wavelengths from 0.4 to 12 micron) in air. Sensor performance is subject to environmental/meteorologic conditions, as well as sensor, platform, background/clutter, and target characteristics. For a given sensor on a platform and a target in background/clutter, a forecaster should be able to determine key performance metrics; for example, maximum detection range based on the forecasted meteorological conditions. In this way, USN commanders can make tactical decisions based on the predicted sensor performance given ambient/forecast weather conditions. Key modeling components within a TDA include the land/maritime surface background, target signature, radiative transfer, and sensor performance models. These models are often interdependent, requiring feedback between them (e.g., radiative transfer between target and background models is needed to compute the contrast of the target in the background, which then feeds into a sensor performance model).
 
 Target Acquisition Weapons Software (TAWS), a successor to Electro-Optic Tactical Decision Aid (EOTDA), was originally developed by the Air Force Research Laboratory (AFRL) and released in 1998. Later a target scene model improvement for selected high-resolution targets was implemented with Multi-Service Electro-optics Signature (MuSES). The USN is looking for an innovative and accurate EO/IR TDA, which would be an alternative/improvement to TAWS. Improvements could include support for three dimensional meteorological inputs. The primary challenge for implementing an EO/IR TDA is the methodical verification and validation (V&V) of the constituent models and submodels being developed. This SBIR topic seeks innovative solutions to the development of an EO/IR TDA with particular focus on the methods proposed to verify and validate developed models. A list of prior V&V efforts on proposed submodels should be made clear in the responses to this solicitation, as well as the proposed means/methods to conduct V&V under a Phase II and/or Phase III.
 
 Work produced in Phase II may become classified. Note: The prospective contractor(s) must be U.S. owned and operated with no foreign influence as defined by 32 U.S.C. § 2004.20 et seq., National Industrial Security Program Executive Agent and Operating Manual, unless acceptable mitigating procedures can and have been implemented and approved by the Defense Counterintelligence and Security Agency (DCSA) formerly Defense Security Service (DSS). This will allow contractor personnel to perform on advanced phases of this project as set forth by DCSA and ONR in order to gain access to classified information pertaining to the national defense of the United States and its allies; this will be an inherent requirement. The selected company will be required to safeguard classified material during the advanced phases of this contract IAW the National Industrial Security Program Operating Manual (NISPOM), which can be found at Title 32, Part 2004.20 of the Code of Federal Regulations.
 Develop a concept for an EO/IR TDA model architecture and verify the radiative transfer model can solve basic thermal transport problems (e.g., conduction, convection, radiation) with analytic solutions. Ensure facets/grid points can be individually sampled to provide their temperature and spectral radiance. Create a land/sea background model where spatiotemporally varying clutter can be added in Phase II. Create a CUBI thermal target model and a generic, band-selectable imaging sensor (e.g., 3-5 micron midwave IR (MWIR) imager) model.
objective: Develop an Electro-Optical/Infrared (EO/IR) Tactical Decision Aid (TDA) for surface and air sensors in maritime, littoral, and inland environments.

title: Autonomous Multi-Intelligence Acoustic Reasoning Agent for Anti-Submarine Warfare
text:
Develop an autonomous Anti-Submarine Warfare (ASW) reasoning agent that fuses passive and active acoustic detections with non-acoustic maritime situational data, environmental acoustic propagation context, and platform/target behavior models to produce explainable contact assessments, track hypotheses, and recommended sensor-tasking actions; and supports deployment on an Unmanned Surface Vehicle (USV) with constrained communications, power, and computing conditions.
 The Department of the Navy (DON) seeks development of an autonomous decision-support and reasoning capability for ASW that can reduce dependence on continuous human interpretation of complex acoustic displays and enable future distributed unmanned ASW operations. Current ASW performance is heavily dependent on trained operators who interpret passive narrowband, passive broadband, Demodulation of Noise (DEMON), and other acoustic products while simultaneously incorporating situational knowledge such as geography, bathymetry, Conductivity Temperature and Depth (CTD) data for sound-speed structure, Global Positioning System (GPS), Automatic Identification System (AIS), organic/non-organic tracks, surface traffic, tactical geometry, and expected target behaviors. This human fusion process is effective but difficult to scale across persistent unmanned systems operating at range, under intermittent communications, and in acoustically cluttered environments.
 
 This SBIR topic requests development of an autonomous ASW agent that can ingest heterogeneous acoustic detections and associated confidence measures, correlate them with non-acoustic common operating picture data, reason over environmental acoustic propagation, and maintain multiple explainable track and classification hypotheses over time. The capability should explicitly account for confusers such as merchant shipping, fishing vessels, biologics, own-force and friendly surface ship contributions, reverberation/clutter, and geographically-dependent propagation effects. The resulting system should not be a single-sensor classifier only; it should demonstrate multi-source temporal reasoning that can explain why a contact is assessed as likely submarine, non-submarine, ambiguous, or requiring additional sensing. The approach should be modular and compatible with Navy acoustic processing and performance-prediction workflows, while allowing Navy-provided threat behavior models, environmental data, and acoustic feature streams to be incorporated without redesign. Submissions should include a description of prior sensor fusion development that will serve as a baseline for the proposed ASW fusion architecture.

The selected contractor and/or subcontractor must be able to acquire and maintain a secret level facility and Personnel Security Clearances. This will allow contractor personnel to perform on advanced phases of this project as set forth by DCSA and ONR in order to gain access to classified information pertaining to the national defense of the United States and its allies; this will be an inherent requirement. The selected company will be required to safeguard classified material during the advanced phases of this contract IAW the National Industrial Security Program Operating Manual (NISPOM), which can be found at Title 32, Part 2004.20 of the Code of Federal Regulations.
 Develop a concept for the proposed software architecture for an autonomous ASW reasoning agent, including data schemas for acoustic detections, Common Operation Picture (COP)/non-acoustic inputs, environmental context, target-behavior priors, uncertainty representation, and operator-interpretable explanations. Demonstrate proof-of-concept using representative or open acoustic and maritime datasets to demonstrate fusion of passive acoustic features with disparate data features. Prepare a Phase I final report that includes a performance assessment plan that quantitively assesses metrics such as track purity, false-track/alarm suppression, classification confidence calibration, explanation quality, latency, and robustness to missing/degraded inputs.
objective: Develop an autonomous Anti-Submarine Warfare (ASW) reasoning agent that fuses passive and active acoustic detections with non-acoustic maritime situational data, environmental acoustic propagation context, and platform/target behavior models to produce explainable contact assessments, track hypotheses, and recommended sensor-tasking actions; and supports deployment on an Unmanned Surface Vehicle (USV) with constrained communications, power, and computing conditions.

title: High Sensitivity Tunneling Magnetoresistive Magnetometers
text:
Modernize United States capabilities to produce ultra-low size, weight, power, and cost (SWAP-C) tunneling magnetoresistive magnetometers with industry leading sensitivities.
 Many Navy systems utilize magnetometer technologies for the remote detection, localization, and classification of ferrous objects. Decades of research into different technologies including optically pumped magnetometers have provided highly sensitive technologies which meet most Navy sensitivity needs. However, higher sensitivity magnetometers also possess increased SWAP-C, which limits their applicability in many Navy applications. 
 
 Therefore, there is a direct need for highly sensitive magnetometers that are also compact, low cost, and low power to support a broader range of Navy mission requirements including one-way attack vehicles, expeditionary warfare, mine warfare, and swarming systems. Over the past 30 years, an adjacent technology known as tunneling magnetoresistance (TMR) has had drastic improvements in system sensitivities, unlocking a potential new regime of magnetometer technologies that exhibit ultra-low SWAP-C while maintaining Navy relevant sensitivities.
 
 Design Requirements:
 -Size: less than 10 mm x 10 mm per axis
 -Power: less than 100 mW per axis
 -Sensitivity: less than 50 pT/rt(Hz) @ 1 Hz
 -Frequency Range: DC-500KHz
 -Dynamic Range: -100 uT to 100 uT
 -Nonlinearity over dynamic range: less than 0.1 %
 -Standardized per unit electrical packaging
 Produce a concept for single-axis TMR sensors that possess a design that satisfies the above criteria and also include a per sensor voltage-to-field calibration for confirmation by stakeholders. Provide an analysis or discussion of the potential tradeoffs in the Phase I report if the design concept cannot meet the design objectives. (Note: Justification for the prior should include comparative analysis of COTS capabilities, U.S. and International.)
objective: Modernize United States capabilities to produce ultra-low size, weight, power, and cost (SWAP-C) tunneling magnetoresistive magnetometers with industry leading sensitivities.

title: Expeditionary Water Quality Sensors
text:
Develop simple-to-use water quality test kits or electronic sensors that require minimal training to enable personnel in the field to rapidly meet Technical Bulletin Medical 577 (TB-MED 577) requirements to certify potable water without liquid reagents.
 Expeditionary forces need updated water testing capabilities to support operations in austere, contested environments. Without proper water testing, water purified in the field are not certified potable for consumption. This creates an unacceptable logistics burden to transport water, or a health risks when consuming untested water; hindering the self-sufficiency, readiness, and lethality required for operations against a pacing challenge. Current approved state-of-the-art water quality testing kits are accurate but cumbersome, and overly complex, requiring chemical reagents, significant operator training, and for some parameters shipping to a certified lab. Present water quality testing methods are not practical for the small, distributed Stand-in Forces operating in expeditionary conditions. 
 
 In the event of detection of certain pathogens and contaminants, confirmation through certified laboratories may be required, necessitating sample transportation to CONUS, host-nation, or ally facilities—a process that can take 4-6 weeks. Delays of this magnitude are operationally unacceptable for forces in contested environments that need immediate assurance of water safety at the point of use. In addition, many critical parameters that impact water safety—including heavy metals, organic chemicals, and other contaminants—are not reliably tested with currently fielded sensors. 
 
 Force Design 2030 compels distributed forces to reduce their reliance on centralized logistics convoys; therefore, small units are increasingly required to produce and consume water at the tactical edge and at the point of need. Without a reliable and practical method to verify water quality in the field, these units face an alarming tradeoff between logistics supply certainty and warfighter health. 
 
 Therefore, the Navy needs simple, field-ready solutions to certify that expeditionary purified water conforms to TB-MED 577 short term potability military field water standards (STW MFWS) without external laboratory support. This SBIR topic seeks the development of new sensors and/or methodologies that will significantly improve existing water testing field kits. Improvements sought include but are not limited to: size and weight, more rapid testing results, simpler procedures requiring minimal training, elimination of liquid chemical reagents, and cost. Proposals can address one or more targeted improvements and can target one or more of the water parameters listed in the STP MFWS, such as physical properties, chemical properties, microbial contamination, chemical warfare agents, or radiological. Resulting improved sensors or methodologies must be integratable into future modernized water testing kits to allow squad- and platoon-level forces to verify compliance with TB MED 577 water safety standards in the field, reducing risk to personnel and decreasing reliance on vulnerable resupply chains. The expected end state of this effort is a fully developed, ruggedized, integratable sensor or set of sensors that enable rapid, automated testing of water quality in expeditionary environments in under 15 minutes (Threshold) / under 5 minutes (Objective), and/or detect all microbial threats in under 1 hour (Threshold) / under 15 minutes (Objective) without incubation or liquid reagents. Modular systems targeting specific critical parameters are equally encouraged and will be evaluated on technical merit.
 Establish the technical feasibility of a preliminary conceptual design(s) of a new sensor or series of sensors, capable of rapidly verifying water quality in austere environments without requiring external laboratory support. Define and develop candidate concepts and sensor technologies. Conduct research that will assess the integration potential of the solution(s) into a portable kit for squad- (~13 Marines) and platoon- (40-50 Marines) level operations. Include approaches that may include modeling, simulation, and benchtop testing to evaluate detection accuracy, operational ruggedness, and ease of operation, all while referencing water safety requirements outlined in TB-MED 577. Deliver a final report documenting the technical progress; results of feasibility analyses; a breakdown of size, weight, power, and cost (SWaP-C) improvements and/or trade-offs; performance projections of candidate concepts and sensor technologies; and a defensible preliminary design concept. Ensure that the new sensor(s) should not require liquid chemical reagents, which are problematic due to a short shelf life and customs clearance. Identify anticipated technical risks, mitigation strategies, and a clear development path for Phase II prototype, fabrication, and validation in the final Phase I report.
objective: Develop simple-to-use water quality test kits or electronic sensors that require minimal training to enable personnel in the field to rapidly meet Technical Bulletin Medical 577 (TB-MED 577) requirements to certify potable water without liquid reagents.

title: Rapid Thermoplastic Patching Capability for Legacy Thermoset Airframe Sustainment
text:
Deliver a rapid, high-strength thermoplastic patching capability for legacy thermoset composite airframes by developing the necessary interfacial enabling technologies to fuse the incompatible polymer systems.
 Current composite airframe repair methodologies rely on a combination of wet-layups, B-staged epoxy prepregs, and bonded pre-cured thermoset patches. While pre-cured patches are the standard for high-quality depot repairs due to their autoclave-consolidated strength and "inspectability", they present significant operational and logistical limitations. All these traditional methods require secondary adhesive bonding (using paste or film adhesives) to attach the repair to the airframe. This secondary bond is the inherent weak link of the repair, demanding long thermal cure cycles (often 4 to 24 hours), strict environmental controls, and burdensome cold-storage logistics (freezers) for the B-staged resins and adhesives. Furthermore, these out-of-autoclave epoxy repairs often struggle to meet the high service temperature requirements of advanced tactical aircraft.
 
 This SBIR topic seeks to evolve the current pre-cured repair methodology by transitioning from secondary adhesive bonding to high-speed fusion welding. The objective is to develop the capability to use pre-consolidated, high-temperature thermoplastic patches (e.g., Carbon/PEEK, Carbon/PEKK) on legacy thermoset aircraft (epoxy/Bismaleimide [BMI]). By replacing the lengthy adhesive cure cycle with a rapid welding process, this technology aims to achieve flight-ready repairs in expeditionary and carrier-based environments in a fraction of the time.
 
 Because thermoplastics melt and thermosets do not, achieving a structural weld between these dissimilar materials is the primary barrier to fielding this capability. The Department of War seeks complete thermoplastic patching solutions that incorporate the requisite chemical or mechanical interfacial enablers—such as plasma surface activation, novel chemical tie-layers, or laser-ablated mechanical interlocking. These enablers must allow the thermoplastic patch to successfully fuse with a fully cured, legacy thermoset airframe using portable ultrasonic, resistance- or -induction welding equipment. The outcome must be a deployable repair process that eliminates cold-storage logistics, restores full structural integrity, meets high service temperature demands, and drastically reduces Aircraft on Ground (AOG) time.
 Develop a conceptual thermoplastic patching process and demonstrate the physical viability of the proposed enabling interfacial technology (e.g., tie-layers, surface functionalization). Establish the feasibility of the conceptual process. Perform coupon-level mechanical testing (such as lap-shear and peel-strength) to empirically prove that the thermoplastic-to-thermoset weld achieves a structural load transfer that is comparable to, or exceeds, baseline epoxy adhesive repairs. Deliver a detailed theoretical model explaining the fusion mechanism, an initial assessment of the repair's thermal limits (ensuring the parent thermoset is not degraded), and a conceptual workflow for field-level application that eliminates the need for depot-level infrastructure or cold-storage consumables.
objective: Deliver a rapid, high-strength thermoplastic patching capability for legacy thermoset composite airframes by developing the necessary interfacial enabling technologies to fuse the incompatible polymer systems.

title: Navy Shipboard Gas Turbine Rotating Detonation Combustor Operation with Diesel Fuel
text:
Develop and demonstrate a scaled high density Rotating Detonation Combustor (RDC) that uses NATO F76 diesel fuel (MIL-DTL-16884R) and perform thermodynamic analysis on developed Navy RDC equipped shipboard gas turbine concepts to determine related performance benefits including reduction of stack up length, efficiency improvements, design limitations, and development gaps.
 As background, the typical arrangement used on U.S. Navy surface combatants consists of four (4) large (20+MW class - GE LM-2500) gas turbines for propulsion and three 3 smaller (3 MW class - Rolls Royce 501-K34) gas turbines for ship service electrical power generation. 
 
 Presently U.S. gas turbine powered warships use simple cycle machines. However, complex cycles with reheat and other cycle enhancements have been considered and analyzed with the potential for increased efficiency. Further examinations have been performed to evaluate improvements in maintainability/reliability, overall generator set power density/stack up length, and alternative configuration installation flexibility for use in overall electric plant designs.
 
 RDCs are advanced power-generation and propulsion devices that operate by propagating one or more supersonic detonation waves continuously around an annular chamber. As fresh fuel and oxidizer are continuously injected into the channel, the rotating shock wave rapidly compresses and ignites the mixture, creating a self-sustaining zone of intense heat and pressure. Thermodynamically, RDCs utilize a detonation-driven pressure-gain cycle, which is most accurately modeled by the Fickett-Jacobs-Salsburg (FJS) cycle and frequently approximated as the constant-volume Humphrey cycle. Unlike conventional gas turbines that rely on the constant-pressure Brayton cycle, the FJS detonation cycle in an RDC generates a substantial net increase in total pressure across the combustor. This inherent pressure gain drastically reduces the workload required by upstream mechanical compressors and significantly boosts the overall thermal efficiency and power output of the gas turbine system. While initial government and industry investigations have centered on the use of RDCs in aerospace applications, future shipboard applications will require a greater understanding of the ability to operate with diesel fuel for long continuous operation as well as a quantification of performance benefits that can be achieved in overall shipboard electric architecture design. 
 
 While not required, discussions with Navy shipboard gas turbine Original Equipment Manufacturers (OEM) are recommended.
 Perform an analysis of an RDC combustor ignition and continuous operation with NATO F76 fuel by the end of the Base period. Assemble and demonstrate an initial limited laboratory experiment/subscale test to verify analysis findings in coordination with Navy personnel. Complete a conceptual design for a combustor prototype and associated liquid fuel system, to include prototype design refinements, fabrication approach, and testing strategy that should include ignition and endurance operation with defined measurements in coordination with Navy personnel and within the scope of a Phase II budget. Prepare a Phase II plan.
objective: Develop and demonstrate a scaled high density Rotating Detonation Combustor (RDC) that uses NATO F76 diesel fuel (MIL-DTL-16884R) and perform thermodynamic analysis on developed Navy RDC equipped shipboard gas turbine concepts to determine related performance benefits including reduction of stack up length, efficiency improvements, design limitations, and development gaps.

title: Rapid Imagery Creation for Navy Training
text:
Develop technology to use historic real-world satellite imagery and then rapidly (10 minutes or less) modify it to reflect a training scenario order of battle (aircraft, ships, vehicles, etc.) to allow imagery analysts to practice their tradecraft underway or ashore in support of maritime exercises.
 Currently, imagery analysts are excluded from, or extremely limited in, participating in dynamic Navy operational and staff training such as Surface Warfare Advanced Team Trainer (SWATT), Information Warfare Advanced Team Trainer (IWATT), Fleet Synthetic Training General Commander/Joint (FST-GC/J), and Commander Training Unit Exercise (COMPTUEX).This is due to the limited ability to dynamically generate the required products for imagery analysts within a reasonable amount of time at a quality that supports training. 
 
 Currently, either summaries are provided to the training audience circumventing the imagery analysts all together or providing GRAPHPLOTS - the equivalence of stick figure drawing - to track the order of battle (OOB) made up of aircraft, ships, vehicles, etc., without any use of actual imagery or geospatial analysis.
 A technology to address this shortfall would need to take real-world geo-rectified imagery as a base and then rapidly adjust/modify the image to reflect the desired OOB and in a National Imagery Transition Format (NTIF) to be provided to the training audience for imagery analysts to process. 
 
 For example, in real-life Port A, identified by Basic Encyclopedia (BE) number, is of high interest and has a collection requirement against it for satellite imagery to be collected. In reality, Port A has three Kilo-class submarines and one Luhu-class destroyer, but in the scenario things have dynamically changed such that one of those submarines is now underway and an additional Luda I-class Destroyer has arrived, requiring the rapid (less than 10 minutes) production of an NITF image depicting two Kilo-class submarines, one Luhu DD, and one Luda I DDG to provide the training audience for analysis. The same would be required for airfields depicting aircraft movement as well.
