This will allow contractor personnel to perform on advanced phases of this project as set forth by DCSA and ONR in order to gain access to classified information pertaining to the national defense of the United States and its allies; this will be an inherent requirement. The selected company will be required to safeguard classified material during the advanced phases of this contract IAW the National Industrial Security Program Operating Manual (NISPOM), which can be found at Title 32, Part 2004.20 of the Code of Federal Regulations.
 Create concept formulation for electro-optical imagery, determine technical feasibility of rapidly generating an NITF image, and validation through the modification of a single image (note: format and quality are not relevant here) to change the depicted order of battle. Determine technical feasibility of infrared (IR), and Synthetic Aperture RADAR (SAR) imagery. Create demonstration standard sufficient to assess preservation of imagery characteristics necessary for realistic imagery-analysis training.
objective: Develop technology to use historic real-world satellite imagery and then rapidly (10 minutes or less) modify it to reflect a training scenario order of battle (aircraft, ships, vehicles, etc.) to allow imagery analysts to practice their tradecraft underway or ashore in support of maritime exercises.

title: Attritable Turbine for Low-Cost Attack Systems (ATLAS)
text:
Design, develop, and prototype a low-cost, limited-life gas turbine engine producing 150-300 lbf of SLS thrust with an estimated engine life expectancy of 10-15 hours, leveraging advanced design and manufacturing techniques to significantly reduce part count, production lead time and scaling, and overall unit cost compared to traditionally manufactured engines in the same class.
 The Department of War has an increasing need for affordable, reliable, and rapidly producible propulsion systems to support the proliferation of attritable Unmanned Aerial Systems (UAS), loitering munitions, and stand-off strike weapons. Current small turbofan and turbojet engines in the 150-300 pounds of thrust (lbf) class often rely on traditional aerospace material and manufacturing processes, resulting in high unit costs and long supply chain lead times. These factors are prohibitive for systems intended to be employed in mass or as expendable assets.
 
 This SBIR topic seeks innovative engineering and manufacturing approaches to design a turbofan engine that meets the thrust requirements while dramatically lowering cost per unit. Proposers should consider advanced design and manufacturing techniques to produce a low-cost engine that can leverage existing industrial base capacity to reduce risk to procurement supply chains. 
 
 Key technologies and design features to consider are:
 Additive Manufacturing: Utilizing Powder Bed Fusion, Directed Energy Deposition and Direct Metal Laser Sintering (DMLS) to consolidate part count and simplify construction. Industrial (Non-Aerospace) Production Capacity: Leverage non-traditional aerospace manufacturing firms to reduce cost. Consider leveraging materials, casting and production techniques found in the automotive sector. Demonstrate a manufacturing pathway that enables rapid scaling and reduces supply chain bottlenecks. Short Life/Expendable Components: Utilizing non-traditional lubrication systems, bearings and electronic sub-components to limit cost. Optimized Materials: Utilize cost-effective materials suited for limited-life/single-use engine operations rather than traditional high-lifecycle aviation materials, where appropriate. 
 Performance metrics of interest include specific fuel consumption (SFC), thrust-to-weight ratio, and operational reliability for mission durations typical of attritable UAS or cruise munitions.
 
 The engine will be fully operational utilizing Navy relevant fuels and demonstrate resilience to harsh maritime storage and launch conditions without significant performance degradation. The engine is expected to demonstrate functionality when subject to storage life of 6-12 months in Maritime environments and meet minimum required performance after exposure to shore-based and shipborne launch environments. 
 
 Notional performance objectives for this SBIR topic are provided in the Tables below:
 
 Table 1: ATLAS engine notional operational envelop and performance objectives.
 Parameter Specification
 Electrical Power Generation [W] 500-1500
 Thrust, SLS [lbf] 150-300
 SFC [lbm/lbf/hr] < 1.5
 Cruise Altitude [ft] 20k 
 
 Table 2: ATLAS engine notional mass and dimensional properties objectives.
 Parameter Specification
 Approximate OML Diameter [in] < =10
 Weight, Dry [lbm] 25-35
 Length [in.] 14-24
 
 
 Table 3: ATLAS engine notional storage & launch conditions.
 Parameter Specification
 Start Altitude Sea Level
 Start Method Air Impingement 
 Storage Duration (Wooden Round) 6-12 months, Maritime Environment
 Launch & Assist Method Rail, Catapult, or Rocket Assist
 Conduct a feasibility study and develop a conceptual design for a 150-300 lbf. turbofan engine.
 Identify the specific advanced design and manufacturing techniques to be utilized, optimizing the finished product for cost and producibility. Provide preliminary conceptual design modeling and simulation data (e.g., computational fluid dynamics, structural, and thermal analysis, cycle model) to validate conceptual design. Develop a comparative cost analysis demonstrating the projected unit cost and production time reductions versus traditional manufacturing baselines. Conduct a proof-of-concept demonstration and/or test campaign of the conceptual design, components, materials and manufacturing methods utilizing component level rig testing or lab testing where applicable. Monitor ongoing program risk and provide status updates throughout program progression. Deliver a Phase II development and testing plan.
objective: Design, develop, and prototype a low-cost, limited-life gas turbine engine producing 150-300 lbf of SLS thrust with an estimated engine life expectancy of 10-15 hours, leveraging advanced design and manufacturing techniques to significantly reduce part count, production lead time and scaling, and overall unit cost compared to traditionally manufactured engines in the same class.

title: Innovative Shortwave Infrared High Energy Laser Source and Coupled Imager
text:
Develop and demonstrate a compact, ruggedized high-energy laser source operating at the 1.9-2.5 micron wavelength with variable Continuous wave and pulsed output [zero to kilowatt kW class average powers] with a time-coupled imaging range gated imaging sensor, capable of real time or near real time doppler data collection & object visualization with ten meter (threshold) to sub-meter (objective) scale range selection, and suitable for maneuvering object discrimination at kilometers of distance at low altitudes, in a quiescent (threshold) or turbulent (objective) maritime atmospheric condition.
 The Navy desires a short wave infrared high energy laser illuminator and coupled range-gated imaging sensor, including optics, operating in 1.9-2.5 micron wavelength to increase engagement ranges in adverse marine atmospheric conditions that include absorption, Mie and Rayleigh scattering, thermal blooming, etc. and able to operate in continuous wave (CW) or pulsed operation modes - at a variable power level up to kilowatt powers (average). Adjustable wavelength tunability to match to optimal atmospheric penetration and transmission within the band specified is required. If the entire band is not accessible, then rationale must be provided for limitation or selections made. In addition, it requires these to be ruggedized, so they are suitable to be installed on maritime platforms (i.e., ships, USMC ground vehicles, and aircraft) and be in a wavelength regime that is considered "eye-safer" when considering issues of defuse reflection or scatter when nearby observers are present. Gimbal and optics development or advancements in the shortwave infrared regimes may be offered but are not the primary technical objective in consideration for this topic.
 
 Recent advances in laser sources [Ref 1] with high beam quality at the 2 micron wavelength, using Holmium and Thulium doped fiber optic-based power gain amplifiers, have shown a potential pathways for innovation to reach higher average powers (in Continuous Wave operation) in the multi-kilowatt regime, within the 2.0 to 2.4 micron (µm) band and falling within an atmospheric spectral short-wave infrared (SWIR) transmission band due to their low absorption of light by atmospheric water vapor. A pulsed system with a pulse gated optical imaging sensor offers the unique opportunity to not only provide a simple Laser Detection and Ranging (LIDAR) capability but also provide doppler-based discrimination information on the imaged objects - which could exceed systems' capabilities typical from the 1.0-1.6 micron near infrared (NIR) band. The marine wave boundary layer (MWBL) can have higher scattering properties when comparing NIR to the selected SWIR bands, and is considered less detectable using widely available commercial, uncooled sensors than standard visible to NIR based illumination systems. A system that can operate in either CW or coupled pulse modes with a time resolved, range gated sensor and with high resolution windowing is the primary objective of this topic.
 
 The Navy and Department of War seeks a unified approach with a scalable prototype device for use in evaluation for Electro-magnetic (EM) Spectrum warfare with an objective of gaining military advantages and achieving freedom of action across missions in support of maritime, surface warfare. However, the one system should show an ability to handle two separate capabilities developed through scaling. The first is development of a small, compact, lightweight SWIR (2.0-2.4 wavelength) high energy laser illuminator and coupled range-gated imaging sensor, including necessary optics suitable for short range sensing from small (group I or II) unmanned aerial vehicles or drones. While shorter ranges are acceptable for these missions (tens to hundreds of meters), the need for higher power still exists to conduct object discrimination at longer range (kilometers) and collect as much information (e.g., doppler shifts) from sensors as is technically possible. These smaller devices may diverge because of the requirements of size, weight and power (SWaP) toward a lower power-ganged diode array of microbolometers that has sufficient optical gain sensitivity to achieve doppler data, at the sacrifice of higher resolution spatial data typically obtained from devices that are based on focal plane arrays. Hybrid approaches combining sensor types shall be considered. Imaged target objects are expected to be in centimeter to meter size, and either stationary or have relatively low velocities (meters per second). 
 
 At the other end of the scale, a desire exists for a larger, fixed placement optical device on a moving or mobile platform (i.e., ground, air or sea-based vehicle) that can accurately discriminate and range objects at significantly greater distances (hundreds of meters to tens of thousands of meters) and are larger (tens of meters in length) with higher velocities (from tens to hundreds of meters per second). These systems require significantly higher source power, larger optics and higher quality vibration control, longer photonic travel distance, shorter pulse lengths, and higher peak power; have longer latency of time from emission to reception; and include the optical distortions that occur during light travel, reflection, and return. These larger devices may favor a combination of both focal plane arrays with coupled microbolometers using highly resolution time coupled range gating techniques, and significant relaxation of SWaP and include potentials for active cooling. However, the complexities of field conditions where the systems are deployed can vary greatly, with humidity (0-100%), rain, fog, particulates, and temperature variation (-55°C to +125°C) are not negotiable for either class of system. The need for higher laser power may be approached by beam combining smaller sources, but simplicity is preferred with ruggedness to dynamic shocks required under this topic, at least initially.
objective: Develop and demonstrate a compact, ruggedized high-energy laser source operating at the 1.9-2.5 micron wavelength with variable Continuous wave and pulsed output [zero to kilowatt kW class average powers] with a time-coupled imaging range gated imaging sensor, capable of real time or near real time doppler data collection & object visualization with ten meter (threshold) to sub-meter (objective) scale range selection, and suitable for maneuvering object discrimination at kilometers of distance at low altitudes, in a quiescent (threshold) or turbulent (objective) maritime atmospheric condition.

title: Co-Packaged Optics (CPO) for Advanced Cryocooled Electro-Optical/Infrared (EO/IR) Sensors
text:
Develop and demonstrate innovative Co-Packaged Optics (CPO) architectures and integration techniques for advanced cryocooled Electro-Optical/Infrared (EO/IR) sensor systems that significantly reduce the number of electrical wirebonds, increase bandwidth density, and withstand rugged maritime environments for deployment in advanced sensing and tactical edge computing platforms.
 Current Department of the Navy (DON) platforms are generating unprecedented volumes of data via advanced radar, SIGINT, and high-resolution imaging sensors. Processing of this data at the tactical edge requires extreme bandwidth but can consume excessive powers, creating significant thermal and signal integrity bottlenecks [Ref 1]. Specifically, for advanced EO/IR sensors that operate in cryocooled temperatures (e.g., 70-140K), the excessive power required to electrically read out the data, i.e., transmit from cold space and receive in warm space, presents a challenging limitation on the size, weight, and power (SWaP) of an integrated dewar cooler assembly. Fiber optics and photonic integrated circuits (PICs) are key optical readout technologies that can offer extreme bandwidth, low power consumption, and mature fabrication but require integrated packaging solutions for next generation DON systems [Ref 2].
  
 CPO offers an integrated solution that considers both optical and electrical elements in EO/IR sensor design, optimizing performance, reliability, and manufacturability. CPO brings the optical transceiver components directly into the same package as the readout integrated circuit (ROIC). This minimizes the electrical channel length or completely eliminates it with photonic interconnects, fundamentally lowering power consumption (energy per bit) and enabling massive bandwidth scaling [Refs 1-4]. To date, commercial CPO solutions are primarily designed for room temperature, climate-controlled hyperscale SI data centers.
  
 This STTR topic seeks to adapt and innovate current CPO technologies for the stringent Size, Weight, Power, and Cost (SWaP-C) and packaging (cryogenically cooled) constraints of advanced Navy EO/IR sensing platforms. The focus of the topic is on the design and development of a CPO architecture that integrates with the ROIC layer of a typical EO/IR sensor chip assembly, enables high-bandwidth cold to warm readout, and operates in cryocooled temperatures.
  
 Proposals must address critical challenges, including:
 ROIC compatibility: PIC interconnect architecture that is compatible with conventional analog and mixed-signal digital ROICs designed in <180 nm node foundries, optimal number of fiber outputs to meet total ROIC bandwidth. Thermal Management: Dissipating heat effectively when dense photonics and ROICs are co-located in a cryocooled integrated dewar assembly. Minimize PIC power consumption to less than 20 mW. Power Efficiency: Choice of electrical-optical conversion scheme and minimizing power consumption (e.g., half-wave voltage for EO modulators, Vpi), PIC waveguide propagation loss, PIC to fiber input/output coupling losses, and stray light scatter. Integration & Packaging: Complementary metal-oxide-semiconductor (CMOS)-compatible substrate materials, 2.5D/3D integration techniques, and cost-effective scalable manufacturing processes. Conduct a feasibility study for a conceptual design of a CPO architecture with full transceiver functionality that addresses the four critical challenges and is tailored for a SWaP-constrained Navy maritime EO/IR sensor system. 
 Deliverables: Perform architectural modeling, signal integrity simulations, and thermal/mechanical modeling. Metrics: Define target performance metrics, such as energy efficiency (e.g., < 10 fJ/bit), bandwidth (e.g., > 1 Tbps), coupling loss (e.g., < 0.5 dB/fiber connection) and estimated mean time between failures (MTBF) under standard military environmental conditions (e.g., MIL-STD-810H). Prepare a Outcome: A comprehensive Phase II development plan that identifies the PIC foundry and packaging facility, including preliminary packaging designs and a proof-of-concept simulation report.
objective: Develop and demonstrate innovative Co-Packaged Optics (CPO) architectures and integration techniques for advanced cryocooled Electro-Optical/Infrared (EO/IR) sensor systems that significantly reduce the number of electrical wirebonds, increase bandwidth density, and withstand rugged maritime environments for deployment in advanced sensing and tactical edge computing platforms.

title: Growth and Production of As2S3 Waveguides
text:
Determine and demonstrate how thin film deposits of As2S3 can be grown on an appropriate cladding material and etched to form a low loss waveguide for photonic applications of the Stimulated Brillouin Scattering (SBS) non-linearity in Radio Frequency (RF) applications.
 Multiple academic papers have indicated that the reverse mode of the SBS interaction between acoustic phonons and coherent 1.55 µm photons can cause Stoke's peak gain on RF sidebands. It is desirable to harvest that effect for application in the burgeoning field of RF photonics. However, for that to happen, it is desirable that methods be developed to optimize the growth and etching of quasi-epitaxial As2S3, the material with the largest known SBS coefficient. In order to achieve low optical loss, achieving extremely low surface roughness of as-deposited films (< 10 nm rms roughness) is required plus ways to preserve that in producing waveguides of around 100 nm thickness and with high confinement bottom and top cladding. While atomic layer deposition (ALD) growth has produced other chalcogenides with very flat, conformal surfaces, it has not been used for As2S3; moreover, that other material was amorphous as deposited and drastically changed optical properties when crystalized. It may be that highly directional growth onto pre-etched substrate mesas produce better performance waveguides in which to produce amplification. Lastly, it is essential to demonstrate a way to achieve extremely low loss signal transfer on and off the die if RF photonics is to outperform conventional electronics in the future. 
 
 Phase I proposals for this STTR topic shall name the deposition and etching techniques that will be developed under the base award and estimate the surface smoothness of both the as-deposited material and the finished waveguides. The work plan must allow the validation of these estimates during the Base award so that the preliminary Phase II plan can define with good certainty the properties achievable in Phase II if awarded.
 
 Measurement of the optical properties of completed waveguides during the Base award is highly desirable. First demonstrations of a method of coupling to the waveguide with losses under 2 dB in the Phase I Option is also desirable. A work division where the non-profit develops the fabrication technology and the company develops the many GHz wide band amplifier and coupling technologies is one possible division of the work. A clear discussion of the dependencies and determinants of the ultimate performance as a photonic amplifier should be included in the initial proposal. 
 
 It is highly desirable that, by the effort's end, how feasible it is that by varying the optical carrier power in and the waveguide length, RF signal gains from 5 to 20 dB can be achieved with total noise figures including all coupling losses of <6 (threshold, 3 objective) dB. Paths to wafer scale fabrication yield above 90% should also be defined.
 Determine the technical feasibility of using the proposed deposition and lithography techniques to produce an in-line photonic amplifier based on the SBS effect in As2S3. Demonstrate the potential compatibility of this material with use of SiN structures including surface grating couplers (desirable). Establish high reliability estimates of the ultimate performance feasible from this combination of materials, fabrication processes, and simple photonic circuit and technology roadblocks.
objective: Determine and demonstrate how thin film deposits of As2S3 can be grown on an appropriate cladding material and etched to form a low loss waveguide for photonic applications of the Stimulated Brillouin Scattering (SBS) non-linearity in Radio Frequency (RF) applications.

title: Validated Modular Autonomy for Undersea Multi-Vehicle Coordination
text:
Develop software modules for existing autonomous undersea vehicles that support and extend existing system autonomy with multi-vehicle coordination behaviors.
 Autonomous undersea vehicles performing expeditionary missions require state-of-the-art cooperative sensing and engagement capabilities. The Navy seeks to enhance those capabilities with modular software designed for reliability and operational effectiveness. The advancement sought is development of a modular coordination layer extending existing single vehicle with decentralized multi-vehicle behaviors to enable autonomous decision making under degraded communications, sensing, and PNT conditions.
 
 The software prototype needs to take in mission requirements provided by existing Navy command and control (C2) systems and sensor data provided by multiple platforms and use those inputs to coordinate mission performance with other vehicles. It should be compatible with modular unmanned autonomy architectures already in use by the Navy, such as the Open Autonomous Underwater Vehicle (OpenAUV) architecture and the Robot Operating System 2 (ROS 2). Within those architectures, the prototype must interface with existing autonomy designed for single-vehicle operations with minimal changes to already established systems. When the prototype is disabled or unnecessary, vehicle performance and behavior must conform to what would be expected of an unmodified single vehicle.
 
 The multi-mission management functions of the software prototype need to use a decentralized C2 scheme that is robust in low-information environments and that degrades gracefully if communications or sensing are limited. The C2 scheme must demonstrate sufficient scalability to effectively manage many vehicles: tens to hundreds. Real-time C2 is a must.
 
 The prototype should assume the primary sensing mode of each vehicle is acoustic. Realistic sensors include forward-look and side-scan sonar, possibly with a synthetic aperture. Cameras may be available, but if so, their field of view should not be assumed to allow for keeping other vehicles in sight. Realistic communications include acoustic modems with transmission rates of 5000 bps or less, possibly much less. Communications methods with higher transmission rates are unlikely to be available and may only be possible at extremely close range.
 
 The prototype should assume that access to radar and satellite systems is extremely limited or non-existent. In particular, the prototype should not depend on regular access to global positioning system (GPS) data, and it should take into account the possibility that each vehicle is subject to position, navigation, and timing errors that increase in magnitude as each mission progresses.
 
 The software prototype must include as an essential component a method of continuous validation that establishes and quantifies risk and trust for all autonomous decision-making, with an emphasis on repeatability. Deliverables must include the documentation and software necessary to implement this continuous validation method, as well as a report quantifying the efficacy of the method.
 
 The ideal prototype will be mission agnostic, instead focusing on a generalized set of multi-vehicle behaviors and objectives.
 
 The software prototype should minimize potential negative impacts on mission effectiveness, vehicle endurance, vehicle survivability, and operator workload. The prototype can include enabling hardware, provided that such hardware can be installed on existing autonomous undersea vehicles. The complexity of any vehicle modifications should be minimized. The prototype software and any accompanying hardware should also minimize their overall power consumption. Deliverable reports should include analysis identifying and quantifying any such impacts.
 Develop a concept for an architecture for a prototype multi-vehicle mission module. Ensure that this architecture should provide an approach for decomposing missions into generalized multi-vehicle behaviors and objectives. Identify and design a method of continuous validation that establishes and quantifies risk and trust for autonomous decision-making. Provide required deliverables that include prototype module architecture designs; documentation for the method of continuous validation; and analysis of how those approaches attain the topic's goals, including both academic research and validated modeling and simulation.
objective: Develop software modules for existing autonomous undersea vehicles that support and extend existing system autonomy with multi-vehicle coordination behaviors.

title: Self-Sustaining Wave Energy Capture for Persistent Autonomous Ocean-Going Systems
text:
Develop a human-portable wave energy capture device able to deploy autonomously and generate sufficient power to effectively recharge autonomous vehicles.
 Unmanned surface and undersea vehicles need regular recharging, and since they often operate far from human contact, their charging systems require a reliable, self-sustaining power source. The Office of Naval Research (ONR) believes the ideal power source will be a wave energy capture device (WECD). WECDs capture kinetic and potential energy generated by the movement of ocean waves on or near the surface of open water. 
 
 The desired WECD must be portable, specifically, designed as a set of components that can each be carried by one or two people who must be able to quickly assemble and disassemble those components. Components designed for one-person carry should weigh no more than 14 kg with largest dimension no greater than 1.9 m, while components designed for two-person carry should weigh no more than 45.4 kg with largest dimension no greater than 2.3 m. The WECD must be able to be relocated to areas of very different depths, including full ocean depth so the WECD's design cannot require placement or anchoring on the sea floor. And since the WECD may need to deploy near the shore, its design must allow it to function in waters as shallow as 100 meters.
 
 Ocean weather conditions can be challenging. The WECD should function reliably at Sea State 6 or less (very rough seas, with wave heights of 4 to 6 meters), and it should be able to survive conditions up to Sea State 8 (very high seas, with wave heights of 9 to 14 meters).
 
 ONR assumes the WECD will be tethered to some device at or near the surface of the water. That tethered system may be an autonomous vehicle in loiter mode, and since loitering involves continuous vehicle movement, the WECD should operate reliably while in motion, and its design should leverage such motion to increase energy capture.
 
 The WECD should produce a minimum of 20 kilowatt-hours (kWh) per day, but more is highly desirable. ONR believes 100+ kWh per day is achievable. Even in calm seas, the ideal WECD should produce sufficient electricity to charge a 2-kWh battery in 6 hours or less. Vehicle movement may be considered when ensuring this minimum level of power generation.
 
 The desired WECD may be needed in areas where human assembly is impractical. Thus, the deliverables must include a prototype device capable of deploying the assembled WECD from the deck of a medium or large autonomous surface vessel. Like the WECD itself, the deployment device (DD) should function reliably in challenging weather conditions: Sea State 4 or less (moderate seas with wave heights of 1.25 to 2.5 meters).
 
 Once deployed, very little of the WECD itself should be visible at the surface of the water. The WECD should minimize any increase in the visibility of the vehicle it is tethered to. This includes surface and airborne observation, both optically and by radar. Acoustic noise generated by the WECD should either be minimized or disguised to seem environmental or biological.
 
 Cost for the WECD and associated DD should be minimized. ONR expects that under certain environmental conditions or mission requirements, WECDs may not be recoverable. At full-rate production, the ideal price will allow for multiple units per million dollars.
 
 Under normal operating conditions, including Sea States of 6 or less, the expected operational duration of the deployed WECD should be at least one month, with three months or more expected if Sea State 4 or less is maintained.
 Develop a concept for a WECD and DD capable of satisfying the listed requirements. Evaluate feasibility of the conceptual design by performing modeling and simulation, supplemented by component-level laboratory tests and water tank tests as appropriate. Provide required Phase I deliverables to include design plans and schematics for the WECD and DD, along with test and evaluation reports that are sufficiently detailed to enable ONR to assess the feasibility of the contractor's proposed approach; and a Phase II plan.
objective: Develop a human-portable wave energy capture device able to deploy autonomously and generate sufficient power to effectively recharge autonomous vehicles.

title: Compact Unmanned Aerial System for Marine Species Monitoring
text:
Develop an inexpensive, compact, and National Defense Authorization Act (NDAA)-compliant Unmanned Aerial System (UAS) - optimized for marine mammal monitoring.
 A major remaining hurdle with marine species management is to know if, and when, measurable short-term behavioral and/or physiological responses of marine species to sound exposure results in biologically significant or meaningful effects on individuals and/or their populations. Advances in UAS methods and technology present unprecedented opportunities to improve the capacity to collect this robust data with minimal disturbance to marine species. However, while UAS methods have led to significant advances in our understanding of marine species' behavior, health, and body condition, thus far many obstacles remain including cost, flight duration, size, and image resolution.
 
 This STTR topic seeks to develop a compact, inexpensive, and NDAA-compliant UAS and payloads designed to collect high-resolution photogrammetry imagery to improve marine mammal monitoring, health measurements, and behavioral sequencing. In particular, the prototype device should contain the following technical parameters: high resolution flat zoom lens camera integrated with a gimbal system; highly maneuverable and flexible payload system; lightweight batteries less than 100 Watt hours; an accurate Light Detection and Ranging (LiDAR) altimeter and range finder integrated with the camera and capable of measuring distances up to 50m or more; and a monitor that is operational in direct sunlight and with polarized sunglasses;. It should be designed for flight times as much as or greater than 40 minutes; be compact and portable in both size and weight such that the UAS and case can fit airline luggage restrictions; have the ability to be quickly calibrated, launched, and caught by hand during small boat-based operations and to tolerate temperature range of -20 degrees to +40 degrees Celsius; and have a minimum weather resistant rating of IP45 to allow for operations in wet conditions; be capable of dynamic home point positioning; and produces minimal noise. 
 
 While there are several existing NDAA-compliant drones available in the marketplace, the desired components and capabilities only exist in piecemeal and further, these UAS are prohibitively expensive for the field. The DON seeks to develop a prototype device to be designed and optimized for marine species monitoring, encompassing all the above technical parameters. Critically, this device must be affordable for the marine research community with the target market price between $10,000 - $15,000.
 Develop concepts for and determine the feasibility of UAS technologies suitable for marine species-focused photogrammetry in a compact, efficient, and cost-effective design, including the identification of components to increase imagery resolution, increase flight time, and decrease size and weight of the prototype device. Develop key component technology milestones and conceptual designs for hardware. Prepare a Phase II plan.
objective: Develop an inexpensive, compact, and National Defense Authorization Act (NDAA)-compliant Unmanned Aerial System (UAS) - optimized for marine mammal monitoring.

title: Multi-Modal Luminescent Paint Systems for Underwater Surface Diagnostics
text:
Develop an integrated, multi-modal luminescent paint system optimized for simultaneous, non-intrusive, large-scale, high-resolution global measurement of wall pressure, shear stress, and temperature fluctuations on complex, curved geometries in underwater environments.
 Quantifying coupled boundary layer interactions along hydrodynamic surfaces require non-intrusive, full-field imaging of surface pressure, temperature, and skin friction (shear stress). While optical diagnostics have revolutionized aerodynamic testing, adapting luminescent paints to hydrodynamic testing in water introduces fundamental physical and application constraints that current state-of-the-art systems cannot overcome:
 • Pressure-Sensitive Paint (PSP): Conventional PSP relies on oxygen-quenching physics. When submerged, oxygen diffusion into the polymer binder is severely inhibited by the liquid boundary layer and low oxygen solubility, rendering standard PSPs insensitive or plagued by extremely slow response times. Furthermore, severe temperature cross-sensitivity corrupts the pressure signal.
 • Temperature-Sensitive Paint (TSP): Accurate dynamic temperature measurements are crippled by the standard utilization of Taylor's frozen-flow hypothesis, which inaccurately assumes turbulent structures remain unchanged as they advect. In water, non-equilibrium flow, high thermal mass and rapid localized diffusion cause this hypothesis to break down, failing to capture true high-frequency temperature fluctuations.
 • Mechano-Luminescent Paint (MLP): MLPs offer a direct optical pathway to map shear stress via mechanical deformation. However, current MLP formulations are in their technological infancy, suffering from poor dynamic range, low luminous efficiency, and signal degradation from material fatigue and hydrostatic pressure cross-talk.
 
 In addition to the above challenges, current formulations are difficult to apply uniformly over large areas. Existing techniques fail to maintain a consistent, repeatable coating thickness on complex, curved, or non-flat surfaces. This inconsistency skews calibration and compromises measurement reliability across large-field hydrodynamic models. Innovative material architectures, such as utilizing distinct, multi-color mechano-luminescent particles or multi-core/shell dye structures, may enable simultaneous, uncoupled optical separation of pressure, shear, and temperature in all flow environments, i.e. gas, liquid, and multiphase flows.
 
 This STTR topic seeks an integrated material, application, and optical processing suite. The system must decouple cross-sensitivities and deliver simultaneous, high dynamic range, full-field quantitative maps of the wall pressure, shear, and temperature fluctuations.
 Develop a concept for advanced formulations for water-compatible PSP, TSP, and MLP systems capable of measuring pressure fluctuations from 10 Pa to 100 kPa, shear stress from 0.1 to 100 Pa, and temperature variations from 0.05 to 20°C, as well as providing uniform spatial sampling capable of resolving unsteadiness up to 50 kHz without relying on Taylor's hypothesis. Evaluate the conceptual system's ability to decouple cross-sensitivities in simultaneous mapping of wall pressure, shear stress, and temperature through analytic modeling and laboratory testing. Identify potential application methodologies (e.g., specialized spray or deposition techniques) that ensure uniform, repeatable adhesion to curved, non-flat structures. Perform an initial cost estimate and identify technical risks to be addressed in Phase II.
objective: Develop an integrated, multi-modal luminescent paint system optimized for simultaneous, non-intrusive, large-scale, high-resolution global measurement of wall pressure, shear stress, and temperature fluctuations on complex, curved geometries in underwater environments.

title: Membranes for Separation, Purification, Compression, and Storage of Carbon Resources from Alkaline Water
text:
Develop a low-cost, robust, energy-efficient, and scalable membrane process to continuously separate, purify, compress, and store carbon dioxide from electrochemically processed alkaline water sources to support the local synthesis of fuels, nutrients, materials, and pharmaceuticals in austere, forward-deployed environments.
 This STTR topic seeks to develop a low-cost, low-energy, low-temperature (not to exceed 50°C), high-throughput nonmetallic membrane process to purify and store carbon dioxide (CO 2 ) (from acidic seawater solutions). Carbon resources harvested from seawater represent a critical renewable feedstock for the localized synthesis of tactical fuels, materials, nutrients, and pharmaceuticals. Developing the capability to generate these resources in-theater or at the tactical edge enhances multi-domain operational sustainment. Current technologies used to recover the dissolved CO 2 produced from electrochemically processed seawater often result in dilution of the CO 2 with air and water vapor that can lead to detrimental sintering and oxidation of catalysts used in thermochemical and biological synthetic approaches. In addition, there are volumetric and compression penalties associated with the dilution of the targeted gas. The proposed membrane process will reduce the complexity, size, and costs associated with supplying pure carbon dioxide resources from alkaline water sources.
 
 The integrated membrane, purification, and compression process will provide equipment, process, design criteria, energy and material balance; and establish operational performance parameters.
 Define a concept for a specific membrane process for the separation and purification of CO 2 from acidified seawater solutions. Define, develop, and perform initial laboratory assessment of the proposed membrane process to validate the technical feasibility of the approach for the capture, purification, and storage of CO 2 from seawater over a pH range of 2 to 5. Perform analysis of the CO 2 to determine yield and purity. Perform analysis on the membrane to determine the membranes' ability to maintain performance, structural and chemical integrity.
objective: Develop a low-cost, robust, energy-efficient, and scalable membrane process to continuously separate, purify, compress, and store carbon dioxide from electrochemically processed alkaline water sources to support the local synthesis of fuels, nutrients, materials, and pharmaceuticals in austere, forward-deployed environments.

title: Domestic Manufacturing of Large Area Raman Laser Materials
text:
Develop scalable domestic manufacturing technologies and processes for large Raman active optical crystals that will enable wavelength agile laser systems for Navy applications.
 The Navy employs laser systems on air- and sea-borne vessels that serve a wide range of applications including laser range finding, target designation, shipboard and airborne LiDAR, and directed energy platforms. Future naval systems require improvements in spectral agility, optical efficiency, and power, with reductions to size and weight while maintaining operation in harsh maritime environments.
 
 Current laser architectures rely upon a limited set of mature gain and nonlinear optical materials including Nd- and Yb-doped yttrium aluminum garnet (YAG), potassium titanyl phosphate (KTP), lithium triborate (LBO), and barium borate (BBO). While these technologies provide reliable performance, wavelength conversion often requires multiple optical stages that increases system complexity, introduces alignment sensitivity, and can limit scalability to higher optical powers and larger apertures.
 
 Raman active optical materials offer a pathway toward compact and wavelength agile laser architectures capable of generating multiple output wavelengths from a single pump source. Such materials may enable simplified optical systems with reduced alignment complexity, improved robustness to vibration and shock, enhanced spectral diversity, and compact eye-safe laser sources. Many Raman laser crystals have been demonstrated to be grown to large sizes at high quality, but broader adoption of Raman active optical materials in these systems hinges on improving domestic production. Many candidate Raman laser materials are produced in small quantities at limited sizes and lack established domestic manufacturing capability and therefore development of domestic manufacturing technologies compatible with large crystal sizes is of importance for future naval laser systems.
 
 Candidate materials shall be compatible with bulk crystal growth processes capable of producing large aperture, high optical quality single crystals and offer a pathway toward crystal sizes of 50 mm and greater.
 
 This STTR topic seeks to develop a prototype manufacturing technology and process which can produce one or more Raman active materials at large crystal sizes with the potential to scale to high throughput. The prototype should minimize reliance on expensive precious metal crucibles. The prototype shall produce Raman active crystals that are large (> 5mm x 5mm x 25mm), achieve laser damage thresholds exceeding 10 J/cm², support self-Raman operation through rare earth doping, and meet the following optical quality criteria:
 
 Objective Threshold Notes
 Refractive Index Homogeneity: Threshold = <10 ppm; Objective = <5 ppm 
 
 Transmitted Wavefront Distortion (at 50mm aperture): Threshold = Lamda/6; Objective = <Lambda/8 
 
 Surface Quality (Scratch-Dig): Threshold = 20-10; Objective = 10-5 (NOTE: The first number relates to the maximum allowable width of a scratch in micrometers, while the second number relates to the maximum allowable diameter of a dig or pit in hundredths of a millimeter.)
 
 Dislocation Density: Threshold = <10 cm^(-2); Objective = < 1 cm^(-2)
 
 Inclusion/Bulk Defect Density: Threshold = <5 inclusions greater than 1µm per cm^3; Objective = No detectable inclusions greater than 0.5µm per cm^3 
 
 Materials of interest include:
 Undoped and doped (Nd, Yb, Er, Tm) potassium gadolinium tungstate (KGW) and Potassium yttrium tungstate (KYW) [Refs 1,2,3]
 Undoped and doped (Nd, Yb, Er, Tm) Barium molybdate and Barium nitrate [Refs 4,5] 
 Other Raman active tungstate, molybdate, nitrate, vanadate or related compelling Raman crystal systems
 
 Alternative material systems are encouraged provided performers demonstrate a credible pathway toward large aperture crystal production and significant Raman gain performance.
 Develop a technical approach and concepts for manufacturing large and high-quality Raman active crystals. Develop and model a growth process and identify methods for optical characterization of grown crystals. Determine the technical feasibility of scaling the process to high throughput and provide a cost analysis. Produce a document containing the technical approach, concepts for manufacturing, growth model details and results, proposed optical characterization process, and approach to scale up the proposed manufacturing concept. Provide a Phase II development plan with performance goals and key technical milestones and that addresses technical risk reduction.
objective: Develop scalable domestic manufacturing technologies and processes for large Raman active optical crystals that will enable wavelength agile laser systems for Navy applications.

title: Persistent, Geochemically-Driven Low-Temperature Power Systems for Subsea Intelligence, Surveillance, and Reconnaissance
text:
Develop a modular, self-sustaining, non-toxic subsea energy-harvesting capability that exploits naturally occurring sediment-seawater geochemical gradients to provide persistent, logistics-free power for distributed Intelligence, Surveillance, and Reconnaissance (ISR) sensor nodes in Arctic marine environments, with reliable operation at -2°C, and providing at least 250mW average net harvested power and storing sufficient energy in an onboard storage subsystem to operate up to a 5W (objective) sensor payload for 10 minutes every 4 hours over a projected 24+ month deployment.
 The Department of the Navy's expanding operational requirements in the Arctic domain demand persistent subsea situational awareness. Current seabed ISR nodes and Unmanned Underwater Vehicle (UUV) docking stations rely on conventional lithium-chemistry batteries. These legacy power sources present severe logistical and operational limitations: they suffer from rapid capacity degradation in extreme cold, possess highly toxic/hazardous chemistries, and require frequent, resource-intensive physical replacement (battery swapping) in highly contested or ice-covered environments.
 
 To achieve persistent, logistics-free ISR, the Navy has a critical need for an environmentally benign, deploy-and-forget power architecture. This STTR topic seeks the development of Seafloor Electrochemical Power Harvesters to generate continuous electrical current by exploiting the natural oxidation-reduction (redox) potential difference between the anoxic marine sediment (mud) and the oxygenated overlying seawater. The proposed approach must demonstrate a credible path to 5W power and 24-month endurance in sub-zero Arctic conditions through a ruggedized seabed electrochemical power-harvesting architecture that maximizes long-term energy extraction while using only indigenous sediment microbial communities and naturally occurring geochemical gradients. Proposed solutions may use abiotic or biologically mediated mechanisms via electrode design, power management, and optimum emplacement.
 
 Biocatalytic Prioritization & Environmental Strictures:
 While purely abiotic electrochemical approaches will be considered, approaches that leverage biologically-mediated processes (e.g., utilizing natural biocatalysis to enhance electron transfer at the anode) will be prioritized due to their potential for higher power density and self-renewing longevity.
 
 However, to prevent any risk of ecological disruption to fragile Arctic ecosystems, solutions must strictly rely on harnessing the naturally occurring, indigenous populations already present in the local sediment. The introduction, deployment, or seeding of any exogenous, synthetic, lab-grown, or non-native biological agents (microbes/bacteria) is strictly prohibited.
 
 By utilizing advanced electrode materials that naturally synergize with the local subsea environment, the system must reduce or avoid reliance on deployable primary batteries for the supported payload while ensuring operational viability in extreme cold and high-pressure conditions.
 Formulate the theoretical electrochemical model for sub-zero geochemical harvesting. Identify and test advanced catalytic electrode materials that maximize electron transfer efficiency at -2°C, prioritizing architectures that optimize interaction with indigenous sediment microbial communities and/or indigenous electroactive microorganisms.
 
 Conduct a benchtop prototype demonstrating the targeted voltage and current density in a simulated cold-water/sediment environment utilizing only native sediment samples, accompanied by a scalable power management design.
objective: Develop a modular, self-sustaining, non-toxic subsea energy-harvesting capability that exploits naturally occurring sediment-seawater geochemical gradients to provide persistent, logistics-free power for distributed Intelligence, Surveillance, and Reconnaissance (ISR) sensor nodes in Arctic marine environments, with reliable operation at -2°C, and providing at least 250mW average net harvested power and storing sufficient energy in an onboard storage subsystem to operate up to a 5W (objective) sensor payload for 10 minutes every 4 hours over a projected 24+ month deployment.

title: Computational Frameworks for the Development and Qualification of Additive Manufacturing-Tailored Wire Feedstock for Naval Directed Energy Deposition
text:
Develop an integrated computational and experimental framework that engineers, qualifies, and specifies advanced metal wire feedstock specifically tailored for wire-fed Directed Energy Deposition (DED). By leveraging Integrated Computational Materials Engineering (ICME) and Super Intelligence / Machine Learning (SI/ML), this capability will enable high-confidence, point-of-need manufacturing of structural naval components by resolving the fundamental feedstock-process mismatch that currently limits DED mechanical performance.
 As the Department of the Navy prepares for contested logistics environments, the ability to manufacture large, mission-critical replacement parts at the point of need has become a strategic imperative. Wire-fed DED is uniquely suited to this role: it operates safely with reactive metal alloys, achieves high deposition rates for large structural volumes, and is robust enough for shipboard and expeditionary deployment. Despite this operational advantage, a persistent and quantifiable performance gap prevents wire DED parts from meeting Navy structural qualification standards without extensive post-processing.
  
 The root cause of this gap is a thermal physics and geometric mismatch. Additive manufacturing (AM) processes span approximately five orders of magnitude in solidification cooling rate, which is the master variable governing grain size, phase selection, and precipitate morphology.
  
 Current wire feedstock is manufactured to welding wire specifications, engineered for arc welding thermal histories rather than the specific precision and cooling rates of robotic DED. The consequences are well-documented:
 Microstructural Deficits: Precipitation-strengthened aluminum alloys exhibit a 40-70% yield strength reduction in DED compared to laser powder bed fusion, driven by insufficient cooling rates to nucleate strengthening dispersoids. Titanium alloys (e.g., Ti-6Al-4V) develop continuous grain boundary alpha films that degrade ductility and fatigue life. Residual Stress Instability: Residual stresses retained from the wire drawing process cause wire tip instability (cast/helix) in the DED melt zone, producing porosity and build failures. Geometric and Surface Topography: Macroscopic inconsistencies in wire diameter dictate volumetric feed-rate errors, causing fluctuating energy-to-mass ratios in the melt pool. Simultaneously, surface roughness (poor smoothness) induces micro-stuttering in the robotic feed conduit and scatters laser impingement, severely destabilizing thermal absorption.  
 No existing ICME framework addresses these deficiencies upstream of the melt pool—every published AM modelling chain begins at deposition, leaving the wire manufacturing sub-chain entirely unmodelled.
  
 The Navy seeks a comprehensive end-to-end computational framework that closes this gap through alloy-process co-optimization. Proposers should develop a model chain that links the entire wire feedstock lifecycle—from primary alloy synthesis and thermomechanical processing through final drawing and surface conditioning—directly to AM deposition dynamics and deposit properties. This model must account for the coupled effects of advanced state variables (e.g., dislocation density, oxide thickness).
  
 The framework should incorporate Super Intelligence/Machine Learning (SI/ML) surrogate models that consume upstream feedstock history to predict how a specific wire lot will respond to DED thermal conditions and should employ SI-guided experimental design to identify the minimum number of physical tests required to achieve robust statistical qualification. The ultimate deliverable is a computational materials passport: a traceable digital record linking a wire lot's manufacturing history to its predicted and validated AM performance, supporting the Navy's Digital Engineering Strategy and enabling condition-based qualification for fleet sustainment.
 Demonstrate the scientific and technical feasibility of the proposed ICME and SI/ML framework for one primary naval alloy system.
 Develop initial multi-scale computational models linking upstream wire manufacturing variables to critical feedstock properties (including strict diametric tolerances, surface topography, and thermomechanical state) and AM deposit behavior, with the specific goal of predicting and mitigating a known and documented performance deficit in the selected alloy. (Note: Models shall be validated against existing data or targeted experiments.)
 Deliver a comprehensive Phase II plan with a clear go/no-go criterion against a defined predictive accuracy target for the novel material/alloy being investigated.
objective: Develop an integrated computational and experimental framework that engineers, qualifies, and specifies advanced metal wire feedstock specifically tailored for wire-fed Directed Energy Deposition (DED). By leveraging Integrated Computational Materials Engineering (ICME) and Super Intelligence / Machine Learning (SI/ML), this capability will enable high-confidence, point-of-need manufacturing of structural naval components by resolving the fundamental feedstock-process mismatch that currently limits DED mechanical performance.

title: Conformal Printed Antennas for Missile and Weapon Composite Airframes
text:
Develop and demonstrate conformal printed antennas for Navy missile, weapon, or aircraft composite airframes, addressing the coupled electromagnetic, structural, and environmental design problem inherent to printing radiating elements on small-diameter, high-curvature carbon-fiber substrates with integrated environmental protection. In particular, the Department is developing a number of low-cost counter-UAS effectors in the 40 mm, 70 mm, and 5" diameters. In order to keep costs down, one approach is to provide in-flight guidance updates until the seeker can detect the threat UAS. To reduce mass, we are seeking technology for printed or conformal antennas and circuitry.
 Rockets, missiles, aircraft, and tactical weapons are extremely weight constrained. Antennas for Global Positioning Systems (GPS) (including anti-jam), command and control, telemetry, datalink, and seeker functions must coexist with structural, thermal, environmental constraints on curved airframes. Conventional fabrication produces these antennas as discrete elements mounted on brackets inside separate radomes, connected to receivers via coaxial cables and connectors. This architecture imposes parasitic mass, parasitic volume, signal loss through cables and connectors, and long-term reliability degradation as connectors corrode and radomes delaminate over shipboard storage life.
 
 Conformal printed antennas integrated directly onto composite airframe surfaces offer substantial advantages: reduced mass, reduced volume, eliminated cable and connector losses, and structural integration with the airframe itself. The technical challenge: printing radiating elements onto curved carbon-fiber substrates couples electromagnetic design with structural design, environmental protection, and the complex electrical interaction between printed conductors and the underlying conducting carbon-fiber substrate.
 
 Multi-material printed electronics, particularly aerosol-jet and inkjet direct-write processes, have matured to where conductors, dielectrics, and substrates can be co-deposited into conformal structures with controlled electromagnetic properties. The unaddressed capability is the integrated design of printed antennas on airframe substrates, with environmental protection co-designed for operational survival.
 
 The antennas shall be designed using direct-write printed electronics methods (aerosol-jet, inkjet, or comparable approaches) capable of multi-material co-deposition on curved composite substrates. Coating or environmental protection schemes shall be integrated into the design from the outset, with explicit treatment of electromagnetic transparency, loss, and detuning effects.
 Define a concept for the target antenna application, including the conventional baseline being displaced and quantitative performance, cost, and lead-time targets. In conjunction with the Navy participants. identify a representative composite substrate and configuration with justification of diameter and curvature (preference for the 70 mm to 130 mm diameter range).Identify a coating or environmental protection scheme appropriate to the target application, with justification against the operational environment. Conduct joint research on the coupled electromagnetic-structural-environmental design problem, including initial design methodology, characterization of electromagnetic transparency and detuning effects of candidate coatings, and characterization of printed conductor performance on carbon-fiber composite substrates. Deliver a final report that includes technology base documentation, coating selection rationale and characterization, and baseline comparison; and a Phase II plan.
objective: Develop and demonstrate conformal printed antennas for Navy missile, weapon, or aircraft composite airframes, addressing the coupled electromagnetic, structural, and environmental design problem inherent to printing radiating elements on small-diameter, high-curvature carbon-fiber substrates with integrated environmental protection. In particular, the Department is developing a number of low-cost counter-UAS effectors in the 40 mm, 70 mm, and 5" diameters. In order to keep costs down, one approach is to provide in-flight guidance updates until the seeker can detect the threat UAS. To reduce mass, we are seeking technology for printed or conformal antennas and circuitry.

title: Photonic-Crystal Surface Emitting Lasers (PCSELS) in the Near-Infrared (NIR)
text:
Develop and demonstrate scalable photonic-crystal surface-emitting laser (PCSEL) architectures that achieve higher output power while maintaining stable, single-mode, diffraction-limited beam quality using innovative photonic-crystal and optical metasurface designs in multi-aperture or integrated photonic configurations.
 The Navy seeks innovations in PCSELs that combine novel in-plane photonic crystal designs with out-of-plane epitaxial and gain structures to overcome the limitations of current approaches and produce the next generation of semiconductor laser technologies. Current PCSEL architectures face power-scaling limitations as device aperture increases because the mode margin between the desired fundamental mode and competing higher-order modes decreases, making stable, single-mode, diffraction operations increasingly difficult at higher powers. Capabilities that enable single mode, high power density, combinable lasers in the one-micron regime are the focus for any near-term transition. Concepts that maximize laser device area above previous limits, either by increasing the number of photons generated per unit area or increasing conversion efficiency, are potential options. Other potential approaches include reducing optical, electrical, and other losses - either with single devices, or through multi-device combinations. For example, stacking multiple gain regions vertically and horizontally, a successful technique used in vertical-cavity surface-emitting lasers ( VCSELs) arrays, may limit current PCSEL designs because of interactions between n++/p++ tunnel junctions in gain layers introducing unwanted absorption. Means to correct this issue through material modification might offer counteracting but beneficial additional total gain from a single device - especially when combined in the far field. Similarly, adding optical features as part of the photonic crystal to extend single-mode operation, especially those with higher conductivity material might reduce thermal distortions and lead to better performance even at the potential limits of vertical heat conduction. Further, adaptive metasurfacing of an existing PCSEL device (through micro- or nano-etching) might create new surface structures that modify laser output to enable more efficient photon conversion through the development of improved cavity properties. 
 
 The potential to demonstrate military utility by showing power scalability greater than single digit watts from an individual PSCEL, while maintaining single mode operation that result in combinable Solid State Lasers (SSLs) sources (through spectral beam combining or coherent beam combining) or other resonant gain media structures - where the result is a single mode - where emissions has already been demonstrated from fiber lasers, but can potentially be replaced by a single PCSEL integrated optical device - opens up the possibility of high energy laser (HEL) single stage output. The Navy desires higher power, higher efficiency laser and optics to increase engagement ranges, even in adverse marine atmospheric conditions. 
 
 The Navy seeks an approach with a scalable demonstration device in the evaluation of new combinable PCSEL devices that support Electro-magnetic (EM) Spectrum warfare dominance with an objective of gaining military advantages through increased laser power and efficiency - achieving freedom of action across missions in support of maritime, surface warfare.
 
 Work produced in Phase II may become classified. Note: The prospective contractor(s) must be U.S. owned and operated with no foreign influence as defined by 32 U.S.C. § 2004.20 et seq., National Industrial Security Program Executive Agent and Operating Manual, unless acceptable mitigating procedures can and have been implemented and approved by the Defense Counterintelligence and Security Agency (DCSA) formerly Defense Security Service (DSS). The selected contractor and/or subcontractor must be able to acquire and maintain a secret level facility and Personnel Security Clearances. This will allow contractor personnel to perform on advanced phases of this project as set forth by DCSA and ONR in order to gain access to classified information pertaining to the national defense of the United States and its allies; this will be an inherent requirement. The selected company will be required to safeguard classified material during the advanced phases of this contract IAW the National Industrial Security Program Operating Manual (NISPOM), which can be found at Title 32, Part 2004.20 of the Code of Federal Regulations.
 Develop, demonstrate, and deliver a small scale, efficient, coupled multi-aperture prototype PCSELs based high energy laser operating at 1.050-1.070 microns, suitable for testing and evaluation in a laboratory with output power measured in watts with a vertical and horizontal beam quality as close to the diffraction limit (M-squared=1.0, in horizontal and vertical dimensions) as possible. The device should include any required power and cooling to support a laser time of no less than 30 seconds. Provide multiple configurations and cross sections for initial laboratory testing. 
 
 Demonstrate the scalability in volume and combinability of individual PCSELs to increase power to achieve higher output power with higher beam quality based on the use of techniques such as nano-meter scale meta-surfacing modifications to die integrated electronic dies - showing improvements compared to standard manufacturing techniques. 
 
 Deliver one prototype to the Naval Research Laboratory to evaluate the performance of the system in terms of power specifications, wavelength, beam quality, and EO efficiency for a prototype laser system that can meet performance goals.
objective: Develop and demonstrate scalable photonic-crystal surface-emitting laser (PCSEL) architectures that achieve higher output power while maintaining stable, single-mode, diffraction-limited beam quality using innovative photonic-crystal and optical metasurface designs in multi-aperture or integrated photonic configurations.

title: Hyperdimensional Neurosymbolic Cyber Course-of-Action Planning and Replanning under Deception
text:
Develop and demonstrate prototype technologies that enable human planners and distributed cyber reasoning elements to generate, compare, explain, and rapidly replan cyber courses of action (COAs) under obfuscation, partial observability, degraded communications, and changing mission constraints using hyperdimensional and neurosymbolic representations that support compact memory, compositional reasoning, analogical retrieval, and low-overhead knowledge sharing. 
 Future cyber operations will be conducted in contested environments in which observations are incomplete, timing is compressed, adversaries actively manipulate defender beliefs, and the state of the mission cannot be fully observed from any single node or operator position. In such settings, success depends not only on detecting malicious behavior, but on understanding what actions remain feasible, what dependencies govern those actions, which alternatives best satisfy mission objectives, and how plans should be revised as assumptions fail or new opportunities emerge.
  
 Current cyber tools do not adequately support this planning problem. Many existing capabilities focus on alerting, anomaly scoring, static attack-path enumeration, or post hoc analytics. These functions are valuable, but they do not provide operators with an integrated capability to construct, compare, and revise cyber COAs as the environment changes. Rule-based playbooks can be brittle under novelty and obfuscation. Optimization and reinforcement-learning approaches may generate recommendations but often provide limited interpretability and can be difficult to adapt when observations are sparse, manipulated, or only partially relevant. Large-model assistants may accelerate interaction, but by themselves do not provide a persistent, auditable, machine-interpretable planning state suitable for operational use.
  
 This topic seeks a new class of cyber planning technologies built around hyperdimensional, vector-symbolic, neurosymbolic, or closely related compositional reasoning methods. Of particular interest are approaches that maintain explicit internal representations of cyber objectives, prerequisites, access dependencies, branching opportunities, constraints, anticipated adversary reactions, and uncertainty in forms that are robust, updateable, and inspectable by both machines and operators. Hyperdimensional and related high-dimensional symbolic representations are of interest when they enable compact encoding of structured cyber context; efficient binding of entities, roles, temporal order, and dependencies; similarity-based retrieval across partially matching situations; graceful degradation under incomplete or deceptive observations; and deployment in resource-constrained or communications-constrained environments where retraining-heavy or centralized approaches are poor fits.
  
 This topic seeks prototype capabilities that support cyber COA planning and replanning as structured decision processes rather than static checklists. Desired systems should represent plans through inspectable mission graphs, task webs, tiled workspaces, or comparable compositional artifacts in which each element captures sub-objectives, preconditions, dependencies, candidate actions, supporting evidence, uncertainty, timing, cost, reversibility, and mission relevance. The system should generate multiple feasible COAs for a stated objective, compare alternatives using explicit decision criteria, identify key assumptions and information gaps, and recommend revisions when new evidence changes branch viability or reveals newly feasible options.
  
 A responsive solution should not treat hyperdimensional or neurosymbolic reasoning as novelty for its own sake. Instead, the proposer should clearly show how the chosen representation materially improves cyber planning performance in one or more of the following ways:
 compact encoding of evolving cyber context and plan structure without exhaustive recomputation; compositional updates as new observations, constraints, or objectives arrive; retrieval of relevant prior plan fragments or analogous situations under partial mismatch; maintenance of competing plan branches or hypotheses under obfuscation and ambiguity; lightweight exchange of decision-relevant symbolic or semantic representation among distributed agents or operator cells; interpretable rationale linking recommended actions to plan structure, assumptions, and uncertainty.  
 Representative operational settings of interest may include distributed mission networks, cyber support to software-reliant tactical platforms, planning for AI-enabled mission systems whose data or control pathways may be degraded or manipulated, or collaborative cyber planning cells operating with intermittent connectivity and incomplete common operating pictures. In these settings, no single operator or software agent may possess the entire relevant state. Accordingly, solutions should support selective sharing of compact, decision-relevant abstractions rather than requiring full-state synchronization, centralized fusion, or cloud-dependent reasoning.
  
 The topic is especially interested in technologies that support one or more of the following planning functions:
 representation of cyber objectives, constraints, prerequisites, opportunities, and dependencies in machine-reasonable structured form; generation of multiple feasible COAs rather than a single opaque recommendation; comparison and ranking of alternative COAs using explicit criteria such as mission value, exposure, time-to-effect, reversibility, resource burden, and uncertainty; rapid replanning when observations are incomplete, delayed, deceptive, or contradictory, or when mission priorities change; distributed coordination through compact semantic or symbolic representation appropriate for degraded communications; operator-facing explanation that identifies why a plan is recommended, what assumptions drive it, what alternatives remain availab
objective: Develop and demonstrate prototype technologies that enable human planners and distributed cyber reasoning elements to generate, compare, explain, and rapidly replan cyber courses of action (COAs) under obfuscation, partial observability, degraded communications, and changing mission constraints using hyperdimensional and neurosymbolic representations that support compact memory, compositional reasoning, analogical retrieval, and low-overhead knowledge sharing.

title: Autonomous Metacognitive Collection Orchestration for Multi-Domain Intelligence
text:
Develop and demonstrate an autonomous, metacognitive artificial-intelligence capability that orchestrates multi-modal intelligence collection across asynchronous sensing streams and produces traceable, causally-informed recommendations for multi-domain operations. The capability shall decide what evidence to collect, when, and why; weigh expected information gain against hard operational constraints including emissions, bandwidth, power, time-to-decision, and access posture; generate Pareto-optimal option-sets accompanied by "why / why-not" traces reproducible from internal system state; and locally refine its internal representation under denial, deception, or distribution shift without offline retraining. Operator interaction is confined to pre-mission intent specification and after-action audit of the decision record, enabling a human-machine formation in which the capability operates at machine speed inside a commander-specified envelope and the human sets intent, constraints, and rules of engagement at mission entry and reviews the auditable decision record at mission exit.
 Modern intelligence, surveillance, and reconnaissance (ISR) enterprises ingest multi-source indicator streams whose native tempos span four or more orders of magnitude. Overhead imagery (EO/IR, SAR, MSI, HSI) arrives at revisit cadences of minutes to hours; RF and SIGINT detections resolve in seconds to minutes; maritime AIS and acoustic returns update continuously at sub-second tempos; and open-source, supply-chain, and pattern-of-life indicators mature over hours to weeks. A single decision of operational consequence, such as whether a vessel of interest is a combatant or a civilian fisher, or whether an observed buildup presages a near-term operation or reflects routine activity, typically turns on whether causally related evidence drawn from several of these phenomenologies can be assembled, reasoned about, and surfaced fast enough and cheaply enough to matter. 
 
 Classical early- and late-fusion pipelines assume temporally aligned inputs and emit single snapshot outputs, useful when cadences match and brittle when they differ by orders of magnitude or when a depended-on sensor is denied. Reinforcement- and active-learning policies can select next observations but treat operational constraints as reward-shaped scalars the optimizer can trade away, and require retraining cycles measured in weeks when priority intelligence requirements or adversary tactics shift in hours. Neuro-symbolic and causal methods contribute structure and interpretability, yet in practice operate over hand-authored graphs and synchronous data, with post-hoc explanations rather than forward-looking traces. Agentic large-language-model orchestrators produce narrative rationalizations whose internal state cannot be audited, and whose plans cannot be inspected for constraint feasibility before execution. What is missing across all of these approaches is a structured, auditable, constraint-feasible substrate whose rationale for each recommendation is transparent, reproducible, and directly inspectable from internal state.
 
 This topic seeks novel approaches to artificial metacognition: an orchestration substrate that reasons about its own reasoning while reasoning about the world. A metacognitive substrate maintains a structured model of evidence-to-outcome relationships across heterogeneous modalities and tempos; tracks its own uncertainty, prediction error, and representational coherence; computes expected information gain for candidate collection actions under hard operational constraints; returns option-sets rather than single collapsed policies; and, when denial, deception, or distribution shift is detected, locally refines its internal model rather than triggering a full retraining cycle. The resulting capability is the computational backbone of a human-machine formation: the autonomous system acts at machine speed inside a bounded operating envelope, while the human commander sets objectives, constraints, and rules of engagement before the mission and reviews the auditable decision record after.
 
 Candidate substrate families for the metacognitive layer include hyperdimensional computing and vector-symbolic architectures; neuro-symbolic architectures that couple learned encoders with symbolic or probabilistic inference; and graph-based reasoning over typed knowledge graphs, causal graphs, and structured inference engines. Hybrids across these approaches are encouraged. This topic is deliberately substrate-agnostic within that class. Offerors are expected to justify their choice on quantitative grounds. Any viable substrate shall provide:
  Compositional, inspectable operators (algebraic, logical, graph-based, or probabilistic) that support real-time assembly and decomposition of multi-source evidence structures, rather than end-to-end learned embeddings whose compositional semantics cannot be examined.  Bounded degradation under partial, corrupted, delayed, or adversarially manipulated input, quantified against a mainstream deep-learning baseline.  Transparent, reproducible reasoning operations that yield auditable explanations directly from internal system state, rather than post-hoc narrative produced by a prompted language model.  Efficient operation under sparse and few-shot regimes, with measurable performance at small label budgets on novel scenario classes.  A credible path to tactical-edge deployment on Size-Weight-and-Power-constrained platforms. 
 Recent work across these areas has independently demonstrated subsets of these properties, including graph-structured anomaly reasoning, compositional multi-modal scene understanding, and interpretable edge AI with online adaptation. 
 
 Converging them into a single autonomous metacognitive orchestration substrate is the objective of this topic. Approaches that rely on monolithic end-to-end deep networks without compositional or causal structure, or on narrative-only explanati
