title: Human Universal Remote
text:
The objective of the Human Universal Remote DP2 SBIR topic is to further develop surface electromyography (sEMG) sensors, piezoelectric micromachined ultrasonic transducers (PMUTs), or other non-invasive sensor modalities as a user interface for warfighter multi-system operations1-6. The cited references serve as representative baselines of the state-of-the-art human machine interfaces and do not limit the scope of acceptable technical approaches. 
 
 The vision is for a single warfighter to execute simultaneous, multi-domain tasks without compromising their primary physical posture or situational awareness. For example, controlling a drone while handling a rifle, or sending/receiving audible, out of line-of-sight communications via radio without speaking. The envisioned system may combine micro-scale ultrasonic cellular stimulation, ultrasound and EMG sensor fusion, and deep learning driven gesture recognition. The system must translate and discern between sub-millimeter muscle contractions and intentional, full-range movements to trigger external system commands. In a series of readiness tests, performers will develop the sensor suite and processing framework to serve as a hands-free, eyes-free human-machine interface for multi-system warfighter operations. 
 Surface electromyography (sEMG) is a proven technique for detecting biomedical voltage measurements from the skin generated by the electrical current of muscle fibers during skeletal muscle contraction and relaxation. These signals, which reflect neuromuscular activity, typically range in amplitude from 0 to 10 millivolts and operate at frequencies between 20 and 450 Hz. While historically used to restore hand function for transradial amputees via non-invasive fiber membrane potential measurement, this topic proposes leveraging state-of-the-art sEMG in concert with other non-invasive muscle sensing modalities to significantly enhance the operational capability of the warfighter. For example, ultrasound is a high-resolution non-invasive sensing modality capable of probing deep muscle tissues and providing complementary information to electromyographic signals. This topic is divided into two distinct, parallel Technical Areas (TAs) that must be addressed concurrently. Proposers must deliver an integrated solution spanning both domains:
  
 Technical Area 1 (TA1): Microphone
 Signal capture will focus on the non-invasive detection and extraction of EMG signals and/or electrical, acoustic deep muscle sensing signals from the user. The approach should include the utilization of signals for arm control as both a command and as biological sensors to understand where muscle activity is occurring and to function as an active indicator of warfighter stress. Hardware systems developed under this Technical Area must reliably detect, isolate, and extract these microvolt-to-millivolt level biopotential signals directly from the warfighter's skin without invasive techniques. Proposers should address the following TA1 criteria:

 Single or multimodal sensor arrays that conform to the forearm or targeted muscle groups

 Integrates with standard-issue warfighter apparel without causing skin irritation or impeding range of motion over extended wear

 Sweat Dynamic movement & collision resistance Electromagnetic interference  Dual-use sensing
 Capture intent-driven neuromuscular firing patterns to facilitate hands-free control of external systems while serving as passive biological monitoring of muscle fatigue, physical overexertion, and cognitive stress Calibration
 The system must be designed for recalibration once during initial outfitting of the sensor array onto the warfighter. Calibration techniques should require minimal to no additional cognitive load and take as much time as to be doable during mission briefing.  
  
 Technical Area 2 (TA2): Speaker
 This Technical Area focuses on translating decoded physiological intent into standardized, platform-agnostic output modalities. The system must reliably differentiate between passive muscle strain and active, intentional micro- and macro-gestures to generate high-confidence external commands. The approach should include command output that translates the processed signals into an actionable trigger via standard communications channels designed for easy integration into Team Awareness Kit (TAK). To prevent over-engineering to a singular use case or platform, the generated signaling protocol should be standardizable for use across multiple external systems. At a minimum, the platform should be built with at least one communications channel using radiofrequency (RF). Example platforms include enabling users to task robotic systems, low-level ISR drones, comms drones, trigger communications, and generate visual indicators directly on a TAK display. title: Domestic Fabrication Of High-Purity Precursor Materials For Advanced Radiation Detection Scintillator Crystals
text:
DTRA seeks to establish reliable, scalable, and secure domestic sources and fabrication processes for high-purity precursor materials or pre-reacted mixes required for the growth of advanced inorganic scintillator crystals, such as LaBr₃:Ce, GGAG:Ce (GGAG), Cs₂LiYCl₆:Ce (CLYC), Cs₂LiLaBr₆:Ce (CLLB), and other materials. These materials are essential for high-resolution gamma spectroscopy and dual gamma/neutron pulse-shape discrimination (PSD) detectors used in Radiation Isotope Identification Devices (RIIDs), handheld identifiers, and other Department of War (DoW) radiation detection systems.
 High-purity precursor materials are the foundational input for all high-performance inorganic scintillator crystals used in the DoW radiation detection and nuclear forensics missions. Current supply chains for key halides (e.g., LaCl₃, LaBr₃, YCl₃, LiCl, CsCl, CeCl3 etc.) and rare earth oxides (e.g., Gd2O3, CeO2, etc.) are heavily dependent on foreign sources. Several of the materials used for inorganic scintillator crystal growth are included in the U.S. Geological Survey (USGS) 2025 List of Critical Minerals. This need is further reinforced by Executive Order 14415, "Securing America's Defense Supply Chains and Ensuring Domestic Acquisition of Critical Materials" (July 20, 2026), which directs the DoW to prioritize domestic sources for critical materials, restrict routine waivers for adversarial foreign suppliers effective January 1, 2027, and require supply chain mapping and mitigation plans from contractors and subcontractors.
 Scaling crystal growth of these scintillators and maintaining consistent performance requires precursor materials with stringent control of purity, stoichiometry, moisture, and trace radioactive contaminants. Poor quality precursor materials often introduce variability that degrades crystal quality, light yield, energy resolution, and PSD figure-of-merit.
 Desired materials typically have the following attributes, confirmed by analytical means and demonstrated by crystal growth results:
 High Chemical Purity: At least ≥4N (99.99%) anhydrous metal halides or pre-reacted mixes; sub-ppm levels of contaminants that interfere with the selected scintillator's performance, such as transition metals (e.g., Fe, Cr, Ni, Cu) and alkali contaminants (e.g., K, Rb). Low Moisture / Oxygen Content: < 50 ppm (minimum) for hygroscopic materials. Precise Stoichiometry Control (for pre-reacted elpasolites): Precise control of multi-cation ratios to enable growth of phase-pure crystals with minimal secondary phases or compositional gradients Radioactive Impurity Control: Minimized 40K, 87Rb, 138La, 176Lu, and U/Th series contaminants to levels supporting low-background detector applications  
 This topic specifically targets the development of domestic synthesis, purification and quality-assurance processes capable of producing scintillator-grade precursor materials at laboratory, pilot, and eventually production scales. The goal is to reduce or eliminate reliance on foreign sources while enabling the next generation of compact, high-performance, ruggedized detectors for WMD detection and nuclear security applications.
 The solution must meet the following minimum specifications:
 Analytical Characterization: Comprehensive analytical characterization confirming chemical purity, low moisture/oxygen content (if applicable) and stochiometric control. Appropriate methods should be used for trace-metal purity or trace moisture measurement. Domestic Feedstock Utilization: Primary use of U.S. or allied-nation sourced precursor materials (e.g. carbonates, oxides, chlorides) and any specialized equipment with documented traceability. Validation Method: Rapid feasibility screening of material performance, which may include small-scale crystal growth and measurements such as powder radioluminescence or optical transmittance. Production Scale: Reliable and reproducible laboratory-scale batches (e.g., 50-100 g) in Phase I; pilot-scale (e.g., 1-5 kg) in Phase II with batch-to-batch consistency. Ultimately, the focus is on material quality and potential for process scale up. Open market commercialization: Process development must lead to high-purity precursor materials made commercially available to the broader U.S. industrial base, rather than exclusive licenses, proprietary arrangements, or other restrictions. Objective specifications (desired but not required for basic consideration):
 Advanced Validation Method: Produced batches must be validated through single crystal growth and complete radiation detection performance benchmarking against commercially available crystals, to include absolute light yield (photons/MeV), energy resolution at 662 keV, and PSD where applicable. Production Scale: Demonstration of multi-kilogram batch yields achieving or with a roadmap to achieve cost competitiveness with foreign-sourced material. Radiopurity: Identification of means to mitigate or minimize naturally occurring radioactive isotopes that impact detector background. Extensibility: Tailoring materials to be directly compatible with transparent ceramic scintillator fabrication processes (e.g. desirable particle size distribution and particle morphology). This effort shall develop reliable domestic manufacturing processes for high-purity scintillator precursor materials while meeting the performance parameters above. Proposed work must include validation. The developed processes and materials will also be tested and validated in Phase II by delivery to DTRA or a designated partner for independent evaluation.

These materials are essential for high-resolution gamma spectroscopy and dual gamma/neutron pulse-shape discrimination (PSD) detectors used in Radiation Isotope Identification Devices (RIIDs), handheld identifiers, and other Department of War (DoW) radiation detection systems.

title: Domestic Scalable Growth Of Large-Format Pixelated CZT Crystals For Advanced Radiation Detection
text:
DTRA seeks to establish reliable, scalable, and secure domestic sources and fabrication processes for large-format monolithic cadmium zinc telluride (CZT) single crystals in the 44 × 44 × 15 mm form factor, optimized for pixelated electrode structures that enable high-performance room-temperature 3D position-sensitive gamma-ray imaging and spectroscopy. These crystals are essential for next-generation compact radiation detection systems supporting WMD detection, nuclear forensics, and other radiation detection efforts within the Department of War (DoW).
 Compact, high-resolution, room-temperature gamma imaging and spectroscopy systems are critical for a number of government agency applications (DoW, DTRA, DOE/NNSA, IAEA, DHS), in addition to a number of commercial applications (nuclear power, medical community). CZT-based 3D position-sensitive detectors provide these capabilities without cryogenic cooling, leveraging the small-pixel effect and depth-of-interaction (DOI) sensing via pixelated anodes and timing readout.
 Current advanced systems rely on high-quality pixelated CZT, but most commercial modules use smaller crystals (~20-22 mm lateral dimensions). Furthermore, finished crystals with a thickness of around 5 mm are readily available for medical imaging; however, thicker crystals are often available from manufacturers by long-lead, custom order. Scaling to monolithic 44 × 44 × 15 mm crystals would significantly increase intrinsic efficiency (particularly for higher-energy gamma rays), reduce the number of crystals and interfaces per imager, improve geometrical coverage, simplify module assembly, and lower overall system complexity while maintaining or exceeding energy resolution targets of <1% FWHM at 662 keV.
 High-performance spectrometer-grade CZT at this scale is currently supplied primarily by a limited number of foreign or foreign-owned sources, creating recognized supply-chain vulnerabilities for critical national security radiation detection hardware. Tellurium feedstock is heavily concentrated overseas, and domestic high-end crystal growth capacity remains limited. Zinc and Tellurium are identified in the U.S. Geological Survey (USGS) 2025 List of Critical Minerals. Additionally, Executive Order 14415 "Securing America's Defense Supply Chains and Ensuring Domestic Acquisition of Critical Materials" (July 20, 2026), and related DoW supply chain initiatives, emphasize the need to strengthen domestic reliance on critical materials and components.
 This topic directly addresses that gap by focusing on domestic crystal growth and machining innovation—including process improvements to the Traveling Heater Method (THM), Accelerated Crucible Rotation Technique (ACRT)-enhanced methods, alternative or hybrid growth techniques, in-situ monitoring, and stoichiometry/defect control—capable of delivering the required size, uniformity, and spectroscopic performance at scalable yield and cost. Successful development will strengthen U.S. supply chain resilience while accelerating technology transition to operational systems. A successful development under this topic should result in CZT material freely available on the commercial market rather than for exclusive or limited use by license or other restrictions. Furthermore, it is not the intent of this topic to develop detector systems utilizing CZT.
 The solution must meet the following minimum specifications:
 Crystal Form Factor: Monolithic single-crystal CZT, nominal dimensions up to 44 × 44 × 15 mm (or equivalent large-format), suitable for pixelation with approximately 22 × 22 pixel anode contact matrix at ~2 mm pitch, a single cathode contact, and a guard ring contact around the edge of each. Material Quality: High spatial uniformity of carrier transport properties (electron μτ and adequate hole properties) across the full crystal volume; low defect density (e.g., Tellurium inclusions, grain boundaries, twins, etc.) sufficient to support high-performance spectroscopic operation; and low current leakage. Performance Target: Demonstrated or projected capability to achieve < 1% FWHM energy resolution at 662 keV when configured with pixelated readout and DOI sensing in a representative detector geometry. Domestic Production: U.S.-based growth process with clear, documented path to scalable yield, lot-to-lot reproducibility, and cost reduction; primary use of U.S. or allied-nation sourced raw materials with traceability. Validation: Precursor and crystal lots must be validated through non-destructive characterization (e.g., IR transmission, X-ray topography, μτ mapping) and, where feasible, proxy electrode testing or delivery to a qualified detector fabricator for performance assessment. Cost: Demonstrate that under high volume production cost per crystal volume is competitive with CZT commercially available from other commercial vendors. Objective specifications (desired but not required for basic consideration):
 Larger or thicker monolithic crystals (e.g., approaching 50 × 50 × 20 mm) with maintained uniformity. Demonstrated full pixelated detector performance meeting or exceeding < 0.8% FWHM at 662 keV in 3D configuration. Production-scale batches (multiple crystals per run) with ≥ 70% single-crystal yield meeting all quality metrics. Cost-competitive pathway versus current foreign-sourced material at equivalent performance. Extensibility to related materials or detector architectures (e.g., array tiling, alternative electrode designs). Conceptualizing approach and proof-of-principle fabrication process. In Phase I, offerors shall perform a thorough assessment of current domestic and allied CZT crystal growth capabilities relevant to large-format detector-grade material. This assessment shall include market research on raw material (tellurium, cadmium, zinc) sourcing, identification of viable U.S. and/or allied feedstock pathways, and an analysis of alternative growth methods capable of achieving the target 44 × 44 × 15 mm form fact
objective: DTRA seeks to establish reliable, scalable, and secure domestic sources and fabrication processes for large-format monolithic cadmium zinc telluride (CZT) single crystals in the 44 × 44 × 15 mm form factor, optimized for pixelated electrode structures that enable high-performance room-temperature 3D position-sensitive gamma-ray imaging and spectroscopy. These crystals are essential for next-generation compact radiation detection systems supporting WMD detection, nuclear forensics, and other radiation detection efforts within the Department of War (DoW).

title: Compact High Energy Density Capacitors For Pulsed Field X-Ray Generators
text:
DTRA seeks ultra-compact, high-voltage, high energy density, capacitors and related advanced dielectric materials to support the development of advanced portable X-ray radiographic imaging systems.
 High energy density capacitors and their constituent dielectrics are vital components for multiple DoW capability needs for high voltage power supplies, Marx generators, high-power microwave sources, and other pulsed-power technologies. The Missile Defense Agency, ONR, NASA and other government agencies have funded efforts into high energy density capacitors for a variety of applications.1 However, it is still very challenging to fabricate high energy density capacitors that reliably meet ultra-compact size constraints for miniaturized high voltage pulse power applications and in a ruggedized field-use system.
 Recent prototype development of compact pulsed X-ray generators for portable radiographic imaging applications has underscored the difficulty of scaling capacitor technologies originally developed for larger directed energy and pulsed power systems down to the ultra-compact sizes needed for man-portable or small unmanned systems. Key challenges include preserving dielectric performance and high-voltage hold-off at reduced dimensions, achieving robust voltage reversal tolerance essential for Marx generator topologies, maintaining long operational lifetimes under pulsed conditions with repetition rates up to 100 Hz, and attaining high manufacturing yields with consistent quality for reliable field deployment. This topic specifically targets the development of reliable fabrication processes and advanced dielectric materials to overcome these miniaturization and ruggedization barriers for X-ray generator pulsed power applications.
 DTRA seeks to develop reliable and efficient fabrication and production processes for compact high energy density capacitors.
 The solution must meet the following minimum specifications:
 Outer Dimensions: No larger than 2 inches x 1 inch x 0.5 inch Voltage Rating: 100kV* Capacitance: ≥ 2nF Voltage Reversal Tolerance: 80%* Operating Environment: Dielectric Liquid or Pressurized Gas (e.g., such as SF6) Operating Temperature: Capable of meeting MIL-STD Ability to survive commercial requirements for shock and vibration (i.e. rough handling) Lifetime: Greater than 100,000 full-charge cycles Duty cycle: Up to 100 Hz Charge/Discharge time: Charging order of 10s of microseconds, discharge order of few nanoseconds *Note: Operating voltage and voltage reversal are the highest priority specifications. DTRA may consider small deviations from the other minimum specifications (e.g. size) if the solution is capable of approaching or meeting the objective voltage and voltage reversal specifications below.
 Objective specifications:
 Voltage Rating: 250kV Capacitance: ≥ 10nF Capacitance Tolerance: ±10% Voltage Reversal Tolerance: 100% Operating Temperature: Capable of meeting MIL-STD Vibration: Capable of meeting MIL-STD Lifetime greater than full-charge 1,000,000 cycles This effort shall develop a reliable manufacturing process for high energy density capacitors while maintaining the performance parameters outlined above. The proposed effort will require that developed capacitors be tested and validated in Phase 2.
 Conceptualizing capacitor design type and proof of principle of manufacturing process. In Phase 1 of this effort, a suitable capacitor type and design will be chosen to meet the above-listed performance parameters. This decision should be informed by extensive modeling, simulation, and market research, and guided by availability of materials needed. Preference is indicated for domestically available materials. Note that while temperature and vibration ruggedization are to meet MIL-STD ranges, formal testing and certification to the MIL-STD specifications is not required during this phase. Following the design decision, material samples will be fabricated and tested to validate performance. Evaluation of success will be weighted towards feasibility of materials to achieve the highest priority specifications: operating voltage and voltage reversal. Additionally, the offerors will define a detailed plan for a scalable prototype manufacturing process to be executed in Phase II, including equipment needs, quality control steps, and risk mitigation. The designed process should demonstrate progress towards production of capacitors that meet the defined performance criteria with particular attention to overcoming the miniaturization and reliability challenges associated with scaling from larger directed energy capacitor designs. The Phase 1 final report should include: details for chosen capacitor design along with relevant modelling, simulation, and market research results, details of the chosen manufacturing process, and test and evaluation results of the proof-of-principle capacitor performance (including but not limited to voltage reversal testing representative of Marx generator operation) and percentage of fabricated material samples that meet specifications via the initial process.
objective: DTRA seeks ultra-compact, high-voltage, high energy density, capacitors and related advanced dielectric materials to support the development of advanced portable X-ray radiographic imaging systems.

title: Low Cost Infrared Seeker
text:
Provide novel infrared (IR) seeker solutions that significantly reduce costs compared to the state-of-the-art onboard interceptor applications. 
 Develop a cost-effective IR interceptor seeker through methods such as novel material development, advanced manufacturing and/or scalability, novel commercial-off-the-shelf (COTS) integration, or other innovations that could reduce costs and maintain acceptable seeker performance. Both full seeker solutions and novel seeker components (focal plane array, readout integrated circuit, cooling system, telescope optics, etc.) are acceptable so long as cost savings are explicitly quantified in the proposal. A "full seeker" solution should include: Cover (if applicable), telescope assembly/ optical system (lenses, mirrors, filters, etc.), the IR sensor (filter, Focal Plane Arrays (FPAs) Readout Integrated Circuit, cooling systems (if applicable, etc.), gimbal system (as applicable), signal processing electronics, and the Final seeker production cost should be less than $150,000 for objective cost or less than $250,000 for threshold. Proposed solutions should be amenable to repeatable high throughput production processes. Proposal should include a plan for demonstration of seeker performance in a ground test facility. Additionally, proposers should identify the threat type(s) (ballistic, hypersonic, cruise missile, etc.) that are relevant to the proposed technology, and any assumptions made concerning the technology or its integration into the missile defense system should be explicitly referenced.

title: Rapidly Deployable Aerial Interdiction Cluster
text:
Demonstrate a rapidly deployable aerial interdiction cluster to be part of the layered missile defense. 
 The Missile Defense Agency seeks novel solutions for a rapidly deployable aerial interdiction cluster for close-in defense against evolving threats to national security assets, including counter-air; counter-drone; electronic warfare; and force protection. The proposed cluster should be capable of transitioning from a standby state to a deployed state and be capable of autonomous, sustained operations. Cluster should contain a number of continuously cycling elements capable of multiple modes of operation (i.e., surveillance, discrimination, electronic warfare, attack). The cluster should contain a high volume of elements that are low size, weight, power, and cost (SWaP-C). The assets should be capable of maneuvering and loitering. Assets should be able to host various sensors and/or effectors capable of interdicting various threats (i.e., hypersonic vehicles, glide vehicles, drones, low-flying aerial objects). Modular cargo bays capable of carrying payloads are desired. System should employ a resilient mesh-node architecture and utilize multiple communication pathways.

title: High Speed Low Size, Weight, and Power (SWaP) Radio Frequency (RF) Communications Systems for Space-to-Space and Space-to-Terrestrial Applications
text:
Provide novel and innovative space communications technologies enabling improved defensive communication capabilities. 
 Specific to this topic, to support the Missile Defense Agency (MDA) mission of developing and deploying a layered Missile Defense System to defend the United States, its deployed forces, and friends from missile attacks in all phases of flight, the MDA seeks improved defensive communication capabilities by increasing bandwidth of new low size, weight, and power, radios and antennas to gigabyte speeds. Small form-factor (.1L) or less volume and low power (<10 W) RF radio utilizing Ku bands or higher (due to National Telecommunication and Information Administration (NTIA) restrictions) capable of transmitting data at speeds of 1.5Gbps or greater in a natural space environment is desired. Technology should also be capable of burst transmission of data through the atmosphere to flight vehicles at speeds of 1 Gbps or greater. Communications system capable of meshed (self-forming, self-healing network, high probability of delivery network) High Assurance Internet Protocol Encryptors (HAIPE) interactions for inclusion into "Zero Trust" platforms and networks. Solutions should consider frequency diversity, antenna diversification, and advanced modulation and coding schemas for security and jamming prevention. At the end of the Phase II, two flight radio payloads would be the deliverables.

title: Modeling UV/VIS/near-IR Observables of Dim Hypersonic Configurations
text:
Develop an innovative model of the ultraviolet (UV), visible (Vis), and near-infrared (near-IR) observables of hypersonic configurations at low- and high-altitudes to facilitate detection of dim, hypersonic vehicles by fast-moving observers. 
 To address dim hypersonic threats in missile defense scenarios, the government desires to enhance current physical modeling tools with the ability to simultaneously predict at-source observable properties in the ultraviolet (UV), visible (VIS), and near-infrared (near-IR) spectral regimes that are founded and built upon Navier-Stokes Computational Fluid Dynamics (CFD) and Direct Simulation Monte Carlo (DSMC) techniques and which accounts for, but is not limited to, vehicle surface heating and ablation, Arrhenius and collisional chemically reacting flows, non-local thermodynamic equilibrium (NLTE) effects, boost and divert jet exhaust interactions with the hypersonic body flowfield, and electro-optical radiative transfer physics-based models. The modeling suite provided by the Joint Army-Navy-NASA Air Force (JANNAF) Exhaust Plume and Signatures Subcommittee (EPSS) [1-4] computes RF and certain IR observables. It is founded on CFD and DSMC flowfield codes, hardbody heating models, and radiative transfer / radar propagation techniques. However, the suite does not model all the underlying chemical and physical mechanisms needed to account for radiative emissions in the identified parts of the electromagnetic spectrum. Phenomenologies that must be enhanced within or added to the suite include, but are not limited to: characterization of thermal protection system response, development of material degradation models, detailed Arrhenius and collisional chemical kinetics models that consistently apply across the continuum and rarefied regimes, and generation of molecular band models for UV, Visible, and near-IR radiative emission. The developed models should be compatible with the JANNAF suite infrastructure. And the resulting assemblage should be able to model realistic hypersonic configurations (such as boost-glide, divert jet, and cruise missiles) under steady, unsteady, and maneuvering flight conditions lasting tens of minutes with high Mach within the atmosphere over a wide range of continuum and rarefied altitudes. The resulting capability is expected to facilitate the acquisition and tracking of dim hypersonic threats in modeling and simulation venues, such as MDA's existing agency framework, and operational scenarios.

title: Mobile Sea-Based Launch Platform
text:

title: Performance Enhancement of Solid Rocket Motors Applied to Existing Systems
text:
Develop and demonstrate enhanced capability/performance of a Solid Rocket Motor (SRM) on an existing missile system without changing system form factor.
 The Missile Defense Agency designs, develops, and delivers advanced missile defense capabilities to protect the United States, its allies, and deployed forces from missile attacks in all phases of flight. Traditional SRM propellant formulations and motor designs are mostly optimized, creating some limitations in regards to capability when form factor is constrained [1]. Methods to enhance and optimize the performance of SRM technology at reasonable cost have been researched for decades, incorporating a variety of potential solution paths such as burn-rate enhancement, particle size modifications, propellant composition optimization, and more [2]. Performance enhancements of SRMs in existing missile systems are desired to provide increased capability to both defensive systems and target systems used to validate defensive capabilities.

title: Low Cost / Rapidly Producible Booster Insulation Methods
text:
This topic will develop affordable, scalable, high production rate insulation technologies for solid rocket motors.
 Solid propellant rockets use insulation to protect motor cases from the high temperature combustion gases and, in the case of composite cases, prevent egress of gases. Heritage methods for insulating motor cases utilize filled polymers with low thermal conductivities which absorb heat as they decompose. The insulation layer is typically applied through time consuming processes on custom mandrels which require significant manual labor. The Government seeks novel insulation material/processing technologies which reduce insulation processing time and/or cost compared to legacy processes for a variety of motor case geometries and sizes. The primary motor case materials of interest for this solicitation are polymer matrix composites, though applicability to metallic cases is also desirable. Proposals developing reusable or low-cost consumable mandrels which can be easily and quickly removed after insulation lay-up and winding are also of interest. The proposed insulation solution must consider stress limitations in the propellant with variations in temperature during storage and operation. The proposed insulation technology should also meet or exceed the insulating ability of the current state of the art with equal or lower inert mass with an increased production rate and/or lower per unit price.

title: Configurable Operator Decision Models for Constructive Test and Evaluation Simulations
text:
Develop and demonstrate a government-configurable software capability that improves the representation, tuning, execution, and validation of human operator decision effects in constructive test and evaluation simulations. The capability shall enable Government analysts to instantiate credible operator behavior models across selectable conditions such as experience level, workload, decision latency, engagement posture, rules of engagement, mission priority, and information availability; execute repeatable scenario ensembles; capture decision traces and outcome metrics; and integrate with Government-owned or Government-approved constructive simulation environments used for missile defense test planning, mission engineering, wargaming, and analysis.
 
 The desired outcome is an analyst-facing prototype that makes operator-dependent effects measurable, repeatable, explainable, and suitable for verification, validation, and accreditation (VV&A) consideration without requiring extensive scenario-specific software development.
 Government problem: Missile defense test and evaluation rely on constructive simulations to examine large numbers of scenarios, explore operational concepts, evaluate system-of-systems interactions, and reduce risk before live flight events. These simulations can represent physical platforms, sensors, weapons, communications, terrain, and threat laydowns, but operator decision effects are often represented by fixed scripts, simplified timing rules, or manually coded behaviors. This can cause analysis results to overstate or understate operational performance because human choices influence detection, classification, engagement, prioritization, communication, and response timing across the kill chain.
 
 Capability gap: The Government lacks a reusable and validated way to generate, configure, execute, and assess operator decision representations across many scenario variations and proficiency levels. Current approaches can require extensive custom programming for each model, scenario, or operator role; may not provide traceable rationale for actions taken during simulation; and may be difficult to compare across test events, analysis teams, or simulation environments. The gap affects the Government's ability to understand sensitivity to operator behavior, evaluate alternate tactics, and support VV&A with documented evidence of intended use, assumptions, limitations, data pedigree, and risk.
 
 Why innovative solutions are likely available: The Government believes innovative small businesses can apply advances from artificial intelligence (AI)-enabled simulation, human behavior representation, synthetic data generation, reinforcement learning, design of experiments, digital engineering, development, security, and operations, and modular simulation integration to address this problem. Related industry capabilities already demonstrate AI-assisted constructive simulation, synthetic data generation, intelligent agents, and integration of commercial simulation toolchains with Government simulation environments. This topic seeks to mature those types of innovations into a Government-purpose capability suitable for missile defense test and evaluation workflows.
 
 Government interest: The Government is not seeking a vendor white paper, a visualization-only training game, or a single hard-coded operator model. The Government is seeking a Direct-to-Phase-II prototype capability that can be adapted to multiple missile defense analysis contexts; that can use Government-provided scenarios, models, data, and subject matter expert (SME) input; that can be evaluated against explicit measures of performance and effectiveness; and that can produce artifacts needed for future transition, reuse, and accreditation.
 
 Desired characteristics:
 Open, modular interfaces for integration with constructive simulations and analysis workflows. Configurable operator roles and behavior profiles that can be reviewed and adjusted by authorized Government analysts or SMEs. Support for scenario ensembles, design of experiments, and repeatable Monte Carlo-style analysis. Decision traceability, data provenance, uncertainty characterization, and explainable outputs suitable for analyst review. 
 Responsible AI, cyber, data-management, and VV&A considerations incorporated from the beginning of Phase II.

title: Multi-Fidelity Transfer Learning for Defense Applications
text:
Use new and evolving Artificial Intelligence (AI) training techniques, algorithms, and protocols to rapidly reduce the resources required to integrate AI into the Missile Defense System (MDS).
 Rapid Artificial Intelligence (AI) integration into the MDS is required for the United States to properly defend itself against its adversaries. The development of robust Artificial Intelligence/Machine Learning (AI/ML) agents for complex missile defense and aerospace applications is often constrained by the computational cost, limited availability, and security restrictions of high-fidelity simulation environments. Transfer learning provides a critical pathway to overcoming these barriers. By initially training agents on low-fidelity models or unclassified representations—where data is abundant and computational demands are reduced—core behaviors, strategies, and decision-making frameworks could be efficiently developed and refined. These pretrained models could then be adapted and optimized in high-fidelity and/or environments at higher classification levels, allowing the agent to leverage its foundational knowledge while rapidly acquiring the nuanced performance required for operational deployment. This staged approach significantly reduces training time, minimizes resource expenditure, and mitigates the risk of overfitting to scarce high-fidelity/classified data. Moreover, it enables iterative development cycles where low-fidelity environments serve as agile testbeds for innovation, and high-fidelity environments refine and validate for mission-readiness. Leveraging transfer learning in this manner not only accelerates capability delivery but also ensures that AI/ML systems achieve the precision, resilience, and adaptability necessary for real-world mission success.

title: Real-World Applications for Prototype ISAC Demonstrations (RAPID) Small Business
text:
Design, develop and demonstrate an innovative 5G/6Gdual-use Integrated Sensing and Communications (ISAC) prototype that provides sensing capabilities without degrading communication performance.
 The Department of War (DoW) seeks to accelerate U.S. leadership in Integrated Sensing and Communications (ISAC), a 5G-Advanced feasibility-study area and a key technology for 3GPP 6G specifications. This project addresses the challenge of adding sensing capabilities to communication networks without degrading the primary communication link across diverse missions and environments, from established bases to remote and contested areas. The goal is to develop innovative, dual-use ISAC prototypes that leverage existing cellular infrastructure including 5G, emerging Open RAN interfaces, and AI-native networking. These solutions should offer a smaller, more cost-effective footprint than separate radar and communication systems. The effort will focus on three pathways: ISAC on fixed infrastructure, ISAC on mobile platforms, and joint AI optimization of radio resources. Success of this project will reduce barriers to market entry, enable new ISAC and AI applications, and strengthen U.S. industrial competitiveness in a field receiving substantial investment from adversaries.
 The following documents are incorporated as part of this topic.
  
 Appendix A - ISAC KPI Framework for RAPID RAPID Statement of Objectives (SOO) This topic solicits Direct-to-Phase-II (D2P2) proposals only; Phase I proposals will not be accepted. Offerors must document that Phase I feasibility has already been established through prior work. Acceptable feasibility evidence includes results from prior research and development performed by the small business; prototype, breadboard, model, simulation, test, demonstration, or experimental results; analytical studies, calculations, trade studies, or modeling and simulation results; data demonstrating performance against relevant technical parameters; prior relevant contract, commercial, internal research, or customer-funded work performed by the small business; and/or peer-reviewed publications, technical reports, patents, or other supporting documentation directly relevant to the SBC's approach. Existing research publications, analytical studies, simulation results, and prototype demonstrations have already established the technical feasibility of dual-use Integrated Sensing and Communications (ISAC) systems leveraging commercial cellular infrastructure, including 5G and emerging 5G-Advanced capabilities. Industry-led standardization efforts, including ongoing ISAC work within 3GPP Release 19 and related 5G-Advanced studies, further validate the viability of the underlying concepts and technologies. As a result, the fundamental scientific and technical feasibility questions that would normally be addressed during a Phase I effort should have already been sufficiently demonstrated. The remaining challenges are focused on system integration, prototype development, performance optimization, and operational evaluation in representative environments.

title: Resilient Tactical Edge Networks
text:
The objective of this Phase II effort is to design, validate, and demonstrate a fully open-source, private 5G network platform for Resilient Tactical Edge Networks—integrating OCUDU, SD-Core, SD-RAN, and OSC components—to provide highly reliable, cost-effective, and scalable wide-area connectivity for autonomous field equipment, precision crop intelligence, and livestock monitoring. This platform will be validated at a representative rural site against specific key performance metrics, establishing a secure, interoperable, and procurement-ready reference architecture that supports both commercial precision agriculture and dual-use DoW mission-support applications.
 The realistic near-to-mid-term serviceable addressable market for private 5G in U.S. agriculture is the subset with real mobility, coverage, reliability, or data-volume pain: row-crop operations running GPS-guided and autonomous equipment, specialty-crop growers using machine vision and agricultural robotics, dairies and feedlots with dense livestock-monitoring deployments, irrigated operations with distributed pump and center-pivot control, and large ranches requiring wide-area coverage for animal and asset tracking. The scale of the opportunity is well documented. USDA Economic Research Service data show about 1.88 million farms in 2024 (roughly 39% of all U.S. land). Only 79% of farms reported internet access of any kind, leaving roughly one in five farms without even basic connectivity. There is also documented evidence that productivity of farms with connectivity is significantly higher than the ones without any connectivity. Furthermore, FCC data show that 39% of rural Americans lack access to minimum fixed broadband speeds, compared with 4% of urban Americans, and coverage on cropland and rangeland specifically is worse still. Public carrier networks will not close this gap on their own; carrier tower economics favor population density, and most agricultural land has almost none.
  
 This segment buys on measurable operational outcomes (machine uptime, yield per acre, input cost per acre, water use, herd health, labor hours saved), not on global platform standardization, and its stated barriers to adoption are consistent and compounding: ROI ambiguity, high capex against tight and cyclical farm margins, no in-house RF/cellular or IT staff, harsh outdoor operating environments, a fragmented device ecosystem spanning tractors, drones, sensors, and wearables, and coverage requirements measured in thousands of acres rather than thousands of square feet. A proprietary private 5G platform from a tier-one vendor addresses almost none of these barriers directly; it is priced and supported for industrial campuses and multi-site enterprise accounts, not a single farm with a handful of mission-critical connectivity problems to solve.
  
 An all-open-source stack removes the structural cost and lock-in that makes proprietary platforms a poor fit for this segment. Because OCUDU's O-CU/O-DU communicate with the rest of the network over open, standardized interfaces (especially the O-RAN 7.2x split to the O-RU), the network can be assembled from whichever RU vendor best fits a given operation's coverage geometry and budget, including high-power CBRS Category B radios and high-gain sector antennas mounted on existing farm infrastructure (grain legs, silos, center-pivot towers, farmstead masts) to maximize covered acres per radio. Together, OCUDU, SD-Core, SD-RAN, and OSC form one integrated, fully open-source 5G stack that a regional systems integrator, agricultural equipment dealer, rural wireless ISP, or electric/telephone cooperative can deploy, support, and price as a right-sized, as-a-service offer for a single operation, instead of selling a broad, vendor-locked platform. That directly answers this market's stated preference for outcome-first, economically flexible offers, and it supports a coexistence posture (private 5G for mobility, coverage, and uplink-intensive problems; existing farmstead Wi-Fi and LPWAN sensors where they already work) rather than a rip-and-replace sale.
  
 The trade-off of an all-open-source stack is that the burden of proving interoperability, stability, and security shifts from a single vendor's warranty to the integrator and the open-source community itself. Agricultural buyers, who by their own account lack in-house cellular and cybersecurity expertise, have little tolerance for integration failures discovered mid-season, when planting, spraying, irrigation, and harvest windows cannot be rescheduled. This is exactly the gap the on-going OCUDU Testing & Validation Plan, and its Radio Access Network (RAN) Testing and Evaluation Center (RTEC)-centered extensions, are designed to close: independently witnessed, multi-vendor testing of device diversity, RU diversity, long-range outdoor RF performance, Core/RIC/SMO integration, and security. The proposal should leverage the current, on-going testing and evaluation activities in RTECs and associated results on this front.
  
 Although this topic is anchored in a specific vertical to ensure a concrete deployment environment, real users, and a defensible commercialization path, proposers should recognize and are required to present the technical work in terms of the generic network performance classes it advances. Improvements made to the OCUDU O-CU/O-DU under this effort (scheduler behavior, mobility management, uplink capacity, stability under sustained load, security features) are expected to generalize across verticals and to benefit the broader community of RAN developers building on OCUDU. The Technical Volume shall include a mapping of each selected use case, and its associated Section 3.0 KPMs, to the performance class or classes it exercises, and shall identify which anticipated OCUDU code or feature enhancements correspond to each class.
  
 For this topic, the dominant performance classes are massive scale and wide-area coverage: maximizing covered

title: Robust and resilient optical modulators for extreme environment applications
text:
The objective of this project is to develop and demonstrate Epsilon-Near-Zero (ENZ)-based optical modulating devices that can be resilient/robust to extreme environments such as high temperatures and strong UV irradiation. 
 This topic solicits new ENZ based optical modulators that can be manufactured by new approaches to improve the techniques explored in the past. If a new material (or approach) is proposed, it would be useful if the proposers discussed why this new material (or approach) is promising. Offerors must address the high temperature stability and durability of ENZ materials in air under either high temperature (up to 800C) and demonstrate ENZ-based modulation device structures, such as metal-insulator-metal or waveguide structure, at MWIR regime. Furthermore, the proposers must address optical light modulation by utilizing electrical or optical tuning, and demonstrate ultrafast switching capability with high-speed, power efficient, and compact optical modulator designs. The successful team will design and demonstrate proof-of-concept devices under high temperatures.
 Phase I seeks complete characterization data of new ENZ material that can be used in extreme environments such as high temperatures and high UV laser irradiation with an ultrafast optical modulation in the MWIR window (3-5 um). Offerors must address the high temperature stability and durability of ENZ materials in air under either high temperature (up to 800C) or intense laser irradiation up to 10 MWcm -2 and demonstrate ENZ-based modulation device structures, such as metal-insulator-metal or waveguide structure, at MWIR regime. If this Phase I is successful, plan to manufacture ENZ-based optical modulators operatable in the near-IR to mid-IR windows in this extreme environment. Documentation may comprise technical reports, peer-reviewed publications, measured data, and design artifacts sufficient to substantiate the scientific, technical, and commercial merit required to enter Phase II.
objective: The objective of this project is to develop and demonstrate Epsilon-Near-Zero (ENZ)-based optical modulating devices that can be resilient/robust to extreme environments such as high temperatures and strong UV irradiation.

title: Wafer-scale low-loss hyperbolic optical material
text:
The overall goal of the R&D effort is to develop wafer-scale, fabrication-ready thin films of a low-loss naturally hyperbolic optical material that operates across the visible to telecommunication wavelength range. Films should be of high optical and crystalline quality, with controlled thickness and orientation, on substrates at least one inch in cross-sectional diameter. 
 Conventional optical systems are limited by diffraction, which sets the smallest features they can pattern, image, or confine to roughly the wavelength of the light used. A class of strongly anisotropic, or "hyperbolic," optical materials can confine and route light far below this limit, enabling a family of compact, low size-weight-and-power photonic components of direct interest to OUSW (R&E). Hyperbolic behavior has historically been realized in artificial metamaterials, which are optically lossy, and difficult to fabricate and scale. Certain naturally occurring crystals exhibit the same behavior with far lower loss, but the available examples operate only in the infrared and have been produced only as small, research-grade crystals by batch methods incompatible with standard microfabrication. There is presently no commercial source of wafer-scale, low-loss hyperbolic material that operates at visible and telecommunication wavelengths in a form compatible with standard semiconductor fabrication, and it is important for the Air Force to establish a domestic supply source for such a material.
 Establish the feasibility of producing the hyperbolic material as wafer-scale, device-grade thin films with the required optical quality and crystalline orientation across the target wavelength range. Characterize and/or predict the optical performance of the films and benchmark it against existing artificial metamaterial approaches. Identify a viable approach for lithographically patterning and integrating the material. 
 As a Small Business Technology Transfer (STTR) effort, the work must be performed in partnership with a research institution; a partner with established expertise in optical measurement of hyperbolic materials is encouraged. Deliverables include a feasibility assessment with supporting analysis and/or preliminary data, quantitative performance projections, and a detailed Phase II plan. Documentation may comprise technical reports, peer-reviewed publications, measured data, and design artifacts sufficient to substantiate the scientific, technical, and commercial merit required to enter Phase II.

title: G-TEAD USAREUR-AF ACE 27-02: Spectrum Enabled Warfare Powered by xTech
text:
The U.S. Army is seeking innovative electromagnetic spectrum operations solutions from eligible small businesses across the U.S. through the Global Tactical Edge Acquisition Directorate (G-TEAD) U.S. Army Europe and Africa (USAREUR-AF) Accelerated Capability Event (ACE) 27-02: Spectrum Enabled Warfare Powered by xTech. This platform offers participants the opportunity to engage with the Department of War (DoW), earn prize money and submit a Direct to Phase II Army Small Business Innovation Research (SBIR) proposal. G-TEAD USAREUR-AF ACE 27-02: Spectrum Enabled Warfare Powered by xTech is a focused open-topic competition designed to identify cutting-edge technology solutions that will drive significant advancements in military capabilities while addressing complex challenges and enhancing national security.
  
 The U.S. Army FUZE Program, in partnership with the USAREUR-AF is executing the Spectrum Enabled Warfare competition as part of the G-TEAD Accelerated Capability Event (ACE) series. This competition addresses Army's need to gain and maintain spectrum superiority by identifying high-potential solutions and accelerating transition through funding and integration into live USAREUR-AF-led exercises. Integrating into a USAREUR-AF-led exercise is critical to: (1) validate capabilities under operationally realistic conditions, (2) inform acquisition and integration decisions, and (3) address near-term gaps to sense, understand, exploit, attack, and protect across a contested electromagnetic environment and connected cyberspace.
  
 The Army recognizes that the DoW must enhance engagements with U.S. small businesses by (1) understanding the spectrum of world-class technologies being developed commercially that may benefit the DoW; (2) integrating the sector of non-traditional innovators into the DoW Science and Technology (S&T) ecosystem; and (3) providing expertise and feedback to accelerate, mature, and transition technologies of interest to the DoW.

title: xTech|Search 10 Competition
text:
xTechSearch is an open-topic competition designed to identify groundbreaking technologies with strong commercial traction that may also provide game-changing capabilities for the Army. This competition will be used to competitively down-select up to 16 finalists who can submit a Phase I Army SBIR proposal for a potential follow-on award of up to $300,000.
 The SBIR|STTR Program has aligned technologies that are experiencing rapid commercial traction with critical Army priorities into four portfolios of priority interest for this competition, each with core technology components identified. While xTech|Search encourages submissions aligned to the following SBIR|STTR portfolios and the associated core technology components, the program also welcomes proposals in any other technology domain with the potential to provide a disruptive advantage to the Army:
  Sensors: Electronic devices used to measure physical parameters, often enabling enhanced automation through the Internet of Things.  Immersive and Wearables: Integration or extension of the real world through digital or simulated reality, such as augmented, virtual, and mixed reality. Wearables focus on smart electronic devices that can be worn by or attached to the user to gather data or provide insight during mission operations.  AI/ML: Technology that incorporates human intelligence into machines (AI) and allows machines to learn from data without explicit programming (ML).  Contested Logistics and Sustainment: Strategic and operational technologies that involve planning and executing the movement and maintenance of forces and materials under adversarial conditions.
